| **Construction / [[tenant improvements]]** | Alter or build out space, often for a new commercial tenant | Moving walls for an office tenant |

> **Exam tip:** Preventive maintenance is the one that best protects long-term value. Tenant improvements are most common in commercial leasing.

### Reports

Managers provide regular statements to the owner: income collected, expenses paid, vacancy, delinquencies, and a cash flow summary. Annual reports and the budget-versus-actual comparison help the owner judge performance.

## Risk management

[[Risk management]] uses four strategies, remembered as **[[ACTR]]**:

| Strategy | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **[[Risk avoidance|Avoid]]** | Remove the activity that creates the risk | Close the swimming pool |
| **[[Risk control|Control]]** | Reduce the chance or size of a loss | Better lighting, sprinklers, handrails |
| **[[Risk transfer|Transfer]]** | Shift the risk to someone else | Buy insurance; require tenant liability insurance |
| **[[Risk retention|Retain]]** | Accept the risk yourself | Large deductible; self-insure small losses |

### Insurance

- **[[Property insurance|Property (fire and hazard)]]:** covers the building and contents.
- **[[Liability insurance|Liability]]:** covers injuries to others on the property.
- **[[Workers' compensation]]:** for employees of the owner or manager.
- **[[Business interruption insurance|Loss of rents / business interruption]]:** replaces income while damage is repaired.
- **[[Multiperil policy|Multiperil / package policy]]:** combines several coverages.
- **[[Coinsurance clause|Coinsurance clauses]]:** the owner must insure to a stated percentage of value (often 80%) to collect full partial-loss claims.

## Trust accounts for tenant funds

Rents and **[[security deposits]]** belong to the owner or tenant, not the manager. They go into a trust account, are never commingled with the manager's own money, and must be fully accounted for. State law sets rules for holding and returning deposits.

## Fair housing and ADA in rentals

All federal fair housing rules apply to leasing: no steering of renters, consistent screening, no discriminatory ads, and reasonable accommodations and modifications for disability. Occupancy limits must be reasonable and applied equally; a policy that effectively excludes children can be familial status discrimination. The ADA applies to the rental office and other areas open to the public.

## Landlord and tenant rights generally

### The landlord's duties

- **[[Quiet enjoyment]]:** the tenant has the right to possess and use the premises without interference from the landlord or anyone claiming superior title. The landlord must give reasonable notice before entering except in emergencies.
- **[[Habitability]]:** most states impose an implied warranty that residential premises are fit to live in (safe structure, heat, water, working plumbing and electrical).

### The tenant's duties

Pay rent on time, avoid damaging the premises, follow lease rules, and return the unit in the same condition, less normal wear and tear.

### Eviction

- **[[Actual eviction]]:** the landlord legally removes the tenant through a court process (often called an unlawful detainer or forcible entry and detainer action) after the tenant breaches the lease. Self-help, such as changing locks or shutting off utilities, is generally illegal.
- **[[Constructive eviction]]:** the landlord's act or failure to act makes the premises unusable (no heat in winter, ongoing severe leak). The tenant may treat the lease as ended, but generally must **move out within a reasonable time** to claim it.

> **Exam tip:** Constructive eviction requires the tenant to actually leave. A tenant who stays and stops paying rent usually can't claim constructive eviction.

Notice periods, security deposit deadlines and warranty of habitability procedures vary by state. Colorado's landlord-tenant specifics are covered in the Colorado module.

lessons.title: Commercial leasing and specialty properties
lessons.body:
## Commercial vs. residential leasing

Residential leases are heavily regulated: landlord-tenant statutes, habitability rules and fair housing law set many of the terms, and most residential tenants pay a flat monthly rent. Commercial leases are treated as deals between business parties who can negotiate almost everything. That means:

- **Longer terms** (often 3, 5, 10 years or more) with renewal options
- **Rent structures that shift expenses to the tenant** (net leases) or tie rent to the tenant's business (percentage leases)
- **Fewer statutory protections** — the written lease controls, so the details matter
- **Space measured and priced by the square foot**, usually quoted as an annual rate (for example, $24 per square foot per year)

> **Exam tip:** If a question says "commercial" and asks who pays taxes, insurance and maintenance, read the lease type. Don't assume the landlord pays.

## Lease types by how rent works

| Lease | Tenant pays | Common use |
|---|---|---|
| [[Gross lease]] | A fixed rent; landlord pays taxes, insurance and maintenance out of it | Residential, small office |
| [[Net lease]] (single net) | Rent plus property taxes | Commercial |
| Double net (NN) | Rent plus taxes and insurance | Commercial |
| [[Triple net lease]] (NNN) | Rent plus taxes, insurance and maintenance/repairs | Single-tenant retail, freestanding buildings |
| [[Percentage lease]] | Base rent plus a percentage of gross sales above a breakpoint | Retail, shopping centers |
| [[Graduated lease]] (step-up) | Rent that rises in scheduled steps | Long office leases, startups |
| [[Index lease]] (escalation) | Rent that adjusts with an index such as the Consumer Price Index | Long-term leases |
| [[Ground lease]] | Rent for land only; tenant builds and owns the improvements during the term | Commercial development |

The exact split in a "single" or "double" net lease varies by market and by lease, so the lease language always controls. What the exam wants you to know: the more "nets," the more of the owner's expenses the tenant pays, and a triple net lease gives the landlord the most predictable income.

A **[[ground lease]]** is usually very long (often 50 to 99 years) so the tenant can finance and recover the cost of the building. At the end of the term the improvements typically revert to the landowner unless the lease says otherwise.

### Percentage leases and the natural breakpoint

A percentage lease charges base (minimum) rent plus a percentage of the tenant's gross sales over a sales level called the [[breakpoint]]. The **[[natural breakpoint]]** is the sales level at which the percentage would equal the base rent:

**Natural breakpoint = annual base rent ÷ percentage rate**

Example: annual base rent is $36,000 ($3,000 a month) and the percentage is 6%.
- Breakpoint = $36,000 ÷ 0.06 = **$600,000**
- The store does $750,000 in sales. Overage = $750,000 − $600,000 = $150,000
- Percentage rent = $150,000 × 6% = $9,000
- Total annual rent = $36,000 + $9,000 = **$45,000**

The parties can also negotiate an **[[artificial breakpoint]]**, a fixed sales figure that is higher or lower than the natural one. If the question gives you a threshold ("6% of sales over $500,000"), use it as given.

### Triple-net pass-through math

In a multi-tenant building, each tenant's share of expenses is usually its **[[pro rata share]]**: the tenant's square footage divided by the building's square footage.

Example: a tenant leases 2,500 sq ft in a 20,000 sq ft building (12.5%) at $20 per sq ft per year base rent. Annual taxes are $48,000, insurance $12,000 and common area costs $40,000 (total $100,000).
- Base rent = 2,500 × $20 = $50,000
- Pass-through = $100,000 × 12.5% = $12,500
- Total annual occupancy cost = **$62,500** ($5,208.33 a month)

> **Exam tip:** Convert monthly to annual (or annual to monthly) before you compare numbers. Most wrong answers on lease math come from mixing the two.

## CAM, tenant improvements and letters of intent

- **[[Common area maintenance]] (CAM)** charges cover the upkeep of shared areas: parking lots, landscaping, lobbies, snow removal, common lighting. Tenants usually pay their pro rata share, often as estimated monthly payments reconciled once a year. Leases may cap annual CAM increases or exclude certain costs (such as major capital replacements).
- **[[Tenant improvements]] (TI)** are changes to the space to fit a tenant's use: walls, finishes, wiring, fixtures. The landlord often offers a **[[TI allowance]]** (a dollar amount per square foot) and the tenant pays any cost above it. Who owns the improvements at the end of the lease is set by the lease; many become the landlord's property.
- A **[[letter of intent]] (LOI)** summarizes proposed key terms (rent, term, TI allowance, options) before the full lease is drafted. It's usually written to be **non-binding** on the main deal, though specific clauses (confidentiality, exclusive negotiation period) may be made binding. Brokers should make sure the LOI says clearly which parts bind and which don't, and suggest legal review.

## Broker cooperation in commercial deals

Commercial transactions often involve a landlord's (listing) broker and a tenant's broker. How they split the fee is set by **[[co-brokerage]] agreements** — the listing agreement and a written agreement between the brokers — not by law or by any trade group. Commercial commissions are often calculated as a percentage of the total rent over the lease term, or as a dollar amount per square foot, and may be paid partly at signing and partly at occupancy. As with all commissions, the rate is negotiable; competing firms must never agree among themselves on rates.

## Business opportunity sales

A **[[business opportunity]]** sale is the sale of an operating business: its name, equipment, inventory, customer lists, leases and [[goodwill]] (the value of its reputation and customer loyalty). Key points:

- The sale is mostly **[[personal property]]**, transferred by a **[[bill of sale]]**, plus an assignment of the lease or a deed if real estate is included.
- The price is often allocated among real estate, equipment, inventory and goodwill, which affects taxes for both sides. Refer the parties to their accountant and attorney.
- A **[[bulk sale]]** is a transfer of a major part of a business's inventory and equipment outside the ordinary course of business. Bulk sale laws were designed to protect the seller's creditors and tax authorities through advance notice. Most states have repealed the old UCC bulk sales article, but some states still require notices (for example, to the state tax department) so the buyer doesn't inherit the seller's unpaid taxes.
- **Licensing caution:** a real estate license may or may not cover selling a business, and selling a business through a stock sale can raise securities issues. Know your state's rules and stay within your competence.

## Oil and gas leases

Land can be split into a **[[surface estate]]** and a **[[mineral rights]]** estate, and each can be sold separately. An owner who sold the surface but kept the minerals still owns the oil and gas below.

In an **[[oil and gas lease]]** the mineral owner is the **[[lessor]]** and the oil company is the **[[lessee]]**. The money terms:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| [[Bonus]] | A one-time payment at signing, usually per mineral acre, kept whether or not anything is produced |
| [[Delay rental]] | A periodic payment that keeps the lease alive during the primary term if drilling hasn't started (many modern leases are "paid-up," prepaying these) |
| [[Royalty]] | The lessor's fractional share of production (such as one-eighth or more), paid free of drilling and production costs |
| [[Primary term]] | The initial period (often a few years) the lessee has to start drilling or production |
| [[Held by production]] | Once production in paying quantities begins, the lease continues past the primary term as long as production continues |

If the primary term ends with no production (and no other clause, such as a shut-in royalty, keeping it alive), the lease generally expires.

## Farm and ranch basics

Rural brokers need to look beyond the house:

- **[[Water rights]]** may be separate from the land and are often worth more than it. Eastern states mostly use **[[riparian rights]]** (owners along a waterway share reasonable use); many western states, including Colorado, use **[[prior appropriation]]** (first to put water to beneficial use has the senior right). Confirm what water rights, well permits and ditch shares actually transfer.
- **[[Mineral rights]]** may have been severed by a prior owner. A title search shows whether the seller owns them.
- A **[[conservation easement]]** is a recorded, usually permanent restriction (often held by a land trust or government agency) that limits development such as subdivision, while the owner keeps ownership and can usually keep farming or ranching. Donating one can bring tax benefits, but it binds future owners and lowers development value.
- **[[Agricultural use]]** often qualifies land for a lower property tax classification, with rules that vary by state. Changing the use can change the tax.
- Check fences, access, grazing or farm leases in place, and outbuildings, and advise buyers to use specialists (water attorneys, surveyors, agronomists).

lessons.title: Technology, MLS/IDX, data security and safety
lessons.body:
## The MLS: a cooperation tool, not a government agency

A [[multiple listing service]] (MLS) is a private organization through which member brokers share information about their listings so other members can help find buyers. Most MLSs are owned by Realtor associations or by groups of brokers. Key points for the exam:

- The MLS is **not a government body** and doesn't license anyone. Membership rules (who can join, fees, required listing input deadlines, data rules) vary from one MLS to another.
- Putting a listing in the MLS is how a listing broker makes the listing available for cooperation. Any offer of compensation to cooperating brokers is a matter of contract between the brokers, and rules on whether and where such offers may appear have changed in recent years, so follow your MLS's current rules.
- Using the MLS doesn't change agency. A broker who finds a buyer through the MLS doesn't automatically represent the seller.
- MLS data belongs to a system with rules about who may see it and how it may be used. Sharing your login or scraping data can break those rules.

> **Exam tip:** MLS rules can't override antitrust law. Brokers in an MLS still can't agree on commission rates or agree to shut out a competitor.

## IDX: showing other brokers' listings on your website

[[IDX]] (Internet Data Exchange) is the MLS feature that lets a participant display other participants' active listings on the participant's own website. Typical MLS rules, modeled on national policy, include:

- **Consent.** Listing brokers are generally presumed to allow IDX display unless they opt out (for all listings or one at a time). A broker who opts out entirely usually loses the right to display others' listings.
- **Seller choice.** A seller can direct the listing broker to keep the listing, or just the address, off the internet. The listing broker must honor that and tell the MLS.
- **Attribution.** The listing firm must be identified in a reasonably prominent place on each listing display, and the MLS is credited as the source.
- **No alterations.** A displaying broker can't change another broker's listing content, and fields the MLS marks confidential (such as remarks meant only for other brokers) aren't shown.

## Fair housing in digital advertising

The [[Fair Housing Act]] bars any advertisement or notice that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on a protected class. HUD's advertising regulation (24 CFR 100.75) adds that choosing media or locations for housing ads in a way that denies particular groups information about available housing is also discriminatory. These rules apply online just as they do in print.

Practical risks:

- **Ad targeting.** Social media and search ad tools let advertisers choose or exclude audiences. Excluding people by sex, family status, religion, national origin or disability, or by age or ZIP code used as a stand-in for familial status or race, can violate the Act even if no discriminatory words appear in the ad. Use broad geographic and interest settings, and use special housing ad categories where a platform offers them.
- **Language.** Describe the property, not the people you want: "three bedrooms near a park," not "perfect for young couples" or "ideal for singles."
- **Search filters and IDX tools.** A website shouldn't let users filter homes by the racial or religious makeup of a neighborhood, and agents shouldn't add commentary that steers ("great schools, if you know what I mean"). Point consumers to objective sources for school and crime data rather than giving your own opinions about neighborhoods.
- **Photos and models.** Using only people of one race or family type across all marketing can signal a preference.

HUD issued detailed guidance on digital ad platforms in April 2024, then withdrew it, along with seven other fair housing guidance documents, effective September 17, 2025 (announced in the Federal Register in April 2026). Withdrawing guidance didn't change the statute or HUD's advertising regulation, so the core rule stands: you can't use where or to whom an ad is shown to keep protected groups from learning about housing.

> **Exam tip:** Intent isn't required for an advertising violation. If the ad, or the way it was targeted, signals a preference based on a protected class, it can violate the Act.

## Electronic signatures: E-SIGN and UETA

Two laws make electronic contracts work:

| | [[E-SIGN Act]] | [[UETA]] |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Federal law (2000) | Uniform state law (1999), adopted by nearly all states, including Colorado |
| Core rule | A signature, contract or record can't be denied legal effect just because it's electronic | Same; an electronic signature satisfies a signature requirement |
| Agreement | No one is required to use electronic records | Applies only when the parties agree to deal electronically (agreement can be shown by conduct) |

**Consumer consent under [[E-SIGN]].** When a law requires that a consumer receive information in writing, an electronic version counts only if the consumer affirmatively consents after being told about the right to get paper copies, the right to withdraw consent, and the hardware and software needed. The consumer must consent electronically in a way that shows they can actually open the records.

**Exceptions.** E-SIGN doesn't cover wills and testamentary trusts, family law matters such as divorce and adoption, court documents, and certain notices, including notices of utility shut-off and notices of default, foreclosure or eviction involving a person's primary residence. Those still need traditional delivery.

Electronic records must also be capable of being kept and accurately reproduced, so keep complete copies in your transaction files.

## Data security and wire fraud

Brokers hold sensitive client information: Social Security numbers, bank statements, loan documents, ID copies. The FTC's guide for businesses boils data protection down to five ideas:

1. **Take stock** — know what personal information you have and where it is.
2. **Scale down** — keep only what you need.
3. **Lock it** — protect what you keep (strong passwords, multi-factor login, encryption, locked files).
4. **Pitch it** — dispose of what you no longer need properly (shred paper, wipe devices).
5. **Plan ahead** — have a plan for responding to a breach.

### Wire fraud

[[Wire fraud]] in real estate is a form of [[business email compromise]]. Criminals break into or imitate the email of an agent, title company or lender, wait until closing, and send "updated" wiring instructions that route the buyer's down payment or the seller's proceeds to their own account. Once the money is gone it's very hard to recover.

What brokers should do:
- Warn clients early and in writing that you and the closing company will **never** change wiring instructions by email.
- Tell clients to **verify wiring instructions by phone using a number they already know** (from the contract, a business card or an independent source), never a number in the email.
- Don't send financial information through ordinary email; use secure portals.
- Use multi-factor authentication on email accounts.

If a wire goes astray, act immediately: the sender should call their bank to request a recall, notify the title or closing company, and file a complaint with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3). Speed matters — funds can sometimes be frozen if reported quickly.

## Agent safety

Real estate work means meeting strangers in empty buildings. Standard safety practices:

- **Meet new prospects at the office first.** Get their full name and contact information and make a copy of their photo ID, and keep it at the office.
- **Share your itinerary.** Tell someone where you're going, who you're meeting and when you'll be back, and set up check-in calls.
- **Use a distress code.** Agree with your office on a code word or phrase that signals you need help.
- **At open houses:** know at least two exits, check every room before you lock up, and don't leave valuables or prescription drugs out (ask sellers to secure them).
- **During showings:** let the prospect walk ahead of you, and park on the street rather than in the driveway so you can't be blocked in.
- **Trust your instincts.** If something feels wrong, leave.

Safety rules must be applied consistently to everyone. Asking only certain prospects for ID, based on how they look or sound, creates a fair housing problem.

lessons.title: The Division and the Real Estate Commission
lessons.body:
## Who regulates Colorado brokers

Colorado real estate brokers answer to two linked bodies:

- The [[Division of Real Estate]] is a state agency inside the Department of Regulatory Agencies. Its director hires the staff (investigators, auditors, attorneys, clerks), enforces the license law, prosecutes violations, and audits brokerage business accounts.
- The [[Colorado Real Estate Commission]] is the policy and decision-making board. It adopts the rules brokers must follow, approves the standard contract forms, and makes the final call on discipline and license denials.

A simple way to remember it: the Division does the day-to-day work; the Commission makes the rules and the final decisions.

## Commission composition

| Item | Rule |
|---|---|
| Members | 5 |
| Appointed by | The governor |
| Broker members | 3, each with at least 5 years of Colorado real estate experience |
| Property management seat | At least 1 of the 3 brokers must have substantial property management experience |
| Public members | 2, representing the public at large |
| Term | 3 years |
| Removal | By the governor for misconduct, neglect of duty, or incompetence |
| Vacancy | Governor appoints someone to finish the unexpired term |

> **Exam tip:** 5 members, 3 brokers + 2 public, 3-year terms, appointed by the governor. The exam likes to swap "governor" for "Senate," "Division director," or "Board of Realtors." Only the governor appoints.

## What the Commission can do

### Make rules
The Commission adopts rules (4 CCR 725-1) that carry the force of law. Violating a Commission rule is itself a ground for discipline.

### Approve forms
Brokers must use a [[Commission-approved form]] when one exists and fits the transaction. The Commission revises forms periodically and sets mandatory-use dates.

### Investigate and audit
The Commission can investigate on its own motion or on a written complaint. It can also send a broker an audit notice. A broker who receives a complaint or audit notice must respond in writing on time with complete answers and the full transaction file. Failing to respond is a separate ground for discipline, even if the original complaint had no merit. The Commission also has subpoena power to compel witnesses and records.

### Hold hearings
Formal disciplinary and license-denial hearings are conducted by an [[Administrative Law Judge]] under the state Administrative Procedure Act. The Commission then decides the case. No license can be denied, suspended, or revoked except by a majority vote of the Commission.

### Discipline licensees
After a hearing, the Commission can:

- Impose an administrative fine of up to **$2,500 per separate offense**
- Issue a public censure
- Place the licensee on [[Probation]] with conditions the Commission sets
- Suspend the license temporarily
- Revoke the license permanently
- Deny a license to an applicant

For minor problems that don't justify formal action but shouldn't be ignored, the Commission can send a [[Letter of Admonition]] by certified mail. The licensee can reject it by asking in writing for a formal hearing within **20 days** of receiving it; the letter is then vacated and the matter proceeds formally.

After a **[[revocation]]**, the Commission won't consider a new license application from that person for **one year**.

The Commission can also act against a brokerage firm itself, suspending or revoking the firm's right to operate, whether or not the firm's responsible broker personally knew about the violation.

### Go to court
The Commission can ask a court for an injunction to stop anyone (licensed or not) from violating the license law.

## Appeals

A Commission decision in a disciplinary case or a license denial is reviewed by the **[[Colorado Court of Appeals]]**, not a district court. The court may stay (pause) the Commission's order, but only after a hearing on whether a stay would endanger the public.

> **Exam tip:** Appeals of Commission orders go straight to the Colorado Court of Appeals.

## Public vs. confidential records

Complaints and investigative files are closed to the public. Stipulations (settlements) and final orders are public records.

## Unlicensed activity

Acting as a real estate broker without a license, or while a license is suspended or revoked, is a **[[class 2 misdemeanor]]**. It applies to individuals and entities alike. The Commission can also seek a court injunction against unlicensed activity, and paying a commission to an unlicensed person is a ground for disciplining the licensee who pays it.

## What happened to the recovery fund?

Many states have a real estate recovery fund that pays consumers who win judgments against licensees. Colorado **repealed its recovery fund in 2005**. Instead, Colorado requires active brokers to carry [[Errors and Omissions Insurance]], which is covered in the next lessons. If an exam question asks how Colorado protects consumers against broker negligence, the answer is mandatory E&O insurance, not a recovery fund.

## Commission position statements

The Commission publishes [[Position Statement]]s (labeled CP-1, CP-2, and so on) in the Colorado Real Estate Manual. They explain how the Commission views common practice issues, such as rebates, office policy manuals, brokers buying property, conflicts of interest, and unlicensed assistants.

Key point: position statements are **guidance, not law**. They describe best practices and how the Commission interprets the statute and rules. Discipline is based on the statute and rules, but ignoring a position statement often means you're close to violating one.

## Broker liability for others

An employing broker is not automatically disciplined for an employee's violation. The Commission can discipline the employing broker if it had **[[actual knowledge]]** of the violation or was **negligent in supervising** the employee.

## Quick review

- Division = staff, enforcement, audits. Commission = rules, forms, decisions.
- 5 members, governor appoints, 3 brokers (5 years' experience, one property management), 2 public, 3-year terms.
- Fines up to $2,500 per offense; letter of admonition can be rejected within 20 days; 1-year wait after revocation.
- Appeals go to the Colorado Court of Appeals.
- Unlicensed brokerage = class 2 misdemeanor.
- No recovery fund since 2005; E&O insurance instead.
- Position statements = guidance, not law.

lessons.title: Getting licensed in Colorado
lessons.body:
## Who needs a license

In Colorado, a person (or firm) is acting as a broker if, **for compensation or the expectation of it**, they do any of the following for another person, even once:

- Sell, buy, exchange, rent, or lease real estate or an interest in it
- Offer to do any of those things, or negotiate them
- List (or agree to list) property for sale, exchange, rent, or lease
- Auction real estate, or offer or agree to auction it
- Deal in real estate options
- Negotiate the sale or lease of a business when real estate or a lease is part of the deal
- Charge a prospective tenant a fee for information about available rentals

A single transaction is enough. "I only did it once" is not a defense.

### Common exemptions

You don't need a license when you are:

- Selling or leasing **your own** property
- A corporation selling its own property through its officers or regular salaried employees (with limits)
- An **attorney** handling a transaction for a client as part of practicing law
- An attorney-in-fact acting **without compensation** under a power of attorney
- A court-authorized fiduciary: receiver, trustee, executor, administrator, conservator, guardian
- A public official performing official duties
- A **salaried [[on-site manager]]** of an apartment building or condominium doing customary duties
- An out-of-state licensed broker receiving a share of a commission or referral fee from a Colorado broker on a cooperative deal (without doing brokerage work in Colorado)

> **Exam tip:** The key trigger is compensation. A friend who helps a neighbor sell for free under a power of attorney is exempt; the same friend taking a "thank-you fee" needs a license.

## License levels

Colorado issues one kind of license, the **[[broker]]** license. There are no salespersons. What changes is the broker's level:

| Level | What it means | Experience to qualify |
|---|---|---|
| [[Associate Broker]] | Works under an employing broker's supervision. Every new licensee starts here. | None beyond pre-licensing |
| [[Independent Broker]] | Runs a one-person brokerage; supervises no other brokers | 2 years of Active licensure |
| [[Employing Broker]] | Runs a firm that employs or engages other brokers; supervises them | 2 years of active practice in the prior 5 years, plus an experience point requirement, plus a 24-hour Brokerage Administration course |

A person licensed as an independent or employing broker can still choose to work as an associate under someone else's firm.

### High level of supervision for new brokers
The license law requires a new broker to practice for at least two years before going independent, and during that time the employing broker must provide a [[High Level of Supervision]]: specific training in office policies, availability for consultation, help preparing contracts, monitoring transactions from contract to closing, reviewing closing documents in advance, and making sure the employing broker or an associate with more than two years of active licensure attends or is available for closings.

## Qualifications for a new license

1. **Age:** at least 18.
2. **Education:** 168 hours of approved pre-licensing courses (48 hours of real estate law and practice, 48 hours of Colorado contracts and regulations, and 72 hours covering trust accounts and record keeping, closings, current legal issues, and practical applications), or a college degree with a real estate major.
3. **Exam:** pass both the national and state portions. A passing score on either portion is valid for **one year**. If you don't file a complete license application within one year of passing, the score expires and you retake the exam.
4. **Background check:** submit **fingerprints to the Colorado Bureau of Investigation** for a state and national criminal history check **before** submitting the application. Applicants must disclose past convictions, pleas (including no contest), deferred judgments, and pending charges, with court documents and a written explanation.
5. **Character:** the Commission looks for honesty, truthfulness, good moral character, and competence.
6. **[[E&O insurance]]:** proof of [[Errors and Omissions Insurance]] is required before you can hold an Active license.

### Active vs. issued Inactive
To be issued **[[Active License|Active]]**, a new broker needs both E&O coverage and an employing broker (or independent status). If proof of E&O or an employing broker isn't provided within **30 days** of the Commission's notice, the license is issued **[[Inactive License|Inactive]]**. You can't do anything requiring a license until the license is actually issued and Active.

> **Exam tip:** Order of operations: education → exam → fingerprints → application within a year of passing → license issued (Active only with E&O and an employing broker).

## Business entities

A brokerage firm can be a sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC, or corporation. The firm must have a qualified, active broker who manages and supervises its licensed activity (the [[Employing Broker]], or an independent broker for a one-person firm). That broker:

- Is personally responsible for earnest money and other trust funds
- Can be held personally liable for the firm's breaches of fiduciary duty
- Must be replaced if they leave. The Division director can issue a **[[temporary license]] for up to 90 days**, with one extension of up to 90 days for good cause, while the firm finds a new employing broker.

Licenses are personal: they can't be transferred, and a broker can't lend their license or name to someone else. An associate broker can't hold themselves out as an employing or independent broker.

## Place of business

Independent and employing brokers who live in Colorado must maintain a Colorado place of business. Associate brokers and inactive brokers are exempt. An employing broker with branch offices must supervise every branch.

## Quick review

- Compensation + a brokerage act = license required; one transaction is enough.
- One license (broker); levels are associate, independent, employing.
- Independent: 2 years active. Employing: 2 years active in last 5, experience points, 24-hour Brokerage Administration.
- 18+, 168 hours, pass exam, fingerprints to CBI before applying, apply within 1 year of passing.
- No E&O or employing broker within 30 days of notice → issued Inactive.

lessons.title: Renewal, CE, license status, and E&O insurance
lessons.body:
## License term and renewal

- A new license expires at midnight on **December 31 of the year it was issued**, no matter when in the year it was issued.
- After that, licenses run on a **three-year calendar cycle**: January 1 of year one through December 31 of year three.
- Renewal opens 45 days before expiration; you pay the fee, certify E&O coverage, and certify continuing education.
- Brokerage firms don't renew separately. The firm's employing (or independent) broker renews.

## Continuing education

| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| Total per 3-year cycle | 24 hours |
| [[Annual Commission Update]] | A new 4-hour course every year; active brokers must take each year's version. Three versions = 12 of the 24 hours |
| Electives | 12 hours of Commission-approved courses |
| Initial (partial-year) license period | No CE required before the first renewal |
| Records | Keep proof of completion at least 4 years |

A missed year's update course **cannot be made up later**. A broker who falls short must use an alternative, such as a 24-hour Broker Reactivation course, passing the state portion of the exam, or completing 72 hours of contracts/regulations and closings coursework. The Reactivation course has limits: an Active broker can't use it in two cycles in a row, and an inactive or expired broker can use it only if the license has been off Active status for no more than 36 months in total.

> **Exam tip:** "24 hours every 3 years, 12 of them from the 4-hour Annual Commission Update, taken every year." That's the most tested CE fact.

## Active and inactive status

An [[Inactive License]] is still a license. The broker renews it and pays fees, but can't do anything that requires a license. Inactive brokers:

- Don't need E&O insurance
- Don't need CE while inactive, but must show CE (or its alternatives) when they reactivate
- Can still be paid by a former employing broker for commissions **earned while Active**

If a license has been inactive for more than three years, reactivation requires passing the state exam or completing 72 hours (48 hours of contracts and regulations plus 24 hours of closings).

Licenses also go inactive **automatically** when:

- E&O coverage lapses or the broker fails to certify coverage
- A broker changes business address or employment without notifying the Commission
- The employing broker's own license is suspended, revoked, or expires (the associates' licenses go inactive until they move to a new employing broker)

## Reinstating an expired license

If you miss the renewal deadline, the license expires and you can't practice. Reinstatement depends on how long it's been:

| Time since expiration | What you pay |
|---|---|
| Within 31 days | Regular renewal fee |
| More than 31 days, up to 1 year | Renewal fee + reinstatement fee of **half** the renewal fee |
| More than 1 year, up to 3 years | Renewal fee + reinstatement fee **equal to** the renewal fee |
| More than 3 years | Treated as a new applicant |

A reinstated license is effective only from the reinstatement date. Any brokerage done while expired is unlicensed activity.

## Notifying the Commission

- **Change of business address or employment:** immediate notice. Without it, the license is automatically inactivated.
- **Leaving a firm:** both the broker and the employing broker must notify the Commission immediately, and the one giving notice must also tell the other party in person or in writing. After leaving, the broker can't do licensed work until the license is transferred to a new employing broker.
- **Transfers:** moving to a new firm requires a transfer to the new employing broker. The former firm can still pay commissions earned while the broker worked there.
- **Convictions and discipline:** written notice within **30 calendar days** of a conviction, guilty or no contest plea (deferred judgments count), a fair housing violation, discipline in another jurisdiction, or a suspension or revocation within the last five years (in Colorado or elsewhere) for fraud, deceit, material misrepresentation, theft, or breach of fiduciary duty.

## Errors and omissions insurance

Colorado requires every **[[Active License|Active]]** broker, and every brokerage firm with more than one broker, to carry [[Errors and Omissions Insurance]] covering all acts that require a license. Exempt: inactive brokers, and attorney-licensees whose malpractice policy covers their real estate work.

### Two ways to get coverage

1. **The Division's [[Group E&O plan|group plan]].** The Division contracts (through competitive bid) with an insurer to offer a group policy open to every licensee. The insurer can't cancel a licensee except for reasons like nonpayment, the license going inactive or revoked, or a denied application.
2. **An [[Independent E&O policy|independent policy]]** bought on the open market, which must meet the Commission's minimums and be certified.

### Minimum terms (individual coverage)

| Term | Minimum |
|---|---|
| Per claim | $100,000 |
| Annual aggregate | $300,000 |
| Defense costs | Paid in addition to limits (not eroding them) |
| Deductible | No more than $1,000 per occurrence |
| Lockbox coverage | At least $25,000 per occurrence |
| [[Extended Reporting Period]] | 365 days available after coverage ends |

A brokerage firm buying its own independent firm-wide policy needs at least **$1,000,000** per claim and aggregate, with a deductible no higher than $10,000.

### Lapses
If coverage lapses, or the broker fails to certify continuing coverage, the license goes **[[Inactive License|Inactive]] immediately**. Doing brokerage while uninsured means acting on an inactive license.

> **Exam tip:** E&O minimums are $100,000 per claim / $300,000 aggregate, deductible no more than $1,000. Inactive brokers are exempt.

## Quick review

- First license expires Dec 31 of the year issued; then 3-year cycles ending Dec 31.
- 24 CE hours per cycle; the 4-hour Annual Commission Update every year.
- Expired: within 31 days = renewal fee; to 1 year = + half; 1–3 years = + full; over 3 years = start over.
- Immediate notice of address/employment changes; 30 days for convictions.
- E&O required for Active brokers; $100k/$300k; lapse = immediate inactive.

lessons.title: Advertising, supervision, and compensation
lessons.body:
## Advertising

Colorado defines advertising broadly: business cards, signs, websites, social media, email signatures, flyers, letterhead, and more, whenever they promote licensed services.

### The firm name rule
- Brokers advertise only under the name shown in the Commission's records.
- Every ad must show the **brokerage firm's name clearly and conspicuously**. (Exception: a broker selling their own property that isn't listed with a firm.)
- Ads can't mislead the public about who the broker or firm is.

### Trade names
A firm may use one [[Trade Name]], filed with the Commission. If the firm uses a franchise or other third party's trade name or trademark, ads must include an independent-ownership statement such as "Each office independently owned and operated."

### Teams
A [[Team]] is two or more brokers in the **same firm** who regularly work together.

- Team names **can't** include words like "realty," "real estate," "Realtors," "company," "corporation," "Inc.," "LLC," or anything implying the team is a separate company.
- Team ads must include the firm's name.
- Team members' names must be provided on request.
- Brokers outside the firm can't use the team's name.

### Internet and social media
- Every viewable page of a broker-controlled website must show the firm name.
- Email, texts, chat, and social media must identify the firm. If space is very limited, the firm name must be no more than one click away.
- **Expired listings must come down within 3 days** of expiration, and a broker must send a written removal request to third-party syndication sites.

### Other advertising rules
- Don't advertise someone else's listing without the listing firm's written permission (the listing firm must be disclosed).
- Advertised price must match what the owner agreed to.
- Designations and awards must be real and verifiable.
- General sales statistics must cite their source and note that the sales weren't necessarily the broker's own.

## Brokerage administration

### Supervision
The [[Employing Broker]] must supervise every associate broker on the firm's license and **all unlicensed staff**: assistants, secretaries, bookkeepers, and on-site managers. The employing broker can delegate some duties in writing to a [[Supervisory Broker]] (a managing broker or team lead), but remains ultimately responsible.

Baseline (reasonable) supervision includes reviewing every executed contract and every transaction file. New associates get the high level of supervision described in the licensing lesson.

### Written policies
Every employing broker must adopt:

- A written policy on which brokerage relationships the firm offers (single agency, transaction-brokerage)
- An [[Office Policy Manual]] that every associate receives and signs, covering how brokers are designated and how confidential information is protected
- A written policy for destroying documents containing personal identifying information

### Competency
A broker who lacks the knowledge for a task must decline it, get the knowledge, get help from a qualified broker or attorney, or co-list with a qualified broker.

## Compensation

### Paid only through your employing broker
An associate broker can accept compensation for brokerage work **only from their employing broker**. A seller who wants to tip a broker directly must pay it through the firm. The firm may pay a broker's wholly owned entity under its compensation agreement. Listings and commissions belong to the **firm**, not the individual broker.

### No payments to unlicensed people
A broker can't pay a commission or anything of value for brokerage work to an unlicensed person. The exception is a [[Referral Fee]] to a broker licensed in another state or country, paid by a Colorado firm only if: that broker actually referred the client, lives and keeps an office in the other jurisdiction, does no brokerage work in Colorado (a Colorado broker does all the advertising, negotiating, and contracting), and the money goes through the Colorado firm.

### Referral fees and RESPA
- Referral fees need a legitimate basis ("reasonable cause"), such as an actual introduction or a referral agreement, and must be legal under RESPA.
- In residential transactions with a federally related mortgage, a broker can't give or accept any fee or [[Things of Value]] for referring settlement services (lenders, title companies, inspectors tied to the loan). This bars kickbacks and inducements from settlement service providers.
- For other transactions, a broker who accepts compensation for referring a provider must disclose it in writing to the person being referred at the time of the referral.
- An [[Affiliated Business Arrangement]] (for example, a firm that co-owns a title company) must be disclosed to the consumer when or before the referral is made, in writing to all parties by contract signing, and reported to the Commission.

### Rebates to consumers
Colorado permits a firm to [[Rebate]] part of its earned commission to its own buyer or seller. That's not paying an unlicensed person. But:

- Put the rebate terms in writing.
- A buyer's rebate must be disclosed to and approved by the buyer's lender and shown on the settlement statement.
- Never pay a rebate outside of closing; undisclosed rebates can amount to loan fraud.

> **Exam tip:** Rebating to your own client is allowed if disclosed; splitting a commission with an unlicensed "bird dog" who found the buyer is not.

### Secret profits
A broker must disclose all compensation to the principal. Taking secret compensation, or using an option to buy a property without disclosing the profit in writing and getting written consent, is a ground for discipline. A broker who charges separately for closing services (other than legal document preparation, which can't be charged for) must itemize those charges and get the written consent of the party being charged.

### Net listings
In a [[Net Listing]], the seller names a net figure and the broker keeps everything above it. Colorado's statute and current Commission rules don't expressly prohibit net listings (many other states do), but the Commission has long discouraged them: there is no Commission-approved net listing form, a court may limit the broker to a usual commission if the arrangement is challenged, and a broker who uses one to take an undisclosed profit can be disciplined for secret compensation.

> **Exam tip:** For Colorado, "net listings are illegal" is too strong; "legal but discouraged, and risky because of secret-profit rules" is the safer answer. On the national exam, remember they are illegal in many states.

### Collecting commissions
In residential deals, a firm can't file a lien or lis pendens or otherwise cloud title to collect a disputed commission without first getting a court judgment. The Commission doesn't decide money disputes between brokers and firms; those go to court or arbitration.

## Quick review

- Firm name on every ad; one filed trade name; team names can't sound like a company.
- Expired listings off the web within 3 days.
- Employing broker supervises associates and unlicensed staff; Office Policy Manual signed by all.
- Associates are paid only by their employing broker; no fees to unlicensed people.
- Rebates allowed with disclosure (and lender approval for buyers); no RESPA kickbacks.

lessons.title: Documents, practice of law, assistants, and discipline
lessons.body:
## Dealing for your own account

When a broker buys, sells, or leases property **for themselves**, they're a principal, but they're still under the Commission's jurisdiction. The broker must disclose in writing, **in the contract or a separate writing at the same time**, that they hold a real estate license. They treat the other party as a customer.

The Commission strongly discourages brokers from buying their own listings. If it happens, the broker should amend or terminate the listing, disclose in writing, and give the seller a right to terminate through closing.

## Conflicts of interest

Brokers and firms have a continuing duty to disclose **in writing** any known [[Conflict of Interest]]. Examples the Commission flags:

- A property manager who owns or has a family or financial tie to a vendor (plumber, maintenance company) used for the owner's property
- An affiliated business arrangement
- A broker who owns 20% or more of an entity selling or leasing its property
- A transaction-broker with a close personal relationship with one party

When in doubt, disclose.

## Handling documents

- Give **copies of every document you prepare** to the parties (or their representatives) **at the time it's prepared**. Failing to provide signed duplicates or closing statements is a ground for discipline.
- Contracts must accurately state the financial terms and itemize things of value paid or received. Changes are made by written amendment.
- Present all offers to the listing broker. If the listing broker can't be reached, go to that broker's employing broker; only if that fails may you present directly to the owner.
- Keep transaction files for **4 years**.
- The broker with a brokerage relationship is responsible for a proper closing and must make sure the client gets a complete, accurate closing statement signed by the broker.

## Listings

- Listing contracts with sellers and landlords must be **in writing before** any brokerage services begin.
- Every listing or other brokerage agreement must have a **[[definite termination date]]**. "Until sold" is not allowed.
- A [[Holdover Clause]] (protection period) can cover only buyers the broker negotiated with during the listing term **and whose names were given to the seller in writing during the term**.
- Listings belong to the firm, not the individual broker. Moving a listing to another firm requires the seller's written consent and the original firm's assignment (or a termination and a new listing).

## Practice of law limits

Real estate brokers aren't lawyers. The rule comes from [[Conway-Bogue]] (1957), in which the Colorado Supreme Court held that filling in standard forms is technically the practice of law, but allowed brokers to do it when:

- The broker is acting as broker in that transaction,
- The broker charges nothing beyond the normal commission, and
- The forms are standard printed forms.

Colorado law now builds on that holding:

- A broker may fill in standard forms when acting as a single agent or transaction-broker.
- If a [[Commission-approved form]] exists and fits, the broker must use it.
- The broker must tell the parties the forms have important legal consequences and they should consult a lawyer before signing.
- A broker can't charge a separate fee for preparing legal documents.
- Brokers can't advise on title exceptions; they must recommend that the client review them and consult an attorney before the deadlines.
- Brokers can't draft custom contract language that goes beyond their competency. That is the [[Unauthorized Practice of Law]].

## Seller financing

Brokers may help market and negotiate a sale that includes seller financing, but:

- Taking a residential loan application or offering or negotiating the terms of a residential mortgage loan (including a seller-carry loan) is [[Mortgage Loan Originator]] work. Colorado's MLO law exempts a real estate broker who represents a seller financing a limited number of residential properties (no more than three in 12 months), but only while acting as a broker; the MLO board's position is that negotiating the financing terms is not brokerage. Without an MLO license, leave the loan terms to the parties, their attorneys, or a licensed MLO.
- For lease-options, lease-purchases, and installment land contracts, there's no Commission-approved form. The Commission strongly urges brokers to involve a Colorado attorney and recommends each party get separate legal advice.
- If a buyer gives a promissory note as earnest money, the seller must be told the note's due date, and if it isn't paid, the broker must promptly notify the seller and deliver the original note.

## Unlicensed assistants

The Commission calls assistants [[Real Estate Administrative Professional]]s (REAPs).

| Unlicensed assistants may | Unlicensed assistants may NOT |
|---|---|
| Do clerical work and fill in forms as directed by a broker | Independently complete standard forms like listing contracts |
| Deliver paperwork and send disclosures | Give opinions or advice about forms or terms |
| Distribute preprinted, objective property information | Negotiate or do anything requiring a license |
| Order title commitments, gather due-diligence documents | Be paid a commission contingent on a closing (risks RESPA and license law problems) |
| Receipt earnest money, deposits, and rents | |
| Provide access, show property, or hold open houses when authorized by the seller or listing broker | |

A licensed assistant whose license is inactive or expired is treated as unlicensed. A licensed assistant must establish a brokerage relationship with the client before doing licensed work, and is paid by the firm.

**Unlicensed [[On-site manager|on-site managers]]** of apartment properties may fill in lease blanks, show units, quote the owner's set rents, arrange maintenance, and collect rents and deposits, but can't negotiate material lease terms. They're paid salary or non-commission income through the firm.

## Sign crossing

[[Sign Crossing]] means going around another firm's exclusive agreement. A broker **may not** negotiate a listing directly with an owner the broker knows has an **unexpired [[exclusive listing]]** with another firm. If the owner contacts the broker first, the broker may discuss a future listing that takes effect after the current one expires or ends. The broker must ask whether a listing exists, get written confirmation that it has expired or been terminated, and if the owner wants out early, tell them to get advice from an attorney.

## Grounds for discipline (highlights)

The statute lists dozens. The exam favors:

- Misrepresentation, false promises, or misleading advertising
- Acting for more than one party without everyone's knowledge
- Failing to account for or remit others' money; commingling or converting trust funds
- Failing to keep records 4 years or produce them on request
- Paying unlicensed persons; taking secret compensation
- Fair housing violations
- Convictions (deferred judgments count) and failing to report them within 30 days
- Failing to supervise; incompetence or "unworthiness"
- Getting a license by fraud; dishonest dealing

## Cooperating with investigations

If you get a complaint or audit notice, respond in writing by the deadline, answer every allegation specifically, include the complete transaction file, and produce records requested. Missing the deadline is grounds for discipline on its own. Reasonable extension requests are granted.

## If your license is suspended, revoked, expired, or inactive

Stop all licensed activity and advertising. An associate broker notifies the employing broker and affected consumers within **7 days**. An independent or employing broker must also account for and disburse trust money within **30 days** and give the Commission a list of affected consumers within 7 days.

## Quick review

- Own-account deals: disclose your license in writing in the contract.
- Copies of documents at the time prepared; files kept 4 years.
- Listings in writing, with a definite end date; holdover only for names given in writing during the term.
- Fill in approved forms, don't draft or charge for legal documents (Conway-Bogue).
- Assistants: clerical yes, negotiating and advising no.
- No sign crossing on an unexpired exclusive listing.
- Respond to complaints on time.

lessons.title: Commission rules in day-to-day practice
lessons.body:
## Why this lesson exists

Earlier lessons covered the rules one at a time. This lesson puts them to work in situations you'll actually face in your first years as a broker, and shows how the Commission expects you to handle them. Keep one idea in mind throughout: **the Commission's reach follows you, not just your listings.** Colorado courts have held that brokers stay subject to the license law and Commission rules even when they act as principals or do things that don't require a license.

## Position statements: guidance, not law

The Commission publishes numbered **[[Position Statement]]s** (often shortened to "CPs") in the Colorado Real Estate Manual. They cover topics such as broker commissions, rebates, conflicts of interest, brokers buying property, assistants, and minimum service requirements.

- Position statements are **not law**. The Commission describes them as non-binding guidance and a set of best practices.
- They explain how the Commission reads the statute and its rules, so they're a good predictor of how a complaint will be judged.
- The binding sources are the statute (C.R.S. Title 12, Article 10) and the Commission's rules.

> **Exam tip:** If a question asks whether a position statement "has the force of law," the answer is no. It's guidance that interprets the law and rules.

## Competency

Colorado requires a broker to have the experience, training, and knowledge needed for the brokerage services they provide, and to keep up with the laws that apply. [[Competency]] is judged task by task: a broker who is competent selling suburban homes may not be competent with a ranch with water rights, a manufactured home, or a property management account.

A broker who lacks competency for a particular task has four acceptable paths:

1. **Decline** the engagement.
2. **Acquire** the knowledge before providing the service.
3. **Get help** from a qualified supervising broker or from legal counsel.
4. **[[Co-listing|Co-list]]** (or otherwise partner) with a broker who is qualified.

What's not acceptable is learning on the client's dime without any of those safeguards. The employing broker must also be competent to supervise the kinds of business the firm does.

## Minimum services can't be waived

Colorado requires every broker providing brokerage services to work either as a single agent or as a transaction-broker, each with duties set by statute. The Commission's position on [[Minimum service requirements]] is that those statutory duties **can't be waived, in writing or otherwise**. A broker can't sell an "entry-only" package that drops required duties. A broker can agree to do *more* than the statute requires, and those extra duties should be written into the agreement.

## Fees and business models

No Colorado law sets commission rates. Compensation is negotiable between the firm and the consumer, and the Commission doesn't regulate fee amounts. Inside the firm, brokers and employing brokers also choose their own business model:

| Model | How the broker's pay works |
|---|---|
| **[[Commission split]]** | Each commission is paid to the firm, which keeps a share and pays the broker the rest (for example, a graduated split that improves as production grows) |
| **[[Desk fee]]** (or flat-fee / 100% model) | The broker pays the firm a fixed monthly fee or per-transaction fee and keeps most or all of each commission |

Either way, the commission is paid **to the firm**, and an employed broker is paid only by their own employing broker. The model doesn't change the employing broker's duty to supervise.

### Independent contractor or employee?

Most Colorado brokers work as [[Independent contractor]]s for tax purposes. Federal tax law treats a broker as a non-employee (a "[[Qualified real estate agent]]") when all three are true:

1. The broker holds a real estate license.
2. Substantially all pay is tied to sales or other output, not hours worked.
3. A written contract says the broker won't be treated as an employee for federal tax purposes.

Tax status and license law are separate questions. An independent contractor is still an associate broker under the license law, and the employing broker must still supervise them.

## Teams

A [[Team]] is two or more brokers **in the same firm** who work together on an ongoing basis. In practice:

- The team name can't use words like "Realty," "Real Estate," "Realtors," "Company," "Corporation," or entity endings like "LLC" or "Inc.," or anything else that suggests the team is its own company.
- Every team ad must clearly and conspicuously show the **firm's** legal or trade name.
- The firm must give the names of team members to a consumer, the Commission, or another broker or firm who asks.
- Brokers outside the firm can't use the team's name.

If a team member wants to buy a team listing, the Commission's guidance calls for the team to get written informed consent from both parties to act as a transaction-broker, then remove the buying broker from the listing contract and wall that broker off from the transaction (a firewall).

## Acting as a principal

When you buy, sell, or lease property for yourself, you're a **[[Principal]]**, but you're still a licensee:

- Disclose **in writing** that you hold a Colorado real estate license. For a purchase or sale, the Commission expects it in the contract itself. For a rental you own and manage, the Division has said a written disclosure in the lease works, as long as it states plainly that you are both an owner of the property and a licensed Colorado real estate broker. Describing yourself only as a licensed "landlord" isn't enough.
- Treat the other party as a customer, and use the Commission-approved brokerage disclosure.
- Buying your own listing is strongly discouraged. If it happens, the Commission expects you to terminate or amend the listing so someone else represents the seller, disclose in writing that you're acting as a principal and had access to confidential information, put your license status in the contract, and give the seller a right to terminate through closing.
- A "guaranteed buy-out" program requires the Commission-approved buy-out addendum where one fits, and the property stays actively marketed.

## Non-brokerage services and other businesses

Many brokers also run side businesses: managing their own rentals, hosting short-term rentals, building, or referring clients to movers, inspectors, or contractors. Two rules follow you there.

**Disclose conflicts.** Brokers have a continuing duty to disclose any [[Conflict of Interest]] in writing. The Commission's examples include a property manager who owns or has a family tie to a vendor used on the owner's property (disclose early, ideally in the management agreement, and let the owner opt out), an [[Affiliated Business Arrangement]], owning 20% or more of an entity whose property you sell or lease, and receiving anything of value for recommending non-settlement providers such as movers or security companies.

**Protect other people's money.** The duty to account for [[Money belonging to others]] applies "whether acting as real estate brokers or otherwise." So security deposits on your own rentals, short-term rental guest deposits, or deposits you take as a builder must go into a [[Trust account]], never your personal or operating account. First check the firm's office policy manual: the firm may require the money to go through its own trust account. If it doesn't, you open your own separate trust or escrow account, keep a journal, do a monthly [[Two-way reconciliation]], and produce the records when the Division asks.

## Signatures, copies, and electronic documents

- Give parties copies of documents you prepare **at the time they're prepared**, and signed copies of listing and sale contracts.
- Colorado's version of the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act says an [[Electronic signature]] satisfies a law requiring a signature, and an electronic record satisfies a law requiring a writing.
- The Commission's definition of a [[Duplicate]] includes photocopies, faxes, and electronic copies that carry a digital or electronic signature. A fully e-signed PDF emailed to the parties is a proper copy.

## When a brokerage relationship ends

A brokerage relationship ends when the work is done, or, if not completed, at the earliest of the agreed expiration date, termination by the parties, or one year after engagement. Some duties **survive** the end, unless the parties agreed in writing to more:

- **Every broker** (single agent or transaction-broker) must still account for any money or property received during the engagement.
- **A [[single agent]]** (seller's or buyer's agent) must also keep confidential the information the client asked to keep confidential, unless the client consents in writing, the law requires disclosure, or the information has become public. A transaction-broker's only surviving duty is the accounting.

Practical follow-through: get any listing advertising down within 3 days of expiration, keep the transaction file for 4 years, and don't start talking to the owner of another firm's unexpired exclusive listing about switching.

## Quick review

- Position statements interpret the rules; they aren't law.
- Lacking competency: decline, learn, get help, or co-list.
- Statutory duties can't be waived; extra duties go in writing.
- Commissions are negotiable; splits and desk fees are business choices.
- Qualified real estate agent: licensed + paid on output + written contract.
- Team names can't sound like a company; team ads show the firm name.
- Principal deals: license status disclosed in writing.
- Other people's money held outside brokerage still goes in a trust account.
- E-signatures count; give copies when documents are prepared.
- After a relationship ends: everyone accounts for money; single agents also keep confidences.

lessons.title: Colorado brokerage relationships and disclosures
lessons.body:
## Why Colorado is different

Most national textbooks teach agency as the default: a licensee who works with a buyer or seller is that person's agent unless something says otherwise. Colorado flips this. Colorado's brokerage relationships law (C.R.S. 12-10-401 and following) gives you three ways to work with a party, bans a fourth, and sets a default you must memorize.

| Relationship | Who the broker works for | Advocate? | Written agreement needed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| [[Seller's agent]] / landlord's agent | Only the seller or landlord | Yes | Yes, before brokerage activity |
| [[Buyer's agent]] / tenant's agent | Only the buyer or tenant | Yes | Yes, before brokerage activity |
| [[Transaction-broker]] | One or both parties, as a facilitator | No | Not to create the relationship (it's presumed), but a written disclosure is required, and any seller or landlord listing must be in writing |
| [[Dual agency]] | Both sides as agents | Not allowed | Prohibited by statute |

## Single agency

A [[single agent]] is a broker engaged by, and representing, only one party. The statute names four single agents: seller's agent, buyer's agent, landlord's agent and tenant's agent. Colorado calls a single agent a [[limited agent]]: the agent's duties are the ones listed in the statute plus any extra duties the parties add in a written contract. Single agency exists only when there is a written agreement with the party being represented, signed before the broker begins brokerage activities for that party.

A single agent may cooperate with other brokers, but may not engage or create [[subagents]]. Old-style "subagency," where every MLS member worked for the seller, is not available in Colorado.

## Transaction-brokerage: the presumed relationship

A transaction-broker helps one or more parties through a transaction (communication, advice, negotiation, contract terms and closing) without being an agent or advocate for anyone.

The key rule: **a Colorado broker is presumed to be a transaction-broker unless a single agency relationship is established by a written agreement.** If a Commission listing or buyer contract leaves the relationship boxes blank, the broker works with the client as a transaction-broker, consistent with the statute.

> **Exam tip:** "No written agency agreement" in a Colorado question almost always points to transaction-broker, not "implied agency" or "no relationship."

## Dual agency is prohibited

Colorado statute says a broker shall not act as a dual agent. Written consent from both sides does not fix it. National-exam answers like "dual agency is legal with informed written consent of both parties" are wrong for the Colorado portion.

## Customers vs. clients

A [[customer]] is a party to a transaction who has not engaged or employed the broker, so there is no brokerage relationship with that person. A party who has engaged the broker, as a single agent or as a transaction-broker, is commonly called the broker's client.

A broker who works for one side may still help the other side's customer with [[ministerial tasks]], once the relationship has been properly disclosed. Examples: showing the property, acting as a scrivener (filling in the form), passing along offers and counteroffers, explaining financing options, and giving information about inspectors, lenders and other services. These tasks do not create an agency or transaction-broker relationship with the customer.

## Required disclosures and their timing

### The written disclosure

Colorado requires brokerage relationships to be disclosed in writing. The Commission rule sets the timing: the written disclosure must be made **before the broker elicits or discusses confidential information** from the consumer (for example, motivation or financial qualifications). The Division describes this as the earliest reasonable opportunity.

What does *not* trigger the requirement: preliminary small talk about price range, location and property style, and answering general factual questions about a property advertised for sale or lease.

The statute adds specifics:

- **[[Transaction-broker]]:** before engaging in brokerage activities, disclose in writing that the broker is not the party's agent and is acting as a transaction-broker.
- **[[Single agent]]:** sign a written agency agreement with the party before engaging in brokerage activities.
- **[[Seller's agent]] working with a buyer:** before engaging in brokerage activities with the buyer, give a written disclosure that the broker is the seller's agent and not the buyer's agent, list the tasks the broker will do for the seller in dealing with the buyer, and state that the buyer is not vicariously liable for the agent's acts.
- **Other parties:** a broker who has a relationship with one party must tell the other parties (or their brokers) about it at the earliest reasonable opportunity.

### Which document makes the disclosure

The disclosure is made on Commission-approved forms:

- When the broker has a signed engagement contract (for example, an exclusive right-to-sell listing or an exclusive right-to-buy contract), that contract states that different brokerage relationships are available and identifies the relationship chosen.
- When the broker works with someone without an engagement contract, the broker uses the matching [[brokerage disclosure]] form: Brokerage Disclosure to Buyer, to Tenant, to Seller (for sale by owner) or to Landlord. These forms include the definitions of the relationships, a box for the relationship (for example, the party is a customer, or the broker is a transaction-broker), and an acknowledgment of receipt.

These disclosures include a signature block so the party can acknowledge receipt. The acknowledgment is **not a contract**. If the party refuses to sign, the broker notes the refusal (and the date) on a copy and keeps that copy, along with the email that delivered the form if it was sent electronically.

> **Exam tip:** Timing is the most tested point. The written disclosure comes **before confidential information is elicited or discussed**. It does not wait for a signed contract, and it is not triggered only by the consumer's questions.

### Definitions of Working Relationships

The Commission-approved [[Definitions of Working Relationships]] form defines seller's agent, buyer's agent, transaction-broker and customer, and states that it is not a contract. Keep two separate rules straight:

1. **The relationship disclosure is always required.** Every broker must disclose the relationship in writing before eliciting or discussing confidential information (see above). The firm's written disclosures must also state that buyer agency, seller agency and transaction-brokerage are available.
2. **The Definitions form is required in one specific situation.** A firm does not have to offer every relationship, but its written office policy must say which ones it offers. If a party asks about a relationship the firm does **not** offer, the broker must give that party the Commission's written definition of it, which is what this form is for. Otherwise the form is a reference for explaining the options.

The Division states that the definitions section of this form is **not, by itself, a brokerage disclosure**. Handing a consumer only this form doesn't satisfy the written disclosure rule.

> **Exam tip:** Firms may choose not to offer single agency. They must still tell consumers that the other relationships exist, must give the Commission's definition if asked about one they don't offer, and must still make the written relationship disclosure before discussing confidential information.

## Working with both sides: change of status

What if the listing broker's own buyer wants to buy the listing? Under Commission rules, one broker (or one team) may **not** be a single agent for one party while being a single agent or transaction-broker for the other. That is dual agency. With proper written disclosure (usually in the listing contract), the broker or team may instead:

1. act as a transaction-broker for both parties;
2. act as a transaction-broker for one party and treat the other as a customer; or
3. act as a single agent for one party and treat the other as a customer.

If the broker moves from single agent for one party to transaction-broker for both, the broker must give the party whose relationship changes the Commission-approved [[Change of Status]] form. It is due when the broker starts assisting both parties as a transaction-broker, and **no later than when that party signs the contract**. The listing and buyer contracts let the client check a box refusing this option ("seller agency only" or "buyer agency only"). If they do, the other party stays a customer. The change applies only to that transaction: when it ends, the broker's relationship with the client automatically goes back to the one designated in the listing contract.

## Designated brokerage and imputed knowledge

In a firm with more than one licensee, the [[employing broker]] designates in writing which broker or brokers will work with a party. The relationship is **only with the [[designated broker]]**. It does not extend to the employing broker, other brokers in the firm, or the firm itself, and the written agreement must say so. A firm made up of a single licensed person has no designated brokerage; the person and the firm are treated as one.

Results of designated brokerage:

- Two different designated brokers in the same firm may be single agents for opposite sides of the same deal. That is **not** dual agency for the employing broker.
- When a designated broker acts as a single agent, that broker's knowledge is **not** imputed to non-designated brokers ([[imputed knowledge]] does not apply) in the firm.
- In transaction-brokerage, information is not imputed between the broker and a party, or among people within the firm.
- Teams: every team member must be a designated broker for the consumer in the same capacity, and all team members must be named in the listing contract.
- The employing broker may substitute or add designated brokers, and must tell the consumer.
- The Commission treats it as a conflict of interest when an employing broker supervises designated brokers on both sides of a deal and a client's confidential information is shared with the employing broker (or when the employing broker represents one side while supervising the designated broker on the other). Brokers have a continuing duty to disclose known conflicts of interest in writing.

## The employing broker's role

The employing broker must:

- adopt a written office policy (the [[office policy manual]]) describing the relationships the firm offers, how brokers are designated, and how confidential information is protected. Each associate broker gets a copy and signs for it;
- supervise associate brokers (with a higher level of supervision for new brokers) and unlicensed staff;
- maintain the firm's trust accounts and transaction records.

The employing broker may supervise a transaction and also be the designated broker in it. Designated brokerage does not reduce the employing broker's duty to supervise or the firm's [[vicarious liability]]. Clients, however, are not vicariously liable for a broker's acts they did not approve, direct or ratify, and the broker must tell them so.

## How long a relationship lasts

A brokerage relationship begins when the party engages the broker and lasts until the engagement is completed. If it is not completed, it ends at the earliest of the agreed expiration date, termination by the parties, or one year after it began. Commission rules separately require every listing or written brokerage agreement to have a definite termination date. After the relationship ends, a single agent must still account for money and property received, and keep confidential any information the party asked to keep confidential (unless the party consents in writing, the law requires disclosure, or the information becomes public). A transaction-broker's remaining duty is to account for money and property.

lessons.title: Broker duties, disclosures and engagement contracts
lessons.body:
## The duty lists you must know

Colorado spells out broker duties in statute, so the exam can ask about them word for word. Learn the three lists side by side.

### Single agent (seller's agent or buyer's agent)

A single agent must:

1. Perform the terms of the written agreement with the client.
2. Exercise reasonable skill and care.
3. Promote the client's interests with the utmost good faith, loyalty and fidelity, including:
   - seeking a price and terms acceptable to the client (a seller's agent need not seek more offers while the property is under contract; a buyer's agent need not look for other properties while the buyer is under contract);
