A landlord who checks credit only for voucher holders
A landlord whose units are all single-family homes
A landlord who owns ten rental units but self-manages
questions.explanation: Landlords with three or fewer rental units are exempt from the source-of-income provisions. A covered landlord may check credit only if it checks every prospective tenant, not just voucher holders.

questions.stem: After a public trustee foreclosure sale of her home, the former owner asks how long she has to redeem. What is accurate under current Colorado law?
choices: She has 75 days after the sale to redeem
She has no right to redeem after the sale
She may redeem until the confirmation deed is recorded
She has 8 business days to file a notice of intent to redeem
questions.explanation: The owner has no post-sale right of redemption in Colorado. Redemption belongs to junior lienors whose liens were recorded before the notice of election and demand, and they file notice within 8 business days.

questions.stem: In a typical Colorado foreclosure of a home loan, who serves as trustee under the deed of trust?
choices: A private trust company chosen by the lender
The county sheriff
The county public trustee
The lender's attorney
questions.explanation: In Colorado, the trustee under a deed of trust is a government official, the county public trustee, who conducts most foreclosures as non-judicial sales. Sheriff's sales occur only in the less common court foreclosures.

questions.stem: A foreclosure consultant agrees to negotiate a forbearance for a homeowner. Under the Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act, when may the consultant collect a fee?
choices: When the homeowner signs the written contract
After fully performing every promised service
After securing the fee with a lien on the home
Once the lender acknowledges receiving the request
questions.explanation: A foreclosure consultant may not collect any fee until every promised service has been fully performed, and may not take a lien or wage assignment to secure the fee.

questions.stem: A licensed broker lists for sale the home of an owner who is behind on the mortgage and facing foreclosure. Is the broker a foreclosure consultant under the CFPA?
choices: Yes, because the owner's loan is delinquent
Yes, unless the broker charges no commission
No, as long as the broker acts within the license
No, but only if the sale is a short sale
questions.explanation: A licensed real estate broker acting within the license, such as by listing the home for sale, is excluded from the definition of a foreclosure consultant.

questions.stem: Which term covers the land, the improvements permanently attached to it, and the legal rights that come with owning it?
choices: Real estate
Land
Real property
Personal property
questions.explanation: Real property is real estate (land plus permanent improvements) together with the bundle of legal rights of ownership. Land is only the earth, subsurface and airspace; real estate adds improvements but not the rights.

questions.stem: A seller agrees to include her freestanding riding mower and patio furniture in the sale of her home. How are these items normally transferred to the buyer?
choices: By a bill of sale
By the deed to the house
By recording a plat
By an appurtenance clause
questions.explanation: Movable items are personal property (chattels), which transfer by a bill of sale. A deed conveys only real property.

questions.stem: A rancher sells his ranch but keeps the right to the oil and gas beneath it. Which right did he keep?
choices: Surface rights
Air rights
Littoral rights
Subsurface rights
questions.explanation: Oil, gas and minerals below the surface are subsurface (mineral) rights, which can be separated from the surface and sold or kept on their own. Air rights cover the space above the land.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an appurtenance that normally transfers automatically when the land is sold?
choices: The seller's freestanding washer and dryer
A recorded easement that benefits the lot
The seller's car parked in the garage
The seller's potted plants on the patio
questions.explanation: Appurtenances are rights and privileges that run with the land, such as an easement benefiting the lot, and pass with the property unless the deed says otherwise. The other items are movable personal property.

questions.stem: A deed describes a parcel as "Lot 12, Block 4, Pine Hills Subdivision, according to the plat recorded with the county." Which description method is this?
choices: Metes and bounds
Lot and block
Rectangular survey
Vertical datum
questions.explanation: Referring to a lot and block on a recorded plat map is the lot and block (recorded plat) method, the most common for urban and suburban homes. Metes and bounds uses courses and distances from a point of beginning.

questions.stem: To describe an upper-floor condominium unit, a surveyor measures elevation from a reference point such as mean sea level. What is that reference point called?
choices: A monument
A base line
A point of beginning
A datum
questions.explanation: Vertical descriptions measure height from a datum, a fixed reference elevation. A monument is a fixed boundary marker, and a point of beginning starts a metes and bounds description.

questions.stem: Which statement about a leasehold estate is correct?
choices: The tenant has possession while the landlord keeps title
The tenant holds title while the landlord keeps possession
It is a freehold estate measured by a person's life
It lasts indefinitely, like a fee simple estate
questions.explanation: A leasehold gives the tenant a right of possession for a term set by the lease; the landlord keeps title. Freehold estates (fee simple, life estate) are ownership interests, and leaseholds are treated as personal property.

questions.stem: Which estate is the most complete form of ownership, with no time limit and no condition that could end it?
choices: Fee simple determinable
Conventional life estate
Fee simple absolute
Estate for years
questions.explanation: Fee simple absolute has no time limit or conditions; it can be sold, willed, or passed to heirs. A determinable fee can end if a condition is broken, and life estates and estates for years end at a set point.

questions.stem: Lena holds a life estate in a farmhouse, and her nephew is the remainderman. Lena plans to tear out and sell the home's hardwood floors. Why can't she?
choices: She holds only a leasehold
Her nephew holds the title now
Doing so would be waste
A life estate can't be leased
questions.explanation: A life tenant may use, rent, sell or mortgage the life estate but must not commit waste, damage that lowers the value for the future owner. Lena does hold a freehold estate, and a life estate can be leased.

questions.stem: Laws in many states that protect part of the value of a family home from certain creditors are called
choices: homestead laws
dower rights
reversion rights
remainder interests
questions.explanation: Homestead laws shield a portion of a family home's value from some creditors. Dower was a historical legal life estate for a surviving spouse, and reversion and remainder are future interests after a life estate.

questions.stem: A corporation takes title to an office building in its own name. How does it hold title?
choices: As tenants in common with its shareholders
In joint tenancy with its shareholders
As a cooperative interest
In severalty
questions.explanation: Severalty means ownership by one person or one legal entity, such as a corporation. The shareholders own stock in the corporation, not the building.

questions.stem: Three tenants in common can't agree whether to sell their rental house, and one owner wants out. What can she ask a court for?
choices: A life estate
A partition
A joint tenancy
A remainder
questions.explanation: Any co-owner can file for partition: the court divides the property or orders it sold and divides the proceeds. She could also sell her own undivided interest without the others' consent.

questions.stem: In a community property state, which asset is generally the separate property of one spouse?
choices: A house bought during the marriage with either spouse's wages
An inheritance one spouse received during the marriage
A car bought during the marriage from joint savings
Savings built from one spouse's salary during the marriage
questions.explanation: Property owned before marriage or received by gift or inheritance is separate property; most property acquired during marriage is community property. Colorado isn't a community property state; it uses equitable distribution at divorce.

questions.stem: What does a condominium owner typically hold?
choices: Shares of stock in the corporation that owns the building
A proprietary lease issued by the building's owners
A right to use a unit for one recurring week each year
Fee title to a unit plus an undivided share of the common areas
questions.explanation: A condo owner holds fee simple title to the unit and an undivided interest, as a tenant in common, in the common elements. Stock plus a proprietary lease describes a cooperative; a recurring week describes a timeshare.

questions.stem: A buyer receives a deed to week 30 of every year in a resort unit. What did the buyer acquire?
choices: A timeshare estate
A timeshare use
A cooperative interest
A life estate pur autre vie
questions.explanation: A timeshare estate conveys a fee interest for a recurring period. A timeshare use is only a contractual or lease-type right to use the property, without real property ownership.

questions.stem: In a trust holding real estate, who holds legal title to the property?
choices: The trustor
The beneficiary
The trustee
The remainderman
questions.explanation: The trustor (settlor) conveys property to the trustee, who holds legal title and manages it for the beneficiary.

questions.stem: Several investors want to fund an apartment project without taking part in management and with losses limited to what they invest. One sponsor will manage and accept unlimited liability. Which form fits?
choices: A general partnership
A joint tenancy
A limited partnership
Ownership in severalty
questions.explanation: A limited partnership has at least one general partner who manages with unlimited liability and limited partners who are passive investors liable only up to their investment. In a general partnership, every partner shares management and unlimited liability.

questions.stem: To avoid corporate income tax on the income it distributes, a real estate investment trust must generally pay out at least what share of its taxable income to owners each year?
questions.explanation: A qualifying REIT must distribute at least 90% of its taxable income. The 75% figure is the share of gross income that must come from real estate sources, and 95% was the older payout rule before 2001.

questions.stem: A developer sells condo units that buyers must place in a mandatory rental pool the developer manages, with each buyer receiving a share of the pooled rents. What is the main concern?
choices: The units become cooperative interests
The buyers hold only a timeshare use
The units become personal property
The offering may be a security
questions.explanation: When buyers give up management control for a passive return, the sale can be a security, which requires securities licensing and registration, not just a real estate license. Buyers still hold fee title to their units.

questions.stem: A recorded utility easement crosses the back of a residential lot. How is it best described?
choices: A specific, voluntary lien on the lot
An encumbrance that limits use of the lot
A general lien on all of the owner's property
A revocable license held by the utility
questions.explanation: An encumbrance is any interest held by someone else that limits use or lowers value. Easements are use encumbrances, not liens, because they don't secure a debt; unlike a license, an easement is an interest in land.

questions.stem: Why do title insurers pay close attention to construction work done on a property shortly before closing?
choices: Recent construction automatically voids any existing title policy
Mechanic's liens may take priority back to when the work began
Building permits are recorded as general liens against the owner
Contractors gain an easement by necessity over the improved lot
questions.explanation: In many states a mechanic's lien's priority dates back to when work began or materials were first delivered, not to when the lien was filed, so an unpaid contractor's lien could outrank later-recorded interests.

questions.stem: A landowner's existing lender agrees to let a new construction loan take first lien position. What does the existing lender sign?
choices: A release of easement
A license agreement
A party wall agreement
A subordination agreement
questions.explanation: A subordination agreement lets an earlier lienholder move behind a later lien, an exception to first in time, first in right. It often happens when a land loan is subordinated to a construction loan.

questions.stem: An owner sells the back half of his land. The back parcel has no road access except across the front parcel he kept, and the deed says nothing about access. What does the buyer most likely receive?
choices: An easement by necessity
A prescriptive easement
A license to cross
An easement in gross
questions.explanation: When a parcel once under common ownership is sold without access to a road, the law creates an easement by necessity. A prescriptive easement requires years of hostile use, and a license is mere revocable permission.

questions.stem: For longer than the state's statutory period, a neighbor has openly driven across a corner of Kim's lot, without her permission, to reach his garage. He never fenced or occupied the corner. What has he most likely acquired?
choices: Title by adverse possession
A license to cross
A prescriptive easement
An easement by necessity
questions.explanation: Open, continuous, hostile use for the statutory period creates a prescriptive easement, a right to use, not ownership. Adverse possession requires exclusive possession, which shared driving across a corner lacks.

questions.stem: A neighbor's new garage extends 2 feet onto Paul's lot. This is an example of a(n)
choices: easement appurtenant
license
encroachment
party wall
questions.explanation: An improvement that extends onto a neighbor's land is an encroachment, usually discovered by a survey. Left alone long enough, it can support an adverse possession or prescriptive easement claim.

questions.stem: Ed adversely possessed a strip of his neighbor's land for 10 years, then sold his house to Fay, who continued the possession. In many states, Fay can count Ed's 10 years toward the statutory period through
choices: tacking
merger
partition
subordination
questions.explanation: Tacking lets successive adverse possessors in privity, such as a seller and buyer, add their periods together. Merger ends an easement when one person owns both parcels.

questions.stem: In a Colorado fee-title adverse possession case where title would vest today, what must the claimant prove?
choices: 10 years of possession and payment of the property taxes each year
18 years of possession with the record owner's written permission
21 years of possession shown by a preponderance of the evidence
18 years of possession and a reasonable, good-faith belief of ownership
questions.explanation: C.R.S. 38-41-101 sets an 18-year period; for title vesting on or after July 1, 2008, the claimant must also show a reasonable, good-faith belief of ownership and prove the elements by clear and convincing evidence. Permission defeats the hostility element.

questions.stem: Local governments get the authority to adopt zoning ordinances from the state through
choices: comprehensive plans
enabling acts
recorded CC&Rs
variances
questions.explanation: States delegate zoning power to cities and counties through enabling acts. The comprehensive plan guides growth, and zoning ordinances carry it out.

questions.stem: A city zones a strip of parks and small offices between a residential neighborhood and a heavy industrial district. This strip is a
choices: spot zone
buffer zone
nonconforming use
setback
questions.explanation: A buffer zone separates incompatible uses, such as homes and heavy industry. Spot zoning benefits a single parcel's owner and conflicts with the comprehensive plan.

questions.stem: Which body typically hears a property owner's request for a variance or an appeal of a zoning decision?
choices: The county clerk and recorder
The homeowners' association
The building inspector
The board of adjustment
questions.explanation: The board of adjustment (zoning board of appeals) hears variance requests and appeals. An HOA enforces private CC&Rs, not public zoning.

questions.stem: After a new home passes its final inspection, which document allows people to legally live in it?
choices: A certificate of occupancy
A building permit
A variance
A recorded plat
questions.explanation: The building department issues a certificate of occupancy after the work passes final inspection. A building permit authorizes construction to begin.

questions.stem: A county requires a developer to pay toward new schools, parks and roads that a new subdivision will need. These charges are
choices: special assessments
ad valorem taxes
impact fees
severance damages
questions.explanation: Impact fees make developers fund public facilities that new growth requires. A special assessment is a lien charged to existing properties that benefit from a specific improvement.

questions.stem: Under the Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act, how long does a buyer of a covered lot generally have to revoke the contract?
choices: Until midnight of the third business day after signing
Until 30 days after receiving the property report
Until midnight of the seventh day after signing
Until the deed to the lot is recorded
questions.explanation: The act requires a property report before signing and generally lets the buyer revoke until midnight of the seventh day after signing. Subdivisions of fewer than 25 lots are exempt.

questions.stem: A buyer acquires an industrial site where a former owner buried hazardous waste years ago. Under the federal Superfund law (CERCLA), the buyer, as current owner,
choices: can be liable for cleanup even though it didn't cause the contamination
is liable only if it personally disposed of hazardous waste on the site
has no liability because the waste was buried before it took title
is liable only for cleanup costs that arise after the date of closing
questions.explanation: CERCLA liability is strict, joint and several, and retroactive: the current owner or operator can be liable regardless of fault. That's why commercial buyers order environmental site assessments.

questions.stem: A subdivision's old recorded restrictions forbid selling homes to people of a certain race. Today these restrictions are
choices: enforceable, because they run with the land
enforceable only by the original developer
enforceable if the HOA votes to keep them
unenforceable
questions.explanation: Deed restrictions that discriminate based on race or another protected class are unenforceable under fair housing law and court decisions, even if they still appear in old recorded documents.

questions.stem: A deed restriction is written as a covenant. If a later owner breaks it, what is the usual remedy?
choices: Automatic return of title to the grantor
A court injunction or money damages
Escheat of the property to the state
An inverse condemnation action
questions.explanation: Breaking a covenant (a promise) is usually remedied by an injunction or damages. A broken condition, by contrast, may let the grantor reclaim title, and courts prefer to read restrictions as covenants.

questions.stem: Neighbors watched for six years as an owner built a fence the CC&Rs prohibit, then sued to force its removal. A court may refuse to enforce the restriction because of
choices: merger
laches
escheat
police power
questions.explanation: Laches is unreasonable delay in enforcing a right. A court may refuse to enforce a restriction when those entitled to enforce it waited too long.

questions.stem: A grandmother deeds a lot to her 10-year-old grandson. Is the deed valid?
choices: No, because a grantee must be of legal age to take title
No, because the grantee must sign the deed to accept it
Only if a court approves the transfer before recording
Yes, because a grantee doesn't need to be legally competent
questions.explanation: The grantor must be competent and must sign, but the grantee only needs to be identifiable; a minor can receive title. The grantee usually doesn't sign the deed.

questions.stem: Which covenant in a general warranty deed promises that the grantor owns the property and has the right to convey it?
choices: Seisin
Quiet enjoyment
Further assurance
Warranty forever
questions.explanation: The covenant of seisin assures ownership and the right to convey. Quiet enjoyment promises no one with better title will disturb possession; further assurance promises to sign papers needed to perfect title.

questions.stem: A seller deeds a lot to Alma, who doesn't record. The seller then sells the same lot to Ben, who knows nothing of Alma's deed and records first. Under a race-notice statute like Colorado's, who holds title?
choices: Alma
Neither, both deeds are void
Ben
Whoever moves onto the lot first
questions.explanation: Under race-notice, a later buyer wins if he took without notice of the earlier deed and recorded first. Ben did both. Colorado's recording statute, C.R.S. 38-35-109, expressly calls itself a race-notice statute.

questions.stem: An abstract of title is best described as
choices: an insurance policy that pays for losses from title defects
a surveyor's drawing of the property's boundary lines
a condensed history of the recorded documents affecting a property
a court judgment that removes a cloud on the title
questions.explanation: An abstract summarizes the recorded documents in the chain of title. It isn't insurance; an attorney reviews it and gives an attorney's opinion of title. A quiet title judgment removes clouds.

questions.stem: Purchase contracts usually require the seller to deliver title free enough from reasonable doubt that a prudent buyer would accept it. This is
choices: marketable title
chain of title
constructive notice
an abstract of title
questions.explanation: Marketable title need not be perfect but shouldn't expose the buyer to likely lawsuits. The chain of title is the sequence of recorded conveyances.

questions.stem: Which statement about a lender's title insurance policy is correct?
choices: It protects the buyer's equity in the property
Its premium is paid monthly with the mortgage payment
It lasts as long as the owner's heirs hold an interest
Its coverage generally shrinks as the loan is paid down
questions.explanation: A lender's policy is usually written for the loan amount, declines as the loan is repaid, and ends at payoff. The owner's policy protects the buyer and lasts as long as the insured or heirs hold an interest; both premiums are one-time.

questions.stem: On a closing statement, dividing this year's property taxes between buyer and seller according to the days each owns the property is called
choices: recording
prorating
acknowledgment
subordination
questions.explanation: Prorations split ongoing expenses and income, such as taxes, rents and HOA dues, between buyer and seller as of the closing date.

questions.stem: A deed of trust contains a power of sale. If the borrower defaults, the lender can generally
choices: foreclose only by suing and getting a court-ordered sale
foreclose through a trustee's sale without a lawsuit
take title automatically by a deed in lieu of foreclosure
keep the property and also collect the full loan balance
questions.explanation: A power of sale allows nonjudicial foreclosure: a trustee sells without a court case. Judicial foreclosure requires a lawsuit. Colorado uses a public trustee for most deed-of-trust foreclosures.

questions.stem: Before the foreclosure sale, a borrower pays the full overdue debt plus costs and stops the sale. Which right did the borrower use?
choices: Statutory redemption
Deficiency judgment
Power of sale
Equity of redemption
questions.explanation: The equity of redemption is the right to pay off the debt and stop foreclosure before the sale. Statutory redemption, where allowed, applies for a set period after the sale.

questions.stem: A foreclosure sale brings $40,000 less than the borrower owed. Where state law allows, what can the lender seek for the shortfall?
choices: A deficiency judgment
A statutory redemption
An equity of redemption
A deed in lieu of foreclosure
questions.explanation: A deficiency judgment is a personal judgment against the borrower for the amount the sale didn't cover, where state law permits it.

questions.stem: Why do lenders often refuse a deed in lieu of foreclosure when the property has junior liens?
choices: A deed in lieu is illegal when junior liens exist
The junior lienholders would receive the title
The lender would take title subject to those liens
The borrower keeps a statutory right to redeem
questions.explanation: In a deed in lieu, the borrower deeds the property to the lender voluntarily, but the lender takes title subject to junior liens. A foreclosure sale would wipe those liens out.

questions.stem: A man's will leaves his ranch to his daughter. What is the daughter called?
choices: A testator
An heir by descent
A devisee
A personal representative
questions.explanation: Real property left by will is a devise, and the recipient is a devisee. The testator is the person who made the will, and descent applies when someone dies without a will.

questions.stem: A widow dies without a will, leaving two adult children. How does her house pass?
choices: By descent under the state's intestate succession law
By devise to the children named in the probate court
By escheat to the state, since no will exists
By adverse possession to whichever child lives there
questions.explanation: Without a will she died intestate, and state intestate succession (descent) laws decide which relatives inherit. Escheat applies only when there is no will and no heirs.

questions.stem: Ana and Ben own a house as joint tenants. Ben's will leaves his share to his brother. When Ben dies, who owns the house?
choices: Ana and Ben's brother as tenants in common
Ana and Ben's brother as joint tenants
Ben's brother alone, after probate
Ana alone, by right of survivorship
questions.explanation: A joint tenant's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenants outside probate and can't be left by will. Ana owns the whole house.

questions.stem: A buyer has a standard-coverage owner's title policy. Later, a neighbor proves a prescriptive easement across the backyard that was never recorded. Is the loss likely covered?
choices: Yes, standard coverage includes all easements
No, unrecorded easements are a standard exception
Yes, prescriptive easements are recorded by law
No, title policies never cover any easements
questions.explanation: Standard coverage excludes matters only an inspection or survey would reveal, including unrecorded easements such as one created by prescription. Extended coverage can remove that exception.

questions.stem: After occupying a parcel openly and adversely for the full statutory period, a claimant wants record title that a buyer would accept as marketable. What should she file?
choices: A partition action
A quiet title action
An inverse condemnation suit
A subordination agreement
questions.explanation: An adverse possessor usually files a quiet title action to get a court judgment establishing her title in the public records, making it marketable. Partition divides property among co-owners.

questions.stem: A home appraised at $410,000 sold two weeks later for $425,000 after a bidding war. The $425,000 figure is best described as the property's
choices: market value
replacement cost
market price
highest and best use
questions.explanation: Market price is what a buyer actually paid. Market value is the appraiser's estimate of the most probable price under typical conditions ($410,000 here); the two can differ when buyers compete or are under pressure.

questions.stem: An appraiser concludes a vacant lot's most valuable use would be a 12-story office building, but zoning allows only three stories. Which highest and best use test does the 12-story building fail?
choices: Physically possible
Legally permissible
Financially feasible
Maximally productive
questions.explanation: Highest and best use must be legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible and maximally productive. A use the zoning doesn't allow fails the legally permissible test, no matter how profitable it would be.

questions.stem: An owner spent $45,000 on an in-ground pool. An appraiser finds the pool adds $15,000 to the home's value. Under the principle of contribution, what is the pool worth?
questions.explanation: Contribution says a component is worth what it adds to value, not what it cost. The pool contributes $15,000; the other $30,000 of its cost is not recovered in value.

questions.stem: A builder in a subdivision of similar two-story traditional homes proposes an ultramodern design that looks nothing like its neighbors. Which principle suggests the unusual design may hurt its value?
choices: Conformity
Anticipation
Contribution
Substitution
questions.explanation: Conformity holds that value is maximized when a property is reasonably similar to its neighbors in style, age and use. A home that departs sharply from the neighborhood tends to lose value.

questions.stem: Which principle of value holds that value is the present worth of expected future benefits, and is the basis of the income approach?
choices: Substitution
Change
Anticipation
Progression
questions.explanation: Anticipation looks forward: a buyer pays today for the benefits (such as income) the property is expected to produce. That is why it drives the income approach. Substitution compares the cost of an equally desirable alternative.

questions.stem: For a single-family home in an active market, an appraiser's three approaches indicate $395,000 (sales comparison), $420,000 (cost) and $380,000 (income). How does the appraiser reach a final opinion of value?
choices: Averages the three to get about $398,333
Reconciles them, weighting sales comparison most
Uses the $420,000 cost figure because it is the highest
Uses the income figure because it is the most conservative
questions.explanation: Reconciliation weights the approach best suited to the property type; it is not a simple average. For a single-family home with many recent sales, sales comparison gets the most weight.

questions.stem: A 2,400 sq ft building would cost $175 per sq ft to replace. Accrued depreciation is $84,000 and the land is worth $110,000. What is the value indicated by the cost approach?
questions.explanation: Cost new: 2,400 × $175 = $420,000. Less depreciation: $420,000 − $84,000 = $336,000. Add land: $336,000 + $110,000 = $446,000. Forgetting the land gives $336,000; skipping depreciation gives $530,000.

questions.stem: An appraiser valuing a 1920s home estimates the cost to build a structure with the same usefulness using modern materials and methods. This estimate is the
choices: replacement cost
reproduction cost
accrued depreciation
effective gross income
questions.explanation: Replacement cost is a building of equal utility built with modern materials, and it is the more common choice. Reproduction cost is an exact replica using the same materials and methods.

questions.stem: A small apartment building has potential gross income of $120,000, vacancy and collection loss of 6%, and operating expenses of $46,800. The owner's annual mortgage payments are $30,000. Using an 8% capitalization rate, what is its value?
questions.explanation: EGI = $120,000 − 6% ($7,200) = $112,800. NOI = $112,800 − $46,800 = $66,000. Value = $66,000 ÷ 0.08 = $825,000. Mortgage payments are debt service, not an operating expense, so subtracting them (giving $450,000) is wrong.

questions.stem: An online home value estimate is produced by software from public-record and recent sales data, without anyone inspecting the home. What is it?
choices: A broker price opinion
A comparative market analysis
An automated valuation model
An appraisal
questions.explanation: An automated valuation model (AVM) estimates value from data alone. Because it can't see condition, upgrades or view, it is least reliable where there are few similar sales. A BPO or CMA is prepared by a broker, and an appraisal by a credentialed appraiser.

questions.stem: In a lien-theory state, who holds legal title to a financed home while the loan is being repaid?
choices: The lender
A trustee chosen by the lender
The borrower
The title insurance company
questions.explanation: Under lien theory, the borrower keeps title and the lender holds only a lien. Under title theory, legal title goes to the lender or a trustee until the loan is paid, while the borrower keeps equitable title and possession.

questions.stem: A seller sells a lot and carries back a loan secured by it. The buyer needs a construction loan, and the construction lender insists on first lien position. Which clause in the seller's loan makes this possible?
choices: Acceleration clause
Defeasance clause
Alienation clause
Subordination clause
questions.explanation: In a subordination clause the lender agrees its lien will rank behind a later lien, which is common when a land loan will be followed by a construction loan. Acceleration, defeasance and alienation clauses deal with default, payoff and transfer.

questions.stem: A developer's blanket loan covers 20 lots. Which clause lets a single lot be freed from the lien when it sells and the developer pays down a set amount?
choices: Release clause
Defeasance clause
Prepayment penalty clause
Acceleration clause
questions.explanation: A release clause lets individual parcels come out from under a blanket loan as they are sold. The defeasance clause is different: it requires the lender to release the whole lien once the entire debt is paid.

questions.stem: A borrower wants to pay off her loan two years early by refinancing. Her lender says she owes an extra fee for doing so. Which clause allows this charge?
choices: Alienation clause
Defeasance clause
Prepayment penalty clause
Subordination clause
questions.explanation: A prepayment penalty clause charges a fee for paying off early. Without one, a borrower may generally prepay. The alienation clause is triggered by a transfer of the property, not by early payoff.

questions.stem: A lender collects one-twelfth of the annual property taxes and homeowners insurance with each monthly payment and holds the money until the bills come due. Where is the money held?
choices: In the broker's trust account
In an escrow (impound) account
In the borrower's PMI policy
With the title company until the next closing
questions.explanation: When the lender collects taxes and insurance along with principal and interest (PITI), it holds them in an escrow or impound account and pays the bills when due.

questions.stem: A lender reviews a borrower's savings to confirm there is enough cash for the down payment, closing costs and reserves. Which of the four Cs of credit is this?
choices: Capacity
Collateral
Credit
Capital
questions.explanation: Capital is the cash for the down payment, closing costs and reserves. Capacity is the ability to afford the payment (income and ratios), credit is payment history, and collateral is the property.

questions.stem: A buyer's broker learns that her client's income is slightly too low to qualify for the loan he wants. What should she do?
choices: Keep the application truthful and refer him to the lender
Suggest he round his income up, since lenders rarely verify it
Advise him to leave a car loan off the application to improve his ratios
Have the seller pay him cash outside closing to show more savings
questions.explanation: Coaching a borrower to misstate income or debts, or hiding payments from the lender, is mortgage fraud. The broker should keep the application truthful and let the lender discuss other loan programs.

questions.stem: A loan's monthly payments are based on a 30-year schedule, but the remaining balance is due in full after 7 years. What is the large final payment called?
choices: Negative amortization
A balloon payment
A prepayment penalty
A buydown
questions.explanation: A partially amortized loan doesn't pay itself off, so a lump sum (the balloon) is due at the end. Negative amortization is a growing balance caused by unpaid interest.

questions.stem: On a fully amortized fixed-rate loan, how do the parts of each payment change over the life of the loan?
choices: The interest portion grows and the principal portion shrinks
The total payment rises each year
Payments cover only interest until the final balloon payment
The principal portion grows and the interest portion shrinks
questions.explanation: Equal payments retire the loan by the end of the term. Early payments are mostly interest because the balance is high; as the balance falls, more of each payment goes to principal.

questions.stem: A buyer who has never served in the military wants a government-backed loan with no down payment on a home in an eligible rural area. Her income is within the program's limits. Which program is designed for this?
choices: USDA Rural Development loan
FHA loan
VA loan
Conventional conforming loan
questions.explanation: USDA Rural Development loans serve eligible rural areas, have income limits and often require no down payment. VA loans also may need no down payment, but they are for eligible veterans and service members.

questions.stem: A seller who owns her home free and clear agrees to take part of the price as a note from the buyer, secured by a deed of trust on the home being sold. This is
choices: a wraparound mortgage
a purchase-money mortgage
a bridge loan
a home equity line of credit
questions.explanation: When the seller acts as lender and takes back a note secured by the property sold, it is seller financing, often called a purchase-money mortgage. A wraparound requires an existing underlying loan, which this home doesn't have.

questions.stem: A buyer makes monthly payments to the seller on a new, larger loan, and the seller keeps paying her own existing loan out of those payments. What could block this wraparound arrangement?
choices: A cap on the new loan's interest rate
A release clause in the new loan
A due-on-sale clause in the seller's loan
A takeout commitment from a permanent lender
questions.explanation: A wraparound leaves the seller's loan in place after the sale. If that loan has a due-on-sale (alienation) clause, the lender can call it due when the property transfers, which defeats the wrap.

questions.stem: A couple has found their next home but hasn't sold their current one. They need a short-term loan that uses the equity in their current home to buy the new one. Which loan fits?
choices: Takeout loan
Package loan
Reverse mortgage
Bridge loan
questions.explanation: A bridge (swing) loan is short-term financing that lets a buyer tap equity in the current home before it sells. A takeout loan replaces a construction loan, and a reverse mortgage pays older owners from their equity.

questions.stem: A buyer's loan on a furnished condo covers both the unit and its furniture and appliances. This is a
choices: blanket loan
open-end loan
package loan
wraparound mortgage
questions.explanation: A package loan covers real property plus personal property. A blanket loan covers several parcels, and an open-end loan lets the borrower borrow more later under the same instrument.

questions.stem: A builder pays the lender an up-front amount so that a buyer's interest rate is lower for the first two years of the loan. This is called
choices: a buydown
a home equity line of credit
an open-end loan
negative amortization
questions.explanation: In a buydown, someone (often the seller or builder) pays the lender up front to reduce the borrower's rate, either permanently or for the early years.

questions.stem: A homeowner gets a revolving line of credit secured by her home, usually in second position. She draws as needed and pays interest only on what she uses. This is a
choices: reverse mortgage
HELOC
bridge loan
construction loan
questions.explanation: A HELOC is a revolving line secured by the home. A reverse mortgage instead pays the owner and its balance grows until the owner sells, moves out permanently or dies.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the secondary mortgage market?
choices: To make loans directly to home buyers
To set the index for adjustable-rate loans
To insure lenders against borrower default
To buy existing loans from lenders
questions.explanation: Loans are made in the primary market. The secondary market buys and sells existing loans, which puts money back in lenders' hands so they can lend again. Uniform documents and standards exist largely so loans can be sold there.

questions.stem: A broker accepts a payment from a lender each time she refers a buyer who gets a federally related mortgage loan. Which penalty can apply under RESPA?
choices: A warning letter for a first offense, with no fine
Loss of that sale's commission, but no fine or prison
A fine of up to $10,000, up to one year in prison, or both
A fine equal to the referral fee, with no possibility of prison
questions.explanation: RESPA Section 8 violations can bring a fine of up to $10,000, up to one year in prison, or both, plus civil liability to the borrower for three times the charge paid for the settlement service involved. A lender's per-referral payment to a broker is exactly the kind of kickback Section 8 bans.

questions.stem: A buyer is financing a home with a federally related mortgage loan. As a condition of the sale, the seller insists the buyer purchase title insurance from a particular title company. Under RESPA this is
choices: prohibited
allowed, because the seller controls the terms of the sale
allowed if the title company gives the seller a discount
allowed if the listing broker discloses it in writing
questions.explanation: RESPA Section 9 bars a seller from requiring, as a condition of sale, that a buyer using a federally related loan buy title insurance from a particular title company; a seller who does so is liable to the buyer for three times the title insurance charges. Neither written disclosure nor a benefit to the seller makes it allowed.

questions.stem: Which federal law requires many lenders to report loan-level data about the applications they receive and the loans they make, so regulators and the public can spot patterns such as redlining?
choices: Equal Credit Opportunity Act
Home Mortgage Disclosure Act
Truth in Lending Act
Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act
questions.explanation: HMDA, implemented by Regulation C, is a reporting law. ECOA prohibits credit discrimination, TILA requires cost-of-credit disclosures, and RESPA covers settlement costs and kickbacks.

questions.stem: Under federal ability-to-repay rules, which loan feature generally keeps a loan from being a qualified mortgage?
choices: A 15-year term
A fixed interest rate
Negative amortization
Full documentation of income
questions.explanation: Qualified mortgages generally avoid negative amortization, interest-only periods, most balloon payments, terms over 30 years and excessive points and fees. A 15-year fixed-rate loan with documented income fits within the rules.

questions.stem: A lender repeatedly persuades a homeowner to refinance, charging new fees each time without any real benefit to the borrower. This practice is
choices: packing
equity stripping
redlining
loan flipping
questions.explanation: Loan flipping is repeated refinancing to generate fees. Packing adds unnecessary products such as credit insurance, and equity stripping is lending against equity without regard to the borrower's ability to pay.

questions.stem: A lender charges higher rates on loans in certain neighborhoods because of the neighborhoods' racial makeup, regardless of the borrowers' credit. This is
choices: redlining
loan flipping
packing
equity stripping
questions.explanation: Redlining is refusing to lend, or lending on worse terms, in certain areas because of their racial or ethnic makeup. It is illegal under fair lending laws.

questions.stem: Annual property taxes of $3,240 are paid in arrears and are unpaid at an April 20 closing. Using a 360-day year, with the seller owning the day of closing, how is the proration shown?
choices: $990 credit to the seller and debit to the buyer
$2,250 debit to the seller and credit to the buyer
$990 debit to the seller and credit to the buyer
$976.44 debit to the seller and credit to the buyer
questions.explanation: Daily rate: $3,240 ÷ 360 = $9. Seller's days: 3 months × 30 + 20 = 110. Share: 110 × $9 = $990. The buyer will pay the whole bill later, so debit the seller and credit the buyer. $976.44 comes from wrongly using 365 days.

questions.stem: A home is worth $420,000. The owner owes $250,000 on a first deed of trust and $40,000 on a home equity line. What is the owner's equity?
questions.explanation: Equity = market value − all loan balances: $420,000 − $250,000 − $40,000 = $130,000. Forgetting the second loan gives $170,000; $290,000 is the total debt.

questions.stem: An investor pays $250,000 cash for a property that produces $20,000 of annual income. What is the simple rate of return?
questions.explanation: Rate of return = annual income ÷ amount invested: $20,000 ÷ $250,000 = 0.08, or 8%. Dividing the other way ($250,000 ÷ $20,000) gives 12.5, which is not a rate of return.

questions.stem: A lot is worth $171,000 after losing 10% of its value. What was it worth originally?
questions.explanation: The current value is 90% of the original: $171,000 ÷ 0.90 = $190,000. Adding 10% of the current value ($171,000 × 1.10 = $188,100) undershoots because the 10% loss was figured on the original value.

questions.stem: An investor buys a property for $750,000, of which $150,000 is land. The building has a 40-year economic life. Using straight-line depreciation, what is the annual depreciation?
questions.explanation: Only the improvement depreciates: $750,000 − $150,000 = $600,000. $600,000 ÷ 40 = $15,000 per year. Dividing the full $750,000 gives $18,750, which wrongly includes the land.

questions.stem: Which expense increases a homeowner's adjusted basis?
choices: Patching drywall
Adding a finished basement
Repairing a broken window pane
Fixing a leaking faucet
questions.explanation: Capital improvements that add value or extend useful life, such as a finished basement, are added to basis. Ordinary repairs and maintenance don't change basis.

questions.stem: A homeowner takes the standard deduction rather than itemizing. Which statement is correct?
choices: She can still deduct her mortgage interest separately
She can deduct her homeowners insurance premiums instead of interest
She can deduct her loan principal payments instead
She gets no separate deduction for mortgage interest or property taxes
questions.explanation: Mortgage interest and property taxes are itemized deductions, so they help only a taxpayer who itemizes. Principal, homeowners insurance and utilities on a personal residence are never deductible.

questions.stem: A couple sells their main home at a $30,000 loss. How is the loss treated for federal income tax purposes?
choices: It is deductible against ordinary income
It is carried over to reduce the gain on their next home
It is not deductible, because it is a personal loss
It is deductible only if they buy another home within two years
questions.explanation: A loss on the sale of your own home is a personal loss and is not deductible. Only gains on a personal residence are taxed, subject to the home-sale exclusion.

questions.stem: An investor buys an office building. Over what period is the building's cost recovered using straight-line depreciation?
choices: 27.5 years
39 years
15 years
It can't be depreciated because it is commercial
questions.explanation: Nonresidential property such as offices, retail and warehouses is recovered over 39 years. Residential rental property uses 27.5 years. Land is never depreciable under either schedule.

questions.stem: How does taking depreciation on a rental property affect the owner when the property is sold?
choices: It lowers basis, which raises the taxable gain
It raises basis, which lowers the taxable gain
It has no effect on basis or gain
It permanently erases tax on that part of the gain
questions.explanation: Each year's depreciation lowers adjusted basis, so the gain on sale is larger. The part of the gain caused by depreciation is taxed under recapture rules, so depreciation defers tax rather than erasing it.

questions.stem: An IRS lien for unpaid federal income tax is best described as
choices: a specific lien on the taxpayer's home only
a lien that always ranks ahead of local property tax liens
a lien that can't reach property acquired after it arises
a general lien on all of the taxpayer's property
questions.explanation: A federal tax lien is a general lien that attaches to all the taxpayer's property, including property acquired later. Local property tax liens are specific liens and, under federal law, can keep priority even over a federal tax lien.

questions.stem: A son inherits his mother's house. She paid $90,000 for it decades ago, and it was worth $480,000 on the date of her death. What is generally his basis?
questions.explanation: An heir's basis in inherited property is generally its fair market value on the date of death, so his basis is $480,000. The mother's $90,000 purchase price does not carry over.

questions.stem: Under FIRPTA, who is generally required to withhold part of the amount realized when the seller is a foreign person?
choices: The seller
The listing broker
The buyer
The county treasurer
questions.explanation: FIRPTA puts the withholding duty on the buyer (the transferee), with some exemptions. In practice the closing company usually handles it for the buyer.

questions.stem: A lot seller carries back a loan to a buyer who plans to build. The construction lender requires first lien position before it will fund. What does the seller's loan usually include to allow this?
choices: A takeout commitment
A subordination clause
A lien waiver from each supplier
A draw schedule
questions.explanation: With a subordination clause the lot seller agrees that its lien will rank behind the construction loan. A takeout commitment is a permanent lender's promise to pay off the construction loan, and lien waivers come from contractors and suppliers.

questions.stem: Who actually issues licenses and certifications to real property appraisers?
choices: The Appraisal Foundation
The Appraiser Qualifications Board
ARELLO
State appraiser regulators
questions.explanation: States license and certify appraisers, using criteria at least as strict as the AQB's minimums. The Appraisal Foundation and its boards set standards and qualifications but license no one, and ARELLO is an association of license regulators.

questions.stem: What is ARELLO?
choices: A private trade association that brokers join for marketing and networking
The federal agency that licenses brokers who work in several states
An association of state and provincial license regulators
The board that writes and interprets appraisal standards
questions.explanation: ARELLO is an association of real estate license regulators. It shares best practices, runs a license verification database and certifies distance-education courses, but it does not license, discipline or write license laws.

questions.stem: An investor's rental building is in excellent condition and rising in value, yet she takes a cost recovery deduction for it every year. Which statement explains this?
choices: She must be claiming external obsolescence
Tax depreciation follows a schedule, not value loss
The land is depreciating even though the building is not
The deduction requires an appraiser to confirm a value loss
questions.explanation: Tax cost recovery is a paper deduction on a fixed schedule whether or not the building loses value. Appraisal depreciation (physical deterioration or functional or external obsolescence) is an actual loss in value. Land never depreciates under either.

questions.stem: A buyer pays $400,000 for a home that appraises at $380,000 and borrows $323,000 on a conventional loan. What is the loan-to-value ratio, and will the lender typically require PMI?
choices: 80.75%; yes, because the LTV is above 80%
85%; no, because PMI applies only to FHA loans
80.75%; no, because the down payment is more than 15%
85%; yes, because the LTV is above 80%
questions.explanation: LTV uses the lesser of price or appraised value: $323,000 ÷ $380,000 = 85%. Conventional loans above 80% LTV typically require PMI, which protects the lender. Dividing by the $400,000 price gives the tempting 80.75%.

questions.stem: A buyer pays $300,000 for a home with a $280,000 loan, and the lender charges 1.5 discount points. How much are the points, and how do they affect the APR?
choices: $4,200; they make the APR lower than the note rate
$4,500; they make the APR higher than the note rate
$4,200; they make the APR higher than the note rate
$420; they have no effect on the APR
questions.explanation: Points are based on the loan: $280,000 × 0.015 = $4,200. The APR includes certain finance charges such as points as well as interest, so it ends up higher than the note rate. Using the $300,000 price gives $4,500.

questions.stem: An office building's NOI is $90,000, and recent sales support a 7.5% capitalization rate. If investors begin demanding a 9% cap rate for similar buildings, what happens to the building's value?
choices: It falls by $200,000
It rises by $200,000
It falls by $135,000
It stays the same because NOI hasn't changed
questions.explanation: At 7.5%: $90,000 ÷ 0.075 = $1,200,000. At 9%: $90,000 ÷ 0.09 = $1,000,000. A higher cap rate means a lower value for the same NOI, so value falls by $200,000.

questions.stem: A seller agrees to sell her house to a buyer for $250,000, well below its $320,000 market value. Later she claims the contract is invalid because the price was too low. Which is most accurate?
choices: The contract is void because the consideration must equal the market value
The contract is voidable by the seller because she received less than fair value
The contract is valid; courts generally don't weigh whether the price was fair
The contract is unenforceable unless an appraisal supports the agreed price
questions.explanation: A contract needs good and valuable consideration from both sides, and courts generally don't judge its adequacy. A low price agreed to by competent parties doesn't make the contract void or voidable.

questions.stem: A buyer and seller sign a written purchase contract that spells out the price, closing date and inclusions. Classified by how it was formed, this contract is
choices: express
implied
unilateral
executed
questions.explanation: An express contract states its terms in words, oral or written. An implied contract arises from conduct; unilateral and executed describe who is bound and stage of performance, not how the contract was formed.

questions.stem: Which statement by a listing broker is most likely puffing rather than a statement of fact a buyer could rely on?
choices: "The furnace was replaced with a new unit just last year."
"This kitchen has the best view in the whole neighborhood."
"The roof on the house is only two years old."
"The basement has never had any water in it."
questions.explanation: Puffing is a vague opinion or exaggeration a reasonable buyer wouldn't rely on as fact. The other statements are specific facts; if false, they would be misrepresentations.

questions.stem: An owner deployed overseas wants her brother to sign the deed conveying her house while she is away. What does the brother need?
choices: A power of attorney from the owner authorizing him to convey the property
A letter from the listing broker confirming that the owner agreed to the sale
Nothing more, because a close family member may sign for an absent owner
A court order declaring the owner legally incompetent to sign contracts
questions.explanation: Someone signing for another person needs proper authority, typically a power of attorney, which is usually recorded when used to convey real property. Being a relative gives no authority to sign.

questions.stem: While reviewing a purchase contract, a seller asks his broker whether a clause would hold up in court and what his legal rights would be if the buyer backed out. What should the broker do?
choices: Explain the seller's legal rights based on the broker's own experience
Rewrite the clause in plain language so that it is clearly enforceable
Tell the seller the clause is standard language that needs no review
Recommend that the seller consult an attorney
questions.explanation: Brokers fill in forms but may not give legal advice or draft original contract language. Questions about legal rights or enforceability should go to an attorney.

questions.stem: A buyer makes an offer on a home. Before the seller responds, the buyer dies. The seller then signs the offer. Which is true?
choices: A contract was formed that is binding on the buyer's estate
The offer ended at the buyer's death, so no contract was formed
The contract is voidable at the option of the buyer's heirs
The seller may choose to enforce the contract against the estate
questions.explanation: An offer terminates if either party dies or becomes incompetent before acceptance. Because the offer no longer existed, the seller's signature couldn't create a contract.

questions.stem: A seller is already under contract with one buyer when a second buyer submits a written offer before closing. What should the listing broker do?
choices: Reject it on the seller's behalf because the home is under contract
Hold it until the first contract either closes or falls through
Present it to the seller promptly; the seller may accept it as a backup
Share its terms with the first buyer so that buyer can match it
questions.explanation: Listing brokers must present all written offers promptly, even when the property is already under contract (in Colorado, C.R.S. 12-10-404 requires this), so the seller can decide whether to accept one as a backup, which is subject to the first contract failing. Holding or rejecting it takes the decision away from the seller, and sharing one buyer's terms with another requires the seller's permission.

questions.stem: A seller hired a particular broker because of his marketing skill. The broker wants to transfer the listing agreement to an unrelated broker. Generally, the listing
choices: can't be assigned without the seller's consent, because it is a personal services contract
can be freely assigned, because most contracts are assignable unless they say otherwise
becomes void the moment the broker attempts to assign it without asking
can be assigned only if the new broker pays the seller separate consideration
questions.explanation: Most contracts are assignable, but contracts that depend on a person's skill, such as a listing agreement, generally can't be assigned without the other party's consent.

questions.stem: A purchase contract makes the buyer's obligation to close depend on the buyer obtaining loan approval by a stated date. This provision is a(n)
choices: right of first refusal
option
amendment
contingency
questions.explanation: A contingency is a condition that must be met before a party is obligated to perform. If it fails, the protected party can usually terminate without default by giving notice by the deadline.

questions.stem: A buyer backs out without legal excuse. The contract lets the seller either keep the earnest money or pursue actual damages. The seller resells to another buyer for $20,000 less and sues the first buyer for that loss. The seller is seeking
choices: specific performance
rescission
liquidated damages
compensatory damages
questions.explanation: Compensatory damages are money to cover the actual loss caused by the breach. Liquidated damages would be the amount agreed in advance, such as the earnest money.

questions.stem: A buyer signs a purchase contract that calls for no earnest money deposit. Which is correct?
choices: It can be valid, because the buyer's promise to pay is consideration
It is void, because every purchase contract requires earnest money
It becomes valid only after the buyer deposits money with a broker
It is valid, but the seller has no remedy if the buyer later defaults
questions.explanation: Earnest money isn't required for a valid contract; the buyer's promise to pay supplies consideration. The seller can still pursue remedies such as damages if the buyer defaults.

questions.stem: A seller breached a purchase contract, but the buyer waited many years to sue, past the deadline state law sets for that kind of claim. The buyer's claim is most likely
choices: still enforceable, because the seller never cured the breach
void from the start, because the seller breached the contract
unenforceable, because the statute of limitations has run
limited to specific performance instead of money damages
questions.explanation: A statute of limitations sets a deadline for filing suit. Once it runs, the claim can no longer be enforced in court.

questions.stem: A homeowner hires a well-known artist to paint a mural in her living room, and the artist dies before starting. The contract is most likely discharged by
choices: novation
mutual release
impossibility
substantial performance
questions.explanation: Impossibility discharges a contract when performance can't be done, such as when a party to a personal-services contract dies. Novation and mutual release require agreement of the parties.

questions.stem: After a purchase contract is signed but before closing, the buyer holds
choices: legal title, while the seller keeps equitable title
a leasehold estate until the closing takes place
no interest in the property until the deed is recorded
equitable title, while the seller still holds legal title
questions.explanation: A signed purchase contract gives the buyer equitable title, an interest in the property, even though the seller keeps legal title until closing.

questions.stem: A lease runs from January 1 through June 30 of the same year. Which is true about ending it?
choices: It ends automatically on June 30 without notice
It is a periodic tenancy that requires notice set by state law
It continues month-to-month until the landlord gives notice
It is a tenancy at will that ends only when either party dies
questions.explanation: A lease with a definite start and end date is an estate for years, whatever its length, and it ends automatically. A periodic tenancy renews itself and requires notice to end.

questions.stem: Which is most likely a material fact that a broker who knows of it should disclose to a buyer?
choices: The listing broker thinks the backyard is the nicest on the block
The state has approved a highway next to the property
The seller will move her furniture out before the closing date
The home's exterior was painted a different color five years ago
questions.explanation: A material fact is one that would affect a reasonable buyer's decision or the price paid; a planned highway next door qualifies. The others are opinions or facts that don't affect value or desirability.

questions.stem: A seller gives the buyer a completed seller's property disclosure statement. Which statement about it is most accurate?
choices: It serves as the seller's warranty that the home has no defects at all
It makes a professional home inspection unnecessary for the buyer
The listing broker should fill it out so that the answers are accurate
It reflects the seller's actual knowledge and doesn't replace an inspection
questions.explanation: The seller completes the disclosure from actual knowledge; the broker shouldn't fill it out. It isn't a warranty and isn't a substitute for an inspection.

questions.stem: A Colorado seller's home was the site of a suicide two years ago. Nothing about the home was physically damaged. Under Colorado law, this fact is
choices: a material fact the seller must disclose on the disclosure form
not a material fact that must be disclosed
a latent defect the listing broker must disclose in writing
required to be disclosed only if the buyer has young children
questions.explanation: C.R.S. 38-35.5-101 provides that facts or suspicions that a property was the site of a homicide, other felony or suicide are not material facts requiring disclosure, and a broker can't be sued for not disclosing them. Stigma isn't a physical defect.

questions.stem: A buyer notices that the neighbor's fence seems to sit several feet inside the lot line shown on the plat, and a shed appears to straddle the boundary. What should the buyer's broker recommend?
choices: A radon test before the inspection deadline passes
Relying on the seller's property disclosure statement
A survey to locate the boundaries and any encroachments
Having the broker measure the lot and report the result
questions.explanation: When boundaries, fences or encroachments are in question, a survey is the expert tool. Brokers should recommend experts rather than act as one.

questions.stem: A landlord is renting a house built in 1960 to a family on a one-year lease. Under the federal lead-based paint rule, which is required before the tenant is bound?
choices: Give the tenant a 10-day opportunity to conduct a lead inspection first
Give the EPA pamphlet and disclose any known lead-based paint
Remove all lead-based paint from the house before the lease begins
Nothing, because the lead-based paint rule applies only to sales
questions.explanation: For pre-1978 housing, landlords must give the pamphlet, disclose known lead-based paint and hazards, and include the warning statement. The 10-day inspection opportunity applies to buyers, not tenants, and the rule never requires removal.

questions.stem: A buyer's inspector finds mold on basement drywall next to a leaking water line. What is the essential first step in addressing the mold?
choices: Paint over the stains with a sealing primer
Install a radon mitigation fan in the basement
Wrap the affected drywall in plastic sheeting
Fix the leak to stop the moisture
questions.explanation: Mold grows wherever there's moisture, so fixing the water source is essential. Covering the mold without stopping the moisture just hides the problem.

questions.stem: Foam insulation blown into the walls of a home in the 1970s is suspected of releasing formaldehyde gas. This insulation is most likely
choices: friable asbestos
radon
UFFI
lead-based paint
questions.explanation: Urea-formaldehyde foam insulation (UFFI) was installed in the 1970s and can release formaldehyde gas. Radon is a soil gas, and asbestos releases fibers, not formaldehyde.

questions.stem: A buyer wants to fill a marshy part of a rural parcel to build a barn. The area is a federally protected wetland. What will the buyer typically need?
choices: A Phase I environmental site assessment report
Flood insurance through the NFIP before building
Approval from the seller's title insurance company
A permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
questions.explanation: Wetlands are protected under the Clean Water Act, and filling or building in them typically requires an Army Corps of Engineers permit. A Phase I assessment relates to contamination and CERCLA defenses.

questions.stem: To hide a known roof leak, a seller paints over the ceiling stains and tells the buyer the roof has never leaked. Before closing, the buyer discovers the leak, wants out of the contract and wants the earnest money back. Which is most accurate?
choices: The buyer must close, because a stained ceiling is a patent defect
The contract is voidable by the buyer, who can seek rescission
The seller may keep the earnest money as liquidated damages
The contract is void, so neither party ever had obligations
questions.explanation: Concealing a known defect and lying about it is fraud, which makes the contract voidable by the victim. Rescission cancels the contract and returns deposits. The stains were hidden, so the defect wasn't patent.

questions.stem: A tenant with a lease option paid a separate option fee. Ten months into the lease, the tenant gives the owner written notice exercising the option. Which is true now?
choices: The option is still unilateral, so the tenant may decline to buy
The owner may refuse to sell if a higher offer comes in first
A bilateral purchase contract binds both the tenant and the owner
The arrangement converts into a right of first refusal
questions.explanation: An option is unilateral until exercised; once the optionee exercises it, it becomes a bilateral purchase contract binding both parties. The optionor can't back out for a better offer.

questions.stem: A buyer's offer on a home built in 1950 includes the Lead Warning Statement and lead disclosure as an attachment, signed along with the contract. This attachment is best described as
choices: an addendum
an amendment
a counteroffer
a contingency
questions.explanation: An addendum is material made part of the contract when it is signed; the federal rule requires the Lead Warning Statement in an attachment to the sales contract. An amendment changes a contract after it is formed.

questions.stem: A purchase contract with a time-is-of-the-essence clause includes an inspection contingency with a deadline. The inspection reveals serious defects, and the buyer gives written notice of termination before the deadline. Which result is most likely?
choices: The buyer is in default, and the seller keeps the earnest money
The seller can get specific performance forcing the buyer to close
The termination isn't effective until the seller signs an amendment
The buyer can terminate without being in default
questions.explanation: When a contingency fails and the buyer gives timely written notice, the buyer can terminate without default, so liquidated damages don't apply. Meeting the deadline matters because time is of the essence.

questions.stem: A seller's listing firm agrees to share part of its commission with the firm working with the buyer. Whom does the buyer's broker represent?
choices: The seller, since the seller's money pays the fee
Both parties, since the fee is shared
The buyer, the party who engaged the broker
The listing firm, since it pays the fee
questions.explanation: Who pays the commission doesn't decide who the broker represents. A buyer's broker paid out of a shared listing fee still works for the buyer.

questions.stem: A broker agrees to help a friend sell her home and says he won't charge a fee. Which statement is correct?
choices: He can still owe the friend full fiduciary duties
An agency exists only once a fee agreement is signed
The friend is a customer rather than a client
He owes no fiduciary duties because no fee is paid
questions.explanation: Agency doesn't require compensation. A broker who acts for someone for free can still be their agent and owe full fiduciary duties.

questions.stem: A listing expired June 30 and includes a 90-day protection period. In August the owner sells, without any broker, to a buyer the listing broker showed the home to in May. The listing broker:
choices: Earns nothing, because the listing term has ended
Earns a fee only if the buyer found it in the MLS
Becomes the seller's agent again for the August sale
May earn the fee under the protection clause
questions.explanation: A protection (carryover) clause lets the broker earn a fee if, within the stated period after the listing ends, the owner sells to someone the broker introduced during the term.

questions.stem: Under the industry practice changes that took effect in 2024, a broker in a NAR-affiliated MLS wants to tour a home with a new buyer. What must be in place first?
choices: Written consent from the listing seller
A written agreement with the buyer
A preapproval letter from the buyer's lender
A signed offer on at least one property
questions.explanation: NAR-affiliated MLS participants working with a buyer must have a written agreement with that buyer before touring a home. The agreement spells out the buyer broker's compensation.

questions.stem: A listing expired and the seller relisted with another firm. A buyer asks the former listing broker why the seller is moving and how low she'll go. The former listing broker should:
choices: Share it once the new listing has closed
Share it, because all duties ended with the listing
Keep it confidential, since that duty outlasts the agency
Share it only if the buyer signs a buyer agency agreement
questions.explanation: Some duties survive the end of an agency. Confidential information learned during the relationship, like motivation and price flexibility, generally stays confidential after the listing ends.

questions.stem: An owner signs a durable power of attorney naming her son. She later becomes incapacitated, and then dies before her home sells. The son's authority:
choices: Survives her incapacity but ends at her death
Survives her death so the son can finish the sale
Ends as soon as she becomes incapacitated
Continues until the home is sold and closed
questions.explanation: A durable power of attorney survives the principal's incapacity, which an ordinary one doesn't. No power of attorney survives the principal's death.

questions.stem: A seller living overseas signs a specific power of attorney so her cousin can sign the deed at closing. Which statement is correct?
choices: The listing agreement already gives the broker this power
The cousin must be a licensed attorney
The cousin must also hold a real estate license
The power of attorney is usually recorded with the deed
questions.explanation: To convey real estate, a power of attorney usually must be recorded along with the deed. The attorney-in-fact doesn't have to be a lawyer, and a listing agreement authorizes marketing, not signing deeds.

questions.stem: A buyer hands his broker an earnest money check. Months later the broker can't show where the money went. Which fiduciary duty has the broker most directly breached?
choices: Obedience
Accounting
Disclosure
Confidentiality
questions.explanation: The duty of accounting requires the broker to account for all money and property entrusted to her and never commingle or convert it.

questions.stem: A buyer client asks her broker whether she should take title with her partner as joint tenants or as tenants in common. The broker should:
choices: Pick whichever form keeps the purchase price lowest
Choose joint tenancy, since couples use it most often
Recommend she consult a real estate attorney
Tell her the choice doesn't matter for a home purchase
questions.explanation: Reasonable care and diligence includes not giving advice outside your expertise. How to hold title is a legal question, so refer the client to an attorney.

questions.stem: A seller tells the listing broker the roof is two years old. Without checking any records, the broker repeats this to buyers as fact. The roof is actually 15 years old, and neither the seller nor the broker knew. The broker's statement is most likely:
choices: Negligent misrepresentation
Fraud
Concealment
Puffing
questions.explanation: Passing along a false statement of fact that the licensee should have verified is negligent misrepresentation. Fraud requires knowing falsity or reckless disregard for the truth; puffing is opinion, not a factual claim.

questions.stem: In states that allow transaction brokerage, a transaction broker typically:
choices: Must be appointed by the employing broker as a dual agent for both parties
Advocates for whichever party pays the commission
Owes both parties full loyalty and confidentiality
Helps the parties close without advocating for either
questions.explanation: A transaction broker (facilitator) helps one or both parties complete the deal without representing either as an advocate. Duties come from state statute, such as honesty, reasonable skill and care, and accounting, but not full loyalty.

questions.stem: Under the general rule, a fact about a property is material when:
choices: The seller personally considers it embarrassing or private
A reasonable buyer would consider it important
It appears in the county public records
The buyer asks about it in writing
questions.explanation: A fact is material if a reasonable person would consider it important in deciding whether, or on what terms, to buy or sell. Physical defects are almost always material.

questions.stem: A buyer asks the listing broker whether the previous occupant had AIDS. What should the broker do?
choices: Answer truthfully, since it's a material fact
Ask the seller for permission to answer
Decline to discuss it
Disclose it only in writing
questions.explanation: Answering or volunteering whether a past occupant had HIV/AIDS or another disability can be treated as disability discrimination under fair housing law, so the broker shouldn't discuss it.

questions.stem: Which of these is a protected class listed in the text of the federal Fair Housing Act?
choices: Religion
Source of income
Marital status
Sexual orientation
questions.explanation: The Act lists seven classes: race, color, religion, national origin, sex, disability and familial status. Sexual orientation isn't in the federal text, though Colorado law covers it.

questions.stem: Which household is protected under the Fair Housing Act's familial status provisions?
choices: A married couple with no children
A grandparent who lives alone
Two unrelated adult roommates aged 22 and 25
A pregnant woman with no other children
questions.explanation: Familial status covers households with a child under 18 living with a parent, custodian or designee, and it also covers pregnant people and anyone in the process of getting custody of a child.

questions.stem: An apartment applicant is in a recovery program and no longer uses illegal drugs. Under the Fair Housing Act, the applicant:
choices: Is protected only in owner-occupied buildings
Is protected, since recovering addicts are covered
Isn't protected, since any past drug use disqualifies
Is protected only if a doctor confirms it in writing
questions.explanation: Current illegal drug use isn't a protected disability, but people recovering from addiction are protected.

questions.stem: A broker tells a Muslim couple that a listed home is "already under contract" when it isn't, to keep them from seeing it. This violates the Fair Housing Act because it:
choices: Is blockbusting aimed at the current owner
Breaches only the duty of obedience to the seller
Falsely represents that housing isn't available
Is a form of redlining by the listing firm
questions.explanation: Falsely saying housing isn't available for inspection, sale or rent because of a protected class (here, religion) is a prohibited act. Redlining involves lenders; blockbusting involves inducing owners to sell.

questions.stem: HUD requires brokerage offices to display the Equal Housing Opportunity poster. If a firm fails to display it, the failure:
choices: Can be treated as evidence of discrimination
