choices: It acts as the buyer's notice to terminate
The extension takes effect anyway because the seller didn't object
The contract continues under its original deadlines
The seller must sign an Agreement to Revive
questions.explanation: If both parties don't sign Part I and the requesting party doesn't receive notice of acceptance in time, Part II works as the requesting party's notice to terminate, based on the contract provisions checked.

questions.stem: Buyer and seller sign an Inspection Resolution in which the seller agrees to give the buyer a repair credit. Who else should the buyer give a copy to?
choices: The county assessor
The Real Estate Commission
The owners' association board
The buyer's lender
questions.explanation: An Inspection Resolution amends the contract, and repairs or credits can change the loan, so the buyer should give the lender a copy.

questions.stem: The contract has no Time of Day Deadline. On the Inspection Termination Deadline, the buyer emails a Notice to Terminate that reaches the seller's broker's inbox at 11:52 p.m. Mountain Time. The seller reads it the next morning. Is the termination timely?
choices: No, because the seller personally didn't receive it until the next day
Yes, because receipt by the seller's broker before 11:59 p.m. counts
No, because termination notices can't be delivered by email
Yes, but only if the seller signs it
questions.explanation: Before closing, delivery to the party's broker or brokerage counts as delivery to the party, and a day ends at 11:59 p.m. Mountain Time when no Time of Day Deadline applies. With a 5:00 p.m. Time of Day Deadline, the same email would be late.

questions.stem: A seller tells the listing broker not to present offers below $600,000. How must this limit be handled?
choices: The broker may follow it based on the seller's oral instruction
The broker must refuse, since every offer must always be presented
Explain pros and cons, then put the limit in the listing contract
The broker must get each buyer's broker's consent to the limit
questions.explanation: A listing broker may limit which offers are presented only after explaining the pros and cons to the seller, and the limit must be written into the listing contract. An oral instruction isn't enough.

questions.stem: A seller receives four offers and wants to send Counterproposals to all four buyers at once. What is the main risk?
choices: More than one buyer could accept, binding the seller twice
Counterproposals can be sent only to the highest offer
The listing broker loses the right to compensation
The original offers stay open and the seller can still accept any of them
questions.explanation: Each Counterproposal is an offer the buyer can accept. Countering several buyers at once can create more than one binding contract if more than one accepts, so this strategy needs care and usually a lawyer.

questions.stem: Under the Exclusive Right-to-Sell Listing Contract, what must happen before the listing broker accepts compensation from someone other than the seller?
choices: The buyer must consent orally
The Commission must approve it
Nothing, if the amount is less than the listing fee
The seller must consent in writing
questions.explanation: The listing contract bars the broker from accepting third-party compensation without the seller's written consent.

questions.stem: During the holdover period, the seller signs an exclusive listing with a new firm, which earns a commission selling to a Submitted Prospect of the first firm. Neither Will/Will Not box was checked in the first listing. Does the seller owe the first firm?
choices: Yes, because the buyer was a Submitted Prospect
No; with neither box checked, nothing is owed to the first firm
Yes, and each firm receives half the commission
No, because holdover clauses can't be enforced in Colorado residential listings
questions.explanation: The Will/Will Not box decides whether the seller still owes the first firm when another firm earns a commission under a new exclusive listing signed during holdover. If neither box is checked, the seller doesn't owe the first firm.

questions.stem: Under an Exclusive Right-to-Buy Contract, the buyer's broker's fee is more than the listing firm pays. When does the buyer owe the unpaid balance?
choices: Only if it was disclosed in writing before the purchase contract
Always, since the buyer owes the full fee no matter who else pays any part of it
Never, because only sellers pay brokerage compensation
Only if the seller refuses to pay it at closing
questions.explanation: Amounts paid by the seller or the listing firm count toward the buyer's broker's compensation. The buyer owes any unpaid balance only if the broker disclosed that amount in writing before the buyer signed a contract with the seller.

questions.stem: A buyer under an Exclusive Right-to-Buy Contract wants to know whether registered sex offenders live near a home. What does the contract tell the buyer?
choices: The seller must disclose any nearby offenders on the Seller's Property Disclosure
The buyer's broker must research it and report in writing
The buyer should get that information from local law enforcement
It is listed in the title commitment
questions.explanation: The Exclusive Right-to-Buy Contract's Megan's Law paragraph tells the buyer that if the presence of a registered sex offender matters, the buyer must get that information from local law enforcement.

questions.stem: A contract includes the Short Sale Addendum. The lienholder's written acceptance hasn't arrived by the Short Sale Acceptance Deadline. What happens?
choices: The seller must pay the shortfall at closing
The contract terminates
The buyer must wait until the lienholder decides
The deadline extends automatically by 30 days
questions.explanation: Under the Short Sale Addendum, if the lienholder's written acceptance isn't received by the Short Sale Acceptance Deadline, the contract terminates. Changing that deadline would take an Agreement to Amend/Extend.

questions.stem: A short sale closes after the lienholder accepts less than the loan balance. What does the Short Sale Addendum warn the seller about?
choices: The lender's acceptance automatically forgives any balance remaining on the loan
The buyer becomes responsible for the deficiency
The listing broker must pay any deficiency from the commission
Unless released in writing, the seller may still owe the deficiency
questions.explanation: The seller may still owe the deficiency unless the lender releases it in writing, and forgiven debt can be taxable. The form strongly urges legal and tax advice.

questions.stem: Under the Commission-approved Closing Instructions, which deed won't the closing company prepare, so that the buyer or seller must supply it or give written instructions for it?
choices: A personal representative's deed
A statutory special warranty deed
A statutory bargain and sale deed
A statutory quitclaim deed
questions.explanation: The closing company prepares standard deeds the contract calls for: general warranty, special warranty, bargain and sale and quitclaim deeds. For a personal representative's or trustee's deed, or a warranty deed listing exceptions beyond the statutory ones, the buyer or seller must provide the deed or written instructions for preparing it.

questions.stem: A seller carrying back financing uses the Commission's Deed of Trust (Due on Transfer – Creditworthy). What does that version allow?
choices: The borrower may transfer the property freely, with no acceleration
The lender may accelerate on any transfer, regardless of the new owner
Acceleration if the new owner after a transfer isn't creditworthy
The Public Trustee must approve each transfer of the property
questions.explanation: The Due on Transfer – Creditworthy deed of trust lets the lender accelerate if the property is transferred to someone who isn't creditworthy. The Strict version allows acceleration on any transfer, and the Assumable version isn't due on transfer.

questions.stem: A buyer is purchasing a small retail building and wants time for a Phase I environmental review and an ADA evaluation. Which Commission contract is built for this?
choices: Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Residential)
Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Commercial)
Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Land)
Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Income-Residential)
questions.explanation: Office, retail, industrial and mixed-use property uses the Commercial contract, which has deadlines for environmental (Phase I/II) review and an ADA evaluation.

questions.stem: A broker is listing a working ranch with grazing land, water rights and two houses. Which approach fits the current Commission forms?
choices: The Commission-approved Farm and Ranch contract
The Residential contract, because people live in the houses on the ranch
The Commercial contract with no addendum
The Land contract with a Residential Addendum for the houses
questions.explanation: There is no farm and ranch contract on the current list. A ranch typically uses the Land contract, which covers water, minerals and growing crops, with a Residential Addendum to bring in the residential disclosures for the houses.

questions.stem: Under the Manufactured Home Contract to Buy and Sell (Lot Lease Only), the park owner refuses to approve the buyer as a tenant. What may the buyer do?
choices: Terminate, since park approval is a condition of the deal
Close anyway and negotiate a lease with the park later
Require the seller to move the home to another park at the seller's cost
Assign the contract to the park owner
questions.explanation: The Lot Lease Only contract depends on the park owner approving the buyer and the home in writing and either assigning the lease or signing a new one. The buyer may terminate if the lease or the approval terms are unsatisfactory.

questions.stem: A seller owns 10 acres and the manufactured home on it, which still has a certificate of title. The land and home are being sold together. Which Commission forms fit?
choices: Manufactured Home Contract to Buy and Sell (Lot Lease Only)
Residential contract alone, since the home is a dwelling
Land contract with the Manufactured Home Addendum
Land contract alone, since the home is personal property
questions.explanation: When the land is sold along with the manufactured home, the Land (or Commercial) contract is used with the Manufactured Home Addendum, which adds the serial number, VIN, certificate-of-title steps and a UCC search. The Residential contract has no manufactured home provisions, and the Lot Lease Only contract is for homes on rented spaces.

questions.stem: A broker's firm signs a guaranteed buy-out with a listing client using the Licensee Buy-Out Addendum. How must the firm treat the listing?
choices: Mark it as under contract in the MLS
Withdraw it from the MLS and other advertising until the buy-out closes
Mark it as sold to the firm
Keep marketing it as active in the MLS and other advertising
questions.explanation: The Commission's position on guaranteed buy-outs requires the broker to keep marketing the property as active. The seller may terminate the buy-out at any time, and the listing stays in effect.

questions.stem: Under the Post-Closing Occupancy Agreement, how is the seller's security deposit handled?
choices: The listing brokerage holds it and returns it at the next closing
The buyer holds it, up to two months' rent
The closing company holds it and releases it 60 days after closing
No deposit is allowed under the form
questions.explanation: The buyer holds the security deposit, which can't exceed two months' rent, and returns it within 30 days after the term ends, as Colorado law requires. Rent is paid to the buyer in advance at closing.

questions.stem: A broker selling her own rental property outside her firm has her attorney prepare the contract instead of using a Commission form. What must that form state?
choices: That the Commission reviewed it
That the buyer has waived the right to consult a separate attorney
Conspicuously, that it is not a Commission-approved form
That the broker acts as the buyer's transaction-broker
questions.explanation: A broker who is a party may have their own attorney prepare a form, but it must conspicuously state that it is not a Commission-approved form. The broker must also disclose their licensed status in writing.

questions.stem: Which property is most likely part of a common interest community under CCIOA?
choices: A townhome whose owner must pay assessments for shared grounds
A rural parcel with its own private well, septic system and no shared property
A single-family home in a city with no HOA
A rental house owned by an LLC
questions.explanation: A common interest community is real estate where owning a unit or lot obligates the owner to pay for common property or other units' expenses. Condominiums, most townhome communities and planned subdivisions with an HOA are typical.

questions.stem: An HOA's declaration bans all political signs and drought-tolerant landscaping. An owner says CCIOA limits such bans. Which statement is accurate?
choices: The declaration controls, because owners agreed to it at purchase
Owners can waive CCIOA's protections in the declaration
CCIOA limits such bans, and owners generally can't waive it
Only the Real Estate Commission can decide the issue
questions.explanation: CCIOA limits what associations can prohibit, including flags, political signs, drought-tolerant landscaping and EV chargers. Its protections can't be waived or varied by agreement except where the Act allows.

questions.stem: An HOA charges each owner a one-time $4,000 to replace the clubhouse roof. This charge is a
choices: regular assessment
working-capital contribution
status letter fee
special assessment
questions.explanation: A special assessment is a one-time charge for a specific need, such as a new roof. Regular assessments are the recurring dues that fund the budget, including reserves.

questions.stem: How is an HOA's statutory lien for assessments perfected under CCIOA?
choices: By recording a separate lien notice each time an owner falls behind
By recording the declaration
By filing a claim with the HOA Information and Resource Center
By obtaining a court judgment against the owner
questions.explanation: Recording the declaration perfects the association's lien, so no separate lien filing is needed. The lien is extinguished unless the association starts enforcement within six years after the full amount of assessments becomes due.

questions.stem: A unit owner delivers a written request to the HOA's registered agent by certified mail for a statement of unpaid assessments. The HOA never responds. What is the effect?
choices: The HOA can't assert a lien for assessments due as of the request date
The HOA may assert whatever amount it later finds was owed on that date
The request expires and must be resent
The buyer becomes liable for any unpaid assessments
questions.explanation: The association must furnish the statement within 14 calendar days of a proper written request, and the statement binds it. If it isn't furnished, the association can't assert a lien for assessments due as of the request date.

questions.stem: Under the Commission residential contract, who pays an association special assessment for a new community pool that was already completed when the buyer signed the contract?
choices: The buyer, because assessments follow ownership
The buyer and seller equally
The seller
Whoever the HOA board designates
questions.explanation: A checkbox decides who pays special assessments levied before closing, but the seller pays special assessments for improvements already installed as of the buyer's signing date.

questions.stem: A buyer asks the broker whether the HOA's declaration would allow her to run a home daycare. What should the broker do?
choices: Interpret the declaration and tell the buyer whether it's allowed
Have her read the documents and get legal advice
Ask the HOA manager for a binding ruling
Tell the buyer that HOA rules can't restrict home businesses
questions.explanation: Brokers should point out restrictions that matter to the buyer and calendar the association document deadlines, but they shouldn't interpret the documents. The buyer should read them and get legal advice on anything complicated.

questions.stem: A buyer's title objection isn't resolved by the Title Resolution Deadline, and the buyer didn't withdraw it. A week later both parties want to go ahead on the same terms with new deadlines. Which form fits?
choices: Agreement to Amend/Extend Contract
Counterproposal
Title-Related Objection Notice
Agreement to Revive Contract
questions.explanation: An unresolved title objection terminates the contract at the Title Resolution Deadline unless the buyer withdraws it. A terminated contract can't be amended; the Agreement to Revive Contract states the termination date, ratifies the contract and sets new deadlines.

questions.stem: The appraisal comes in low and the buyer timely objects. Before the Appraisal Resolution Deadline, the parties agree to cut the price by $10,000. How should they document it?
choices: An Agreement to Amend/Extend Contract signed before the deadline
A Counterproposal from the seller
A note in the buyer's broker's transaction file
An Agreement to Revive Contract signed once the resolution deadline has passed
questions.explanation: Changes to a signed contract, such as a price reduction after an appraisal objection, are made with an Agreement to Amend/Extend signed by both parties. It has to be done before the Appraisal Resolution Deadline, or the unresolved objection terminates the contract.

questions.stem: A broker lists her own home for sale through her own brokerage firm. Which statement is accurate?
choices: She may use any attorney-drafted contract she prefers
She needn't disclose her license because she is the owner
She uses Commission forms and discloses her license in writing
She must have another firm list the home
questions.explanation: A broker selling her own property through her firm must use the Commission-approved forms when appropriate and, as a principal, must disclose in writing that she's licensed. A broker selling outside the firm may use other forms.

questions.stem: A Colorado sale has just closed at the title company. What should happen with the signed closing statement and other closing documents?
choices: The title company keeps them, and the broker only needs to request copies if a dispute comes up
They go to the brokerage firm right after closing for its transaction file
The broker keeps them personally until the next Division audit
They are filed with the Real Estate Commission within 30 days
questions.explanation: Commission rules send closing statements and other closing documents to the brokerage firm right after closing for the transaction file, and the employing broker's supervision still applies. They aren't filed with the Commission.

questions.stem: After signing, the buyer and seller want to change how the closing company disburses a credit, but the new instruction conflicts with their purchase contract. What is needed?
choices: A new Closing Instructions form signed only by the closing company
A letter from the listing broker directing the closing company
An Agreement to Amend/Extend Contract signed by the buyer and seller
Nothing, because party instructions automatically override the contract
questions.explanation: When party instructions conflict with the contract, the buyer and seller must sign an amendment (Agreement to Amend/Extend Contract). A broker can't change the parties' deal by letter.

questions.stem: Under Colorado's good funds law, which payment may a closing company make before the buyer's funds are available for immediate withdrawal?
choices: Up to $500 for incidental items such as recording fees and tax certificates
The listing brokerage's commission, if the listing contract allows it
The seller's loan payoff, to stop interest from accruing
Any disbursement at all, as long as the buyer and seller both approve it in writing beforehand
questions.explanation: The good funds law (C.R.S. 38-35-125) bars disbursement until funds are available for immediate withdrawal, but lets the provider advance a small amount (up to $500) for incidentals like tax certificates and recording fees. Commissions and payoffs must wait for good funds.

questions.stem: Buyer A gets a deed to a Colorado home but doesn't record it. The seller then deeds the same home to Buyer B, who knows nothing about Buyer A's deed and records first. Who generally prevails?
choices: Buyer A, because the first deed delivered always controls
Neither, until a court decides who paid more
Buyer A, as long as A recorded within one year
Buyer B, because Colorado is a race-notice state
questions.explanation: Under Colorado's race-notice statute (C.R.S. 38-35-109), an unrecorded deed isn't valid against a later buyer who records first without notice of it. That's why the closing company records the deed right away.

questions.stem: At a Colorado closing, the title company typically gets which document from the county treasurer to confirm the taxes owed on the property?
choices: A real property transfer declaration
A certificate of taxes due
An improvement location certificate
A status letter
questions.explanation: The certificate of taxes due comes from the county treasurer and shows taxes owed; the contract says who pays for it. The transfer declaration reports the price to the assessor, and a status letter comes from the owners' association.

questions.stem: A Colorado home sells for $360,000. The buyer pays $72,000 down and finances the rest. What is the state documentary fee?
questions.explanation: The documentary fee is one cent per $100 of the full consideration, not just the down payment: $360,000 / 100 = 3,600 x $0.01 = $36.00. $7.20 wrongly uses only the $72,000 down payment.

questions.stem: The buyer takes over the seller's existing loan with a $150,000 balance. How does the assumed loan appear on the closing statement?
choices: Debit buyer, credit seller
Credit buyer only, like a new loan
Debit seller only, like a payoff
Credit buyer, debit seller
questions.explanation: An assumed loan is part of how the buyer pays the price, so the buyer is credited; the seller gets less cash because the buyer is taking over the debt, so the seller is debited. A new loan is buyer-only and a payoff is seller-only.

questions.stem: A Colorado brokerage manages a rental, but the owner, not the firm, will hold the tenant's security deposit. What must the tenant be told?
choices: Nothing, as long as the deposit is no more than two months' rent
In writing, who holds the deposit and how to get it back
Only orally, at move-in, that the owner has the money
That the deposit is nonrefundable because the firm doesn't hold it
questions.explanation: When the owner rather than the firm will hold security deposits, the tenant must be told in writing who holds the deposit and how to get it back.

questions.stem: Unless the management agreement says otherwise, when does a Colorado property management firm generally owe the owner an accounting?
choices: Once a year, with the owner's tax documents
Only when the owner asks for one in writing
Within 30 days after each month ends
At the end of the management agreement
questions.explanation: Owners get regular accountings, generally within 30 days after the end of each month unless the management agreement provides otherwise.

questions.stem: A tenant lived in a Colorado apartment for three years. At move-out the carpet shows ordinary traffic wear, and there's a large burn hole the tenant caused. What may the landlord deduct from the deposit?
choices: A reasonable amount for the burn hole only
The full cost of new carpet throughout the unit
Nothing, because carpet wear is always the landlord's cost
The traffic wear only, since burn damage needs a separate lawsuit
questions.explanation: Deductions must be for actual cause and in reasonable amounts. Damage beyond normal use, like a burn hole, can be deducted, but normal wear and tear never can.

questions.stem: A landlord sells a Colorado rental house with a tenant in place. What does Colorado law require regarding the tenant's security deposit?
choices: The landlord must return it to the tenant on the closing date
The new owner must collect a new deposit from the tenant within 10 days
The deposit is forfeited to the landlord when ownership changes
Within 60 days, transfer it to the new owner and notify the tenant, or return it
questions.explanation: When a rental is sold, the landlord or its agent has 60 days to either transfer the deposit to the new owner and notify the tenant, or return it to the tenant less lawful deductions. That's why the closing statement moves deposits from seller to buyer.

questions.stem: A tenant's guest clogs the plumbing and floods the bathroom, making it unusable. Is the landlord in breach of Colorado's warranty of habitability?
choices: Yes, because the warranty can't be waived
No, because the condition was caused by the tenant's guest
Yes, unless the landlord starts repairs within 96 hours
No, because plumbing problems are never treated as a habitability issue under Colorado law
questions.explanation: Conditions caused by the tenant, household members or guests are not a breach by the landlord. The warranty is nonwaivable, but it covers conditions the landlord is responsible for.

questions.stem: A Colorado farm owner wants to keep the land but sell its irrigation water rights to a city. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Water rights may be sold separately, using the same formalities as a real estate conveyance
Water rights can't be separated from the land they serve, so the city must buy the farm too
Water rights transfer only by a bill of sale, like personal property
Water rights end when the owner stops farming and can't be sold
questions.explanation: A Colorado water right is property in its own right and can be severed and sold separately. It is conveyed with the same formalities as real estate, usually by a recorded deed (shares in a mutual ditch company are the exception).

questions.stem: Under the Colorado residential contract, what must the buyer acknowledge receiving about the home's drinking water?
choices: A water quality test from a certified lab
A water court decree confirming that the seller's water rights are senior to every neighbor's rights
The Seller's Property Disclosure or Source of Water Addendum stating the potable water source
A letter from the State Engineer approving the sale
questions.explanation: The buyer acknowledges receiving either the Seller's Property Disclosure or the Source of Water Addendum disclosing the potable water source, plus a copy of the current well permit if there's a well.

questions.stem: A developer wants a non-exempt well to serve a multi-home subdivision from groundwater connected to a stream. What will the well generally need?
choices: Only a household-use-only permit from the county
An augmentation plan approved by the water court
A riparian rights certificate from the State Engineer
A change in owner name form filed within 60 days
questions.explanation: Pumping tributary groundwater takes water senior users are entitled to, so a non-exempt well generally needs a water-court-approved augmentation plan that replaces those depletions. The change in owner name form is for transferring an existing exempt well.

questions.stem: A title commitment for a Colorado ranch shows that a prior owner reserved the mineral rights. What does this mean for the buyer?
choices: The reservation expires automatically when the ranch sells
The buyer may evict any mineral developer from the surface
The buyer owns the minerals unless the deed says otherwise
The buyer gets the surface; the mineral owner may reasonably use it to develop the minerals
questions.explanation: Severed minerals create a split estate: the buyer owns the surface but not the minerals, and the mineral owner generally may make reasonable use of the surface to develop them. The broker should refer the buyer to the title commitment and legal counsel.

questions.stem: How often does a Colorado county assessor revalue real property?
choices: Every odd-numbered year, based on classification and use on January 1
Every year, based on the property's classification and use as of December 31
Every four years, or sooner whenever the property is sold to a new owner
Only when the owner files a protest
questions.explanation: Colorado reappraises real property every odd-numbered year, based on its classification and use on January 1. Mill levies, by contrast, are set by each taxing authority every year.

questions.stem: A home is in a special taxing district that has issued general obligation debt. Under Colorado law, which statement is correct?
choices: Only the listing broker must disclose the district, and an oral disclosure is enough
No disclosure is required if the district's debt is paid by developers
The contract must include a bold disclosure that owners may face higher mill levies, and the seller has the duty
The buyer must get the county assessor's approval before closing
questions.explanation: Every residential sales contract must contain a bold disclosure that special taxing districts may carry debt and that owners may face higher mill levies. The duty is the seller's, and a buyer who doesn't get it can sue for damages.

questions.stem: A seller's home is in a metropolitan district organized in 2012. Under a 2024 Colorado law, what must the seller give the buyer?
choices: The district's official website, on or with the Seller's Property Disclosure
Copies of every district budget for the past five years
A certificate from the district stating that it has no debt
A copy of the district's service plan, recorded with the deed
questions.explanation: Since 2024, a seller of residential property in a metropolitan district organized on or after January 1, 2000 must give the buyer the district's official website, on the Seller's Property Disclosure or a document delivered with it.

questions.stem: Each seller below lives outside Colorado and signs no exemption affirmation. Which sale requires NO Colorado nonresident withholding?
choices: A $250,000 rental house sold by an Arizona resident
A $95,000 vacant lot sold by a Utah resident
A $180,000 lot sold by an out-of-state corporation with no Colorado place of business
A $400,000 vacation cabin sold by a Texas resident
questions.explanation: No Colorado withholding is required when the sales price is $100,000 or less. The other sales exceed $100,000 and have no exemption, so the closing company withholds the lesser of 2% of the price or the net proceeds.

questions.stem: A landlord owns four single-family rental homes and no other rental units. An applicant for one of the homes wants to use a federal housing choice voucher. Under Colorado law, the landlord:
choices: Must accept the voucher, because source of income is protected
May refuse only if the applicant's credit score is low
Must accept the voucher but may charge a higher deposit
Is not required to accept federal housing choice vouchers for those homes
questions.explanation: Colorado lets a landlord who owns five or fewer single-family rental homes, and no more than five rental units in total, decline federal housing choice vouchers for those homes (C.R.S. 24-34-502(1.7)). The general three-or-fewer-units source-of-income exemption doesn't fit here, but this separate voucher rule does.

questions.stem: In a Colorado public trustee foreclosure of a non-agricultural home, when is the sale generally set?
choices: 30 days after the borrower's first missed payment, once the lender sends a demand letter
110 to 125 days after the notice of election and demand is recorded
215 to 230 days after the Rule 120 hearing
One year after the notice of election and demand is recorded
questions.explanation: For non-agricultural property, C.R.S. 38-38-108 sets the sale 110 to 125 days after the notice of election and demand is recorded. The 215-to-230-day window applies to agricultural property.

questions.stem: What does the highest bidder at a Colorado public trustee foreclosure sale receive at the sale?
choices: A certificate of purchase
A public trustee's confirmation deed
A general warranty deed from the borrower
A notice of election and demand
questions.explanation: The highest bidder gets a certificate of purchase. After the redemption periods for junior lienors run with no redemption, the public trustee issues a confirmation deed to the certificate holder.

questions.stem: A Colorado homeowner who is behind on payments sells her home in a short sale to an investor who won't live there. Which approach fits Colorado practice?
choices: Close without lender approval and let the lender sue for the shortfall
Have the broker assure the seller there will be no tax consequences
Use the standard contract with the Commission-approved Short Sale Addendum and recommend legal and tax advice
Use the Foreclosure Protection Act contract, which is required for every short sale
questions.explanation: A short sale needs the lender's approval to accept less than the payoff. Using the Commission's Short Sale Addendum is part of what keeps a short sale outside the CFPA's equity-purchaser rules, and because of possible tax and deficiency consequences, brokers should recommend legal and tax advice.

questions.stem: A Spanish-speaking homeowner in foreclosure is selling to an investor using the Commission's CFPA contract. What should the broker do about the Homeowner Warning Notice?
choices: Translate it personally to save the seller time
Skip it, since the seller has a broker
Read it aloud in English at closing and have the seller initial each page
Make sure it is translated, without translating it personally
questions.explanation: If the seller's main language isn't English, the Homeowner Warning Notice must be translated, and the broker should not translate it personally.

questions.stem: A duplex closes April 20 with both leases assigned to the buyer. The seller collected April rent totaling $2,400 and holds two $1,500 security deposits. Using a 30-day month with the buyer owning the closing day, what is the correct handling of these items?
choices: Debit seller and credit buyer $3,880; tenants are notified in writing of the transfer
Credit seller and debit buyer $3,880; tenants are notified in writing of the transfer
Debit seller and credit buyer $880; the deposits are refunded to the tenants at closing
Debit seller and credit buyer $1,980; the deposits are prorated like the rent
questions.explanation: Buyer's rent days are April 20-30 = 11: $2,400 / 30 x 11 = $880. Deposits transfer in full, not prorated: $3,000. Total $3,880, debit seller and credit buyer, and the tenants must be notified in writing that their deposits moved to the new owner.

questions.stem: A U.S. citizen who lives in Arizona sells a Colorado rental for $300,000 and signs no exemption affirmation. After the loan payoff and costs, her net proceeds are $4,500. How much must the closing company withhold for Colorado?
choices: $0, because she is a U.S. citizen
questions.explanation: Colorado withholds the lesser of 2% of the price ($6,000) or the seller's net proceeds ($4,500), so $4,500, not the sum of the two. U.S. citizenship matters for FIRPTA, not Colorado withholding, which turns on residency.

cards.back: Real estate = land plus permanent improvements. Real property = real estate plus the bundle of legal rights of ownership.
Possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, and disposition.
By a bill of sale, not a deed.

Method of attachment, Adaptability, Relationship of parties, Intention, Agreement. A written agreement overrides the others; courts treat intention as the key test (some prep courses key method of attachment).
Business equipment a tenant installs. It stays the tenant's personal property and must be removed before the lease ends.
Annual crops planted by labor. They're personal property; a tenant farmer may return to harvest them after the lease ends, if the tenant didn't cause the lease to end.
A right or improvement that runs with the land and passes with the deed, such as an easement appurtenant.
Riparian: owners along rivers and streams. Littoral: owners along lakes and oceans.
Water rights go to the first to put water to beneficial use ("first in time, first in right"). Colorado uses this system.
Describes a parcel by distances and directions from a point of beginning; it must return to the POB. Monuments generally control over distances.
Legal description by reference to a recorded subdivision plat.
6 miles × 6 miles = 36 square miles = 36 sections.
1 mile × 1 mile = 1 square mile = 640 acres.
Section 1: northeast corner of the township. Section 36: southeast corner.

cards.front: Acreage of the N 1/2 of the SW 1/4 of a section
Fee simple determinable vs. condition subsequent
cards.back: "So long as" = determinable, reverts automatically (possibility of reverter). "On condition that" = grantor must act (right of reentry).
A life estate measured by the life of someone other than the life tenant.
Remainder: goes to a named third party when a life estate ends. Reversion: goes back to the grantor or grantor's heirs.
Damage or neglect by a life tenant that lowers the property's value for the future owner. It isn't allowed.
Estate for years, periodic tenancy, tenancy at will, tenancy at sufferance.
Ownership by one person or one entity.
Possession, Interest, Time, Title (PITT).

cards.front: Effect of a joint tenant selling their share
cards.back: The buyer becomes a tenant in common; the remaining owners stay joint tenants with each other.

cards.front: Colorado presumption for conveyance to two or more people
cards.back: Tenancy in common, unless the deed expressly declares a joint tenancy (C.R.S. 38-31-101).

cards.front: Does Colorado recognize tenancy by the entirety?
cards.back: No. C.R.S. 38-31-201: an attempted tenancy by the entirety creates a joint tenancy.

cards.front: Is Colorado a community property state?
cards.back: No. Colorado divides marital property by equitable distribution.
Fee title to the unit plus an undivided interest as tenant in common in the common elements.
Shares in a corporation that owns the building plus a proprietary lease; usually treated as personal property.
Property tax and special assessment liens generally come before all other liens, whatever their recording date.
Appurtenant: has dominant and servient parcels and runs with the land. In gross: benefits a person or company and has no dominant parcel.
Merger, release, abandonment, end of necessity or purpose, and (in some states) non-use of a prescriptive easement.

Open, notorious, continuous, exclusive, hostile (adverse) for the statutory period. Colorado: 18 years (C.R.S. 38-41-101), plus clear and convincing proof (cases filed since July 1, 2008) and a good-faith belief of ownership (title vesting since that date).
Government powers: Police power, Eminent domain, Taxation, Escheat.
Public use and just compensation. The legal process is condemnation.
A suit by an owner seeking compensation when government action has effectively taken or damaged the property.
A use that was legal before the current zoning; it's grandfathered but usually can't be expanded or rebuilt after destruction.
Relief from strict zoning requirements (setback, height) because of a hardship unique to the property.
Allows a use the ordinance permits under conditions, such as a church or school in a residential zone.
Rezoning one parcel inconsistently with the comprehensive plan to benefit one owner; often illegal.
Issued after final inspection; allows a building to be legally occupied.
The more restrictive rule generally governs.
Writing, competent grantor, identifiable grantee, consideration recital, granting clause, legal description, grantor's signature, delivery and acceptance.
General: warrants against defects from any time. Special: only defects arising during the grantor's ownership.
No warranties; conveys whatever interest the grantor has, if any. Used to clear clouds on title.
A later buyer wins only if they had no notice AND recorded first. Colorado's statute (C.R.S. 38-35-109) is race-notice.
Survey and inspection matters: encroachments, boundary disputes, parties in possession, unrecorded easements and mechanic's liens.
Owner's: protects the buyer, usually for the price, lasts while the owner or heirs hold an interest. Lender's: protects the lender for the loan amount.

cards.front: Equity of redemption vs. statutory redemption
cards.back: Equity: pay off and stop foreclosure before the sale. Statutory: buy back after the sale, where state law allows.
Testate: dies with a will (devise). Intestate: dies without a will (descent under state statute); no heirs = escheat.
Value = estimated worth to typical buyers; price = what was actually paid; cost = what it took to build.
Demand (with purchasing power), Utility, Scarcity, Transferability.
A buyer won't pay more than the cost of an equally desirable substitute. Basis of the sales comparison approach.

cards.front: Highest and best use: four tests
cards.back: Legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, maximally productive.
A component is worth what it adds to value, not what it cost.
Regression: best house on a modest street loses value. Progression: modest house among nicer homes gains value.
Value = present worth of expected future benefits. Drives the income approach.
Adjust the comp, never the subject. Comp better → subtract; comp worse → add.
Land value + (cost new − accrued depreciation).
Reproduction = exact replica, same materials. Replacement = same utility, modern materials.
Physical deterioration, functional obsolescence, external (economic) obsolescence.
External (economic) obsolescence — the cause is off the property.
No. Only improvements depreciate.
PGI − vacancy/collection loss = EGI; EGI − operating expenses = NOI; NOI ÷ cap rate = value.
Debt service (mortgage P&I) and the owner's income tax depreciation.
GRM = price ÷ monthly gross rent (1–4 units). GIM = price ÷ annual gross income (larger/commercial).

cards.front: Best approach for a church or fire station
cards.back: Cost approach — special-purpose property with few sales and no rental income.
Weighing the approaches to reach one final value opinion — not a simple average.
CMA/BPO = broker's market estimate. Appraisal = credentialed appraiser's formal opinion. Never call a CMA an appraisal.
Automated valuation model: software estimate from data, no inspection. Weak where sales are sparse.
Note = the debt (promise to pay). Mortgage/deed of trust = pledges property as collateral (lien).

cards.front: Parties to a deed of trust
cards.back: Trustor (borrower), beneficiary (lender), trustee. In Colorado, the trustee is usually the county public trustee.
Mortgagor = borrower (gives the mortgage). Mortgagee = lender.
Lien: borrower holds title, lender has a lien. Title: title conveyed to lender/trustee until paid.
On default, lender can declare the entire balance due.
Lender can call the loan if the property is transferred; blocks unapproved assumption.
Lender must release the lien when the debt is paid in full.
Subordination: lien agrees to rank behind a later lien. Release: frees parcels from a blanket loan as they're paid off.
Assumption: buyer becomes personally liable. Subject to: buyer pays but isn't personally liable.
1% of the loan amount (not the price). Prepaid interest to lower the rate.
Loan ÷ lesser of price or appraised value.
The lender, on a conventional loan with a small down payment (classically LTV above 80%).
Principal, interest, taxes, insurance — the full monthly housing payment.
Housing (front-end) = housing payment ÷ gross monthly income. Total (back-end) = housing + other debts ÷ gross monthly income.
Index = market rate, changes. Margin = lender markup, fixed. Rate = index + margin, limited by caps.
Payments don't cover interest, so unpaid interest is added and the balance grows.
FHA insures (mortgage insurance premiums). VA guarantees (no monthly MI; funding fee; eligibility certificate).
Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy loans. Ginnie Mae (in HUD) guarantees securities of government-backed loans; doesn't buy loans.
Seller keeps legal title until paid; buyer has possession and equitable title.
For older owners with equity; lender pays owner, balance grows; repaid on sale, permanent move-out or death.
No kickbacks, referral fees or unearned fee splits for settlement services on covered loans.
Written disclosure at or before referral; consumer not required to use affiliate; only return on ownership received.
Down payment amount/%, number of payments or term, payment amount, finance charge amount.
Delivered or mailed no later than the 3rd business day after the lender receives the application.
Consumer must receive it at least 3 business days before consummation.

cards.front: Changes that restart the 3-day CD wait
cards.back: APR becomes inaccurate, loan product changes, or a prepayment penalty is added.
Name, income, SSN (for credit report), property address, estimated value, loan amount sought.
Race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, public-assistance income, exercise of consumer credit rights.
3 business days on certain refinances/home-equity loans on a principal residence; not for purchase loans.
1 acre = 43,560 sq ft. 1 section = 640 acres = 1 sq mile.
Part = Whole × Rate; Rate = Part ÷ Whole; Whole = Part ÷ Rate.

cards.front: Price needed for a desired net
cards.back: (Desired net + dollar costs) ÷ (1 − commission rate).
360: every month = 30 days (annual ÷ 360). 365: actual days (annual ÷ 365).

cards.front: Taxes paid in arrears at closing
cards.back: Debit seller, credit buyer for the seller's share.
Income = Rate × Value. Cap rate = NOI ÷ value; value = NOI ÷ cap rate.
1 mill = $1 per $1,000 of assessed value. Tax = assessed value × mills ÷ 1,000.

cards.front: Monthly interest on an amortized loan
cards.back: Balance × annual rate ÷ 12. Payment − interest = principal reduction.
Market value − all loan balances.
Original = current ÷ (1 − loss rate). $180,000 after a 10% loss → $200,000.
Basis = original cost (plus certain acquisition costs). Adjusted basis = basis + capital improvements − depreciation and casualty losses.
Gain = Amount realized (price − selling costs) − Adjusted basis.
No. Only capital improvements (adding value or extending life) increase basis; ordinary repairs don't.

cards.front: Does the mortgage payoff affect taxable gain?
cards.back: No. Gain depends on amount realized and adjusted basis, not the loan balance.
Held one year or less = short-term (ordinary income rates). Held more than one year = long-term (lower rates).
Up to $250,000 single; up to $500,000 married filing jointly.

cards.front: Home-sale exclusion: ownership and use test
cards.back: Owned and lived in as a main home at least 2 of the 5 years before sale. Years needn't be consecutive.

cards.front: How often can the home-sale exclusion be used?
cards.back: Generally not if used on another home within the past 2 years; no lifetime limit.

cards.front: Loss on sale of your own home — deductible?
cards.back: No. Losses on personal-use property aren't deductible.

cards.front: Mortgage interest and property tax deductions
cards.back: Deductible only if the homeowner itemizes; dollar limits/caps are set by Congress and change.
No. Only buildings and other improvements can be depreciated.
27.5 years, straight-line.
39 years, straight-line.
(Cost − land value) ÷ 27.5 (residential rental) or ÷ 39 (nonresidential).
Depreciation lowers basis, increasing gain at sale; the depreciation portion of the gain is taxed under separate rules (often a higher rate). Depreciation defers tax, it doesn't erase it.
Real property held for investment or business use, exchanged for other such real property. Not a primary residence, a personally used vacation home, or property held for sale.
45 days to identify replacement property in writing; 180 days (or return due date incl. extensions, if earlier) to acquire it. Both run from the sale.
Cash, debt relief or other non-like-kind property received in an exchange. Gain is taxable up to the boot.
Holds the exchange proceeds so the investor never controls the cash. The investor's own agent or broker generally can't serve.
At least one payment is received after the year of sale; gain is reported proportionally as payments come in.

cards.front: Federal tax lien vs property tax lien
cards.back: IRS lien is general (all property); property tax lien is specific (one parcel). A property tax lien with priority under local law stays ahead even of an earlier-filed federal tax lien.
Generally fair market value on the date of death.

cards.front: Broker's role on client tax questions
cards.back: Recognize the issue and refer the client to a CPA or tax attorney; don't give tax advice.
Funds released in stages as work is completed and inspected; interest usually paid only on amounts drawn.
The permanent long-term loan that pays off the interim construction loan when the building is finished.
One loan (usually one closing) that funds construction and then converts to a permanent mortgage.
The Appraisal Standards Board of The Appraisal Foundation.
Sets minimum education, experience and exam criteria for appraisers; states license and certify using them.
Trainee → licensed residential → certified residential → certified general (all property types).
Allowed: give comps, ask to correct errors or explain. Prohibited: requesting a target value, tying pay or future work to the value.
Association of Real Estate License Law Officials — an association of license-law regulators. It licenses no one.

cards.front: Five essential elements of a real estate contract
cards.back: Competent parties, offer and acceptance, consideration, legal purpose, and a writing (Statute of Frauds).
Requires contracts for the sale of real property (and, in many states, leases over one year) to be in writing and signed to be enforceable.
Promise for a promise; both parties bound. Example: purchase contract.
Promise for an act; only one party bound. Example: option before exercise.
Express: terms stated in words (oral or written). Implied: created by the parties' conduct.
Executory: obligations remain. Executed: fully performed (e.g., after closing).
No legal effect at all. Examples: illegal purpose; party previously adjudicated incompetent.
Valid until the protected party disaffirms. Examples: minor's contract; fraud, duress, undue influence.
Appears valid but a court won't enforce it — e.g., an oral real estate sales contract or one past the statute of limitations.
Voidable by the minor only; the adult stays bound.
Fraud is intentional deception about a material fact; misrepresentation can be innocent or negligent. Both can make a contract voidable.
Duress: threats or force. Undue influence: abusing a position of trust or control.
Mutual mistake of a material fact can void a contract; a one-sided mistake usually doesn't.
Vague opinion or exaggeration ("best view in town"); not misrepresentation because it isn't a statement of fact.
Something of legal value exchanged — money or a promise. Earnest money isn't required; the promise to pay is consideration.
Rejects and ends the original offer and creates a new offer with roles reversed.

cards.front: When can an offer be revoked?
cards.back: Any time before acceptance is communicated to the offeror, even if it says it will stay open (unless it's an option).
Acceptance, rejection, counteroffer, revocation, expiration, death or incapacity of a party, destruction of the property.
When the unconditional acceptance is communicated (delivered) to the offeror or the offeror's agent.
Acceptance must match the offer exactly; any change makes it a counteroffer.
Present all offers promptly; the seller decides. Don't share terms with other buyers without seller permission.
Give electronic signatures and records the same legal effect as paper when parties agree to transact electronically.
Optionee pays for the right (not obligation) to buy at a set price within a set time; optionor must sell if exercised.
Optionor = owner who grants the option and is bound. Optionee = holder of the right to buy.
Right to match a third-party offer if the owner decides to sell. No set price; owner can't be forced to sell.
Assignment: assignor stays secondarily liable. Novation: new contract/party; original party released.

cards.front: Can a listing agreement be assigned?
cards.back: Generally no without consent — it's a personal service contract with the broker.
Condition that must be satisfied before a party must perform (financing, appraisal, inspection, sale of home).
Makes contract deadlines strict; missing one is a breach.
Addendum: added when the contract is signed. Amendment: changes the contract after formation; all parties sign.
Court order to perform as promised; mainly a buyer's remedy because land is unique.
Damages amount agreed in advance; commonly the earnest money. Must be reasonable, not a penalty.
Money to cover the actual loss caused by a breach.
Cancels the contract and returns parties to their original positions.
Deadline to file suit; after it runs the claim is unenforceable. Length varies by state.
Performance, mutual release, novation, impossibility, operation of law, breach.
The buyer's interest under a signed purchase contract before closing; seller still holds legal title.
Lease with a definite beginning and end; ends automatically, no notice needed.
Renews automatically period to period (e.g., month-to-month) until proper notice.

cards.front: Tenancy at will vs. at sufferance
cards.back: At will: no set term, both consent, ends on notice or death. At sufferance: holdover without landlord consent.
Gross: landlord pays property expenses. Net: tenant pays some or all (triple net = taxes, insurance, maintenance).
Base rent plus a percentage of gross sales, often over a threshold; typical in retail.
Ground: land only, tenant builds. Graduated: scheduled step increases. Index: rent tied to an index such as CPI.
Lease option: tenant may buy. Lease-purchase: tenant agrees to buy.

cards.front: Assignment vs. sublease of a lease
cards.back: Assignment: entire remaining interest; assignee pays landlord. Sublease: part of interest; subtenant pays original tenant.
A fact that would affect a reasonable buyer's decision or the price paid.
Latent: hidden, not found by ordinary inspection — must be disclosed if known. Patent: visible on reasonable inspection.
Property with a psychological stigma (death, crime, illness) but no physical defect. Colorado: not a material fact requiring disclosure (C.R.S. 38-35.5-101).
Most housing built before 1978.
10 days to inspect or do a risk assessment; may be changed by written agreement or waived.
3 years after closing or the start of the lease.
Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home.
EPA: fix the home at 4 pCi/L or higher.
Crumbling asbestos that releases fibers — the dangerous condition. Intact asbestos is often left or encapsulated.
Strict, joint and several, and retroactive; current owners can be liable for past contamination.
Review of past uses and records to identify possible contamination; supports CERCLA defenses.
Protected under the Clean Water Act; filling usually requires an Army Corps of Engineers permit.
FEMA zone (A or V) with 1% annual flood chance; flood insurance required with federally backed or federally regulated loans.

cards.front: Broker response to a suspected hazard
cards.back: Disclose what you observed and recommend an expert inspection.
Client (principal) = represented, owed fiduciary duties. Customer = unrepresented third party, owed honesty and disclosure.
Express (words), implied (conduct), ratification (approval after the fact), estoppel (principal's conduct led others to believe it).
Principal approves, after the fact, an act the agent did without authority.
Principal's words or conduct led a third party to reasonably believe an agency existed, so the principal can't deny it.
No. A broker acting for free can still owe fiduciary duties.

cards.front: Does who pays the commission decide who the agent represents?
cards.back: No. Representation comes from the agency agreement, not the source of the fee.
Authority for one specific act or transaction. Example: listing broker, buyer's broker.
Authority over a range of acts in one business. Example: property manager.
Broad authority to do anything the principal could delegate, e.g., under a general power of attorney.
Broker paid no matter who sells during the term, even the owner.
One broker; owner can sell on their own and owe no commission.
Several brokers; only the procuring cause is paid; owner selling alone pays nobody.
Broker keeps everything above the seller's net figure. Banned in many states; Colorado has no approved form, and secret profits are grounds for discipline.
The broker whose efforts started the unbroken chain of events that produced the sale.
Broker can still earn a fee if the owner sells, after the listing ends, to a buyer the broker introduced during the term.

cards.front: Ways agency ends by operation of law
cards.back: Death or incapacity of either party, destruction or condemnation of property, bankruptcy, change in law.
Agent holds a stake in the property; the principal can't revoke it, and it survives the principal's death.
Survives the principal's incapacity but ends at death.
Obedience, Loyalty, Disclosure, Confidentiality, Accounting, Reasonable care.
Follow only lawful instructions. Refuse illegal (e.g., discriminatory) ones.
Disclosure: tell your client everything material. Confidentiality: keep the client's private info from others.
Honesty, fair dealing, reasonable care, disclosure of known material (latent) defects.
Exaggerated opinion or sales talk ("stunning view"). Not usually actionable.
False statement of fact the licensee should have known was false.
Where allowed: informed, written consent of both parties. Undisclosed dual agency is illegal everywhere. Colorado prohibits dual agency entirely.
Employing broker assigns different licensees in the same firm to buyer and seller, each with full duties to their client.
Assists one or both parties without advocacy; duties set by state statute. Colorado has its own rules (see Colorado module).
Disclose license status and personal interest in writing first; never use a straw buyer.
Race only; NO exemptions; enforced directly in federal court. Revived by Jones v. Mayer (1968).
Race, color, religion, national origin, sex, disability, familial status.

cards.front: When were sex, disability and familial status added?
cards.back: Sex: 1974. Disability and familial status: 1988 amendments.
Child under 18 living with parent/custodian/designee; includes pregnancy and someone gaining custody.

cards.front: Sexual orientation / gender identity under federal FHA
cards.back: Not listed in the Act. HUD's 2021 memo treating them as sex discrimination was withdrawn on Sept. 17, 2025. Colorado law expressly protects them.
Directing buyers/renters toward or away from areas based on a protected class.
Inducing owners to sell by suggesting a protected class is moving in. Also called panic peddling.
Lender refuses or limits loans in an area because of its racial/ethnic makeup.
Owner of max 3 homes, no broker, no discriminatory ads; one non-occupant sale per 24 months.
Owner-occupied building with up to four units living independently.
At least 80% of occupied units have a resident 55+, published policies, age verification. Exempt from familial status only.
Accommodation = change in rules/policies (provider bears cost). Modification = physical change (tenant pays in private housing).
HUD complaint: 1 year. Private lawsuit: 2 years.
Public accommodations and commercial facilities, e.g., brokerage and leasing offices. Not private dwelling units.
Price fixing, group boycotts, market allocation, tie-in arrangements.
Licensed; pay based on sales output; written agreement saying not an employee for tax purposes.
Scrub every 31 days; call 8 a.m.-9 p.m.; EBR 18 months after transaction / 3 months after inquiry; honor company DNC 5 years.
Honor within 10 business days; opt-out must work 30 days after sending; include physical postal address.
Commingling: mixing client and broker funds. Conversion: using client funds for yourself.

cards.front: What unlicensed assistants may NOT do
cards.back: Show property, negotiate, discuss terms, host open houses alone, or be paid per closing for licensed activity.
Best net operating income for the owner, and preserving/increasing property value.
Percentage of gross rents collected (sometimes plus leasing fees).
Preventive: prevent problems (best protects value). Corrective: fix what's broken.
Avoid, Control, Transfer (insurance), Retain.
Actual: tenant removed by legal process. Constructive: landlord makes unit unusable and tenant moves out.
Tenant's right to use the premises without interference by the landlord or someone with superior title.
Usually means rents are too high (if the property is in good condition).
Gross: tenant pays fixed rent; landlord pays taxes, insurance, maintenance. Net: tenant pays rent plus some or all of those expenses.
Tenant pays base rent plus property taxes, insurance and maintenance. Landlord gets the most predictable net income.
Tenant pays rent plus (typically) taxes and insurance; exact split depends on the lease language.
Annual base rent ÷ percentage rate. Percentage rent is paid only on gross sales above the breakpoint.
A negotiated sales threshold for percentage rent that differs from the natural breakpoint.

cards.front: Percentage lease: $24,000/yr base, 4% over natural breakpoint, $750,000 sales — total rent?
Pro rata share in a multi-tenant building
cards.back: Tenant's square footage ÷ building's square footage; used to allocate taxes, insurance and CAM.
Rent increases by set amounts on a set schedule.
Rent adjusts according to an outside index, such as the Consumer Price Index.
Lease of land only, usually long-term (often 50–99 years); tenant builds and improvements typically revert to the landowner at the end.
Common area maintenance: tenants' shares of costs for shared areas (parking, landscaping, lobbies), usually reconciled yearly.
Landlord's contribution (often $ per sq ft) toward customizing the space; tenant pays costs above it.
Summary of proposed lease or sale terms before the full contract; usually non-binding on the main deal.

cards.front: Who sets commission splits between cooperating commercial brokers?
cards.back: The brokers and parties by agreement — never law, an association or the MLS.
Sale of an operating business (equipment, inventory, goodwill, lease); mostly personal property, transferred by bill of sale.
Transfer of a major part of a business's inventory/equipment outside the ordinary course; some states still require notice to creditors or tax authorities.

cards.front: Oil and gas lease: lessor vs. lessee
cards.back: Lessor = mineral owner granting drilling rights. Lessee = oil company receiving them.
Bonus: one-time payment at signing, kept regardless. Royalty: lessor's fractional share of actual production, free of production costs.
Payment that keeps an oil and gas lease alive during the primary term when drilling hasn't begun.
Lease continues beyond the primary term as long as oil or gas is produced in paying quantities.
Recorded, usually permanent limit on development, held by a land trust or agency; owner keeps title and can usually keep farming.

cards.front: Is the MLS a government agency?
cards.back: No. It's a private broker cooperation system; membership rules vary by MLS.
Internet Data Exchange: lets MLS participants display other participants' listings on their websites, with listing-firm attribution and no alterations.

cards.front: Can a seller keep a listing off the internet?
cards.back: Yes. Seller can direct the listing broker to withhold the listing (or address) from internet display under typical MLS rules.

cards.front: Digital ad targeting and fair housing
cards.back: Choosing audiences or locations so a protected class doesn't see housing ads can violate the Fair Housing Act, even with neutral wording.
E-SIGN: federal law (2000). UETA: uniform state law (1999), applies when parties agree to deal electronically. Both give e-signatures legal effect.
Wills/testamentary trusts, family law, court documents, utility shut-off notices, and default/foreclosure/eviction notices for a primary residence.

cards.front: Wire instructions arrive or change by email — what to do?
cards.back: Verify by phone using an independently known number. If money was sent, call the bank for a recall at once and file with IC3.
Take stock, scale down, lock it, pitch it, plan ahead.
Meet new prospects at the office, copy ID, share your itinerary, use a distress code word, know your exits — apply rules to everyone equally.

cards.front: Colorado Real Estate Commission: how many members?
cards.back: 5, appointed by the governor.
3 brokers (5+ years Colorado experience; one with property management experience) and 2 public members.
3 years.

cards.front: Who removes a commissioner, and why?
cards.back: The governor, for misconduct, neglect of duty, or incompetence.

cards.front: Division of Real Estate vs. Commission
cards.back: Division = staff, investigations, audits, enforcement. Commission = rules, approved forms, final decisions on discipline.
$2,500 per separate offense.

cards.front: Disciplinary actions available to the Commission
cards.back: Fine, censure, probation, suspension, revocation; letter of admonition; license denial.

cards.front: Letter of admonition: how to contest it

Landlord generally needs cause to evict or refuse to renew a tenant who has lived there 12+ months; no-fault grounds need ~90 days' notice. Check current law.
Prior appropriation: first in time, first in right.
With the same formalities as real estate, usually by recorded deed; ditch company shares by stock assignment.
Buyer acknowledges Seller's Property Disclosure or Source of Water Addendum and, if a well, the current well permit.

cards.front: Who files the well change-in-ownership form?
cards.back: Buyer completes it; closing company submits it to Division of Water Resources within 60 days after closing.
Water-court-approved plan replacing a well's stream depletions so senior rights aren't injured.
Actual value x assessment rate = assessed value; assessed value x mill levy (mills/1,000) = tax.
Bold notice in every residential contract: districts may have debt and raise mill levies; seller's duty.
Seller gives buyer the district's official website (districts organized on/after Jan 1, 2000).
FIRPTA: foreign-person sellers (IRS). Colorado: nonresident sellers (Dept. of Revenue).
Creed, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, marital status, ancestry, veteran/military status, source of income.

cards.front: Deadline to file a housing charge with the CCRD
cards.back: Within one year of the alleged discriminatory act.
The county public trustee, under a deed of trust (non-judicial).
110–125 days after the notice of election and demand is recorded.
Notice of intent to cure 15+ calendar days before sale; pay by noon the day before sale.
Junior lienors only; owner has no post-sale redemption. Intent to redeem within 8 business days.
Protects homeowners in foreclosure from equity-stripping by foreclosure consultants and equity purchasers.

cards.front: Is a broker a foreclosure consultant?
cards.back: Not while acting within the license; but an investor-broker can be an equity purchaser.
Can't be collected until every promised service is fully performed.
Until midnight of the 3rd business day after signing or noon the day before the sale, whichever is first.

cards.front: When can't the CFPA contract be used?
cards.back: Seller leaseback, seller repurchase right, or buyer assuming the loan — an attorney must draft.

cards.front: On a six-column settlement worksheet, what are the three column pairs?
cards.back: Seller debit/credit, buyer debit/credit, and broker (cash) debit/credit.

cards.front: In the broker (cash) column, what does a debit mean? A credit?
cards.back: Debit = money received into the closing. Credit = money paid out.

cards.front: What is a double entry on a closing worksheet?
cards.back: An item between buyer and seller: one is debited and the other credited the same amount, usually with no cash entry.

cards.front: What is a single entry on a closing worksheet?
cards.back: An item between one party and an outsider (lender, county, title company, brokerage); it hits that party's column and the cash column.
Buyer credit; cash debit (received). Never a seller entry.
Buyer credit; cash debit. The seller's side is not affected.

cards.front: Payoff of the seller's loan: worksheet entries?
cards.back: Seller debit; cash credit (paid to the seller's lender).
Debit seller, credit buyer. No cash moves.
Debit seller, credit buyer. The seller takes a note instead of cash; no cash entry.

cards.front: Accrued interest on an assumed loan (paid in arrears)?
cards.back: Debit seller, credit buyer for the seller's days; the buyer's next payment covers them.

cards.front: Lender escrow reserve that transfers with an assumed loan?
cards.back: Credit seller, debit buyer (the seller funded it; the buyer gets it).

cards.front: Unpaid current-year Colorado property taxes at closing?
cards.back: Seller's share: debit seller, credit buyer. Colorado taxes are paid in arrears.

cards.front: Unpaid prior-year Colorado taxes at closing?
cards.back: Seller debit for the full amount, paid out to the county treasurer. Not prorated.

cards.front: Rent the seller collected for days after closing?
cards.back: Debit seller, credit buyer for the buyer's days.

cards.front: Tenant security deposits when leases are assigned?
cards.back: Debit seller, credit buyer for the full amount. Not prorated.

cards.front: Seller concession toward the buyer's closing costs?
cards.back: Debit seller, credit buyer.

cards.front: Who pays the owner's title policy if neither box is checked in the Colorado contract?
cards.back: The seller (who also selects the title company).

cards.front: Colorado documentary fee: rate and worksheet entry?
cards.back: $0.01 per $100 of consideration (none at $500 or less), on the full price. The contract doesn't assign it: debit whichever party the problem says pays, and credit cash.

cards.front: How is the balance due to the seller entered?
cards.back: Seller debit (to balance the seller columns) and cash credit (paid out).

cards.front: How is the balance due from the buyer entered?
cards.back: Buyer credit (to balance the buyer columns) and cash debit (received).

cards.front: Quick formula: seller's cash at closing?
cards.back: Seller credits − seller debits.

cards.front: Quick formula: buyer's cash to close?
cards.back: Buyer debits − buyer credits.

cards.front: Cash column won't balance but both party pairs do. Likely cause?
cards.back: A single-entry item is missing its cash entry (or a cash entry is missing its party entry).

cards.front: Does a lender's Closing Disclosure satisfy the Colorado broker's closing statement duty?
cards.back: No. The broker who works with a party must still see that the party gets an accurate, complete closing statement signed by the broker.

glossary.definition: Giving up a right or use on purpose, shown by conduct and not just by non-use. It can end an easement or a nonconforming use.
Federal rule that a lender must make a reasonable, good-faith determination that a borrower can repay most residential mortgage loans.
A condensed history of all recorded documents affecting a property, usually reviewed by an attorney.
Loan provision letting the lender declare the entire balance due on default.
The offeree's unconditional agreement to the exact terms of an offer, communicated to the offeror.
A non-breaching party's choice to simply let a breach go and not pursue any remedy.
Acquiring title to property that is added to or left on land you own, such as trade fixtures a tenant leaves behind after the lease ends.
The fiduciary duty to account for and safeguard all money and property entrusted to the agent, without commingling or converting it.

A brokerage firm's written policies describing the checks and balances it uses over the people who handle trust money, such as who may sign, deposit and reconcile. Colorado firms must keep them with their trust account records.
The slow addition of land by water depositing soil along a shore or riverbank. The added land belongs to the owner of the land it attaches to.
A formal declaration before a notary or other officer that a signature is genuine and voluntary. Most states require it before a deed can be recorded.
A unit of land area equal to 43,560 square feet.

License status that lets a broker do work requiring a license. In Colorado it requires current errors and omissions insurance and an employing broker (or independent status); without them the license is Inactive.

Avoid, Control, Transfer, Retain. A memory aid for the four ways a property manager handles risk. Transfer usually means shifting the risk to an insurer; retain means accepting it, often through a deductible or reserve.
Removal of a tenant by the landlord through legal process.

Knowing about something directly, as opposed to being treated as knowing it because you should have. The Commission can discipline an employing broker who had actual knowledge of an employee's violation.
What a person actually knows, from seeing, hearing, or reading it.
The assessor's market-based value of property for property tax purposes.

Annual Commission Update. The update course the Colorado Real Estate Commission issues every year, which every active broker must complete. Each year's version counts toward the continuing-education hours needed to renew, and a missed year can't be made up later.
Latin for "according to value." Ad valorem property taxes are based on a property's value.

Americans with Disabilities Act. A 1990 federal civil-rights law; its Title III requires public accommodations and commercial facilities to be accessible to people with disabilities. Private homes generally fall under the Fair Housing Act instead, but brokers who handle commercial property or run an office must consider the ADA.
Additional material attached to and made part of a contract when it is signed.
The section of a Commission form where negotiated, transaction-specific terms are written. This language is not Commission-approved and must not amount to the broker practicing law.
A loan whose interest rate changes periodically based on an index plus a margin, within caps.
Basis increased by capital improvements and reduced by depreciation and casualty losses; subtracted from the amount realized to find gain.
A fair housing complaint filed with HUD within one year of the discriminatory act; HUD investigates and tries conciliation.
A judge who conducts formal disciplinary and license-denial hearings for the Commission under the state Administrative Procedure Act.
A fact a reasonable person would consider significant that works against a party's interest. Brokers must disclose those they actually know.
Gaining title to another's land by open, notorious, continuous, exclusive, and hostile possession for the statutory period.

Affiliated business arrangement. Under RESPA, a setup in which a broker or brokerage has an ownership interest in a settlement service provider, such as a title or mortgage company, and refers clients to it. It is legal only if the relationship is disclosed in writing, the client isn't required to use that provider, and the only return is from ownership, not per-referral payments.
A situation where a broker or firm has an ownership interest in a settlement service provider it refers business to; requires disclosure to consumers and the Commission.
A relationship in which one person (the agent) is authorized to act for another (the principal) in dealings with third parties.
Agency found when a principal's words or conduct led a third party to reasonably believe someone was their agent.
An agency in which the agent also has an ownership or financial stake in the property; the principal can't revoke it, and it doesn't end at the principal's death.
A person or firm authorized to act on behalf of a principal.
The Commission form, signed by both parties, used to change deadlines or other terms of a signed contract.
A Commission form, new for 2026, that brings back a contract that has already terminated. The parties state the termination date, ratify the contract and set new deadlines.
Use of land for farming or ranching, which often qualifies it for a lower property tax classification.
Any transfer of title to property, whether voluntary (deed or will) or involuntary.
Loan provision letting the lender call the loan due if the property is sold or transferred.

Administrative law judge. A judge who conducts formal hearings in contested license-denial and disciplinary cases. In Colorado the ALJ hears the case and issues an initial decision, the Real Estate Commission makes the final decision, and the Court of Appeals reviews it.
A negotiated later date for delivering earnest money, instead of delivering it with the contract.
A change to the terms of an existing contract, signed by all parties after the contract is formed.
Federal disability law; Title III requires public accommodations and commercial facilities to be accessible.
Paying down a loan with regular payments of principal and interest so the balance reaches zero by the end of the term.
The sale price minus selling expenses such as commission and seller-paid closing costs.
The 4-hour course the Commission issues each year that every active broker must complete; three versions count for 12 of the 24 CE hours per cycle.
The yearly cost of credit, including interest and certain finance charges such as points.
Appraisal principle: value is the present worth of the future benefits a property is expected to produce. It underlies the income approach.
Federal laws, mainly the Sherman Act, that prohibit agreements restraining competition.
A formal, unbiased opinion of value prepared by a state-licensed or certified appraiser.
The contract deadline by which the appraisal must be received.

The contract deadline by which the buyer may terminate or object if the appraisal wasn't received by the Appraisal Deadline or comes in below the purchase price. If the buyer does nothing, that right is gone.
The contract deadline for resolving a buyer's appraisal objection. If it isn't resolved in writing by then, the contract terminates unless the buyer withdraws the objection in writing first.
The board of The Appraisal Foundation that writes and interprets USPAP.
The board of The Appraisal Foundation that sets minimum education, experience and exam criteria for appraiser credentials.
Entry-level appraiser credential; the trainee may appraise only under the supervision of a certified appraiser.
An increase in a property's value over time. New value = original value × (1 + rate).
A right or improvement that belongs to the land and passes with it on transfer, such as an easement appurtenant.
