Annual percentage rate. The yearly cost of a loan expressed as a percentage, including interest plus certain finance charges such as points and some fees. TILA requires it to be disclosed so borrowers can compare loans, and it is usually higher than the note's interest rate.

Appraiser Qualifications Board. The board of The Appraisal Foundation that sets minimum education, experience and exam criteria for appraiser credentials. States do the actual licensing and certifying of appraisers.

Association of Real Estate License Law Officials. An international association of government agencies that regulate real estate licensees. It supports regulators and promotes consistent license laws but does not license anyone itself.
aliases: Association of Real Estate License Law Officials

glossary.definition: Adjustable-rate mortgage. A loan whose interest rate changes periodically to the current index plus a fixed margin, limited by rate caps. Exam questions often ask you to compute the new rate as index plus margin, then apply the caps.
A negotiated sales figure, higher or lower than the natural breakpoint, above which a percentage lease tenant starts paying percentage rent.
Appraisal Standards Board. The board of The Appraisal Foundation that writes and interprets USPAP, the standards appraisers must follow.
A fibrous mineral once used in building materials that is hazardous when friable (crumbling).
Actual value times the assessment rate; the value the mill levy is applied to.
Percentage set by law that converts actual value into assessed value.
Owners' shares of a common interest community's common expenses, allocated by the declaration and secured by a statutory lien.
Transfer of a party's contract rights (and usually duties) to another; the assignor stays secondarily liable.
A Commission optional form a landlord-seller uses to transfer existing leases and security deposits to the buyer at closing. The buyer assumes the landlord's obligations.
A Colorado broker working under the supervision of an employing broker; the level every new licensee starts at.
The owners' association's governing documents, insurance list, assessments, financial records and construction-defect notices that the seller provides to the buyer.
The contract deadline by which the seller, at the seller's expense, delivers the association documents (governing documents, financials, minutes and similar records) to the buyer.

The contract deadline by which the buyer may terminate if the association documents are unsatisfactory, in the buyer's sole subjective discretion. If the documents arrive late, the buyer has 10 days after receipt (and no later than closing).
A Commission deed of trust version under which a transfer of the property doesn't let the lender call the loan due, so the loan can be assumed.
An attorney's written opinion, based on reviewing an abstract or the public records, about who holds title and what defects exist.

A Division review of a brokerage firm's trust accounts, records, and disclosures to check compliance with the license law and Commission rules. Firms can be picked randomly, under a stipulation, or after a complaint or investigation.
Water-court-approved plan that replaces depletions from well pumping so senior water rights aren't injured.
A computer model that estimates value from sales and public-record data without an inspection.

Automated valuation model. Software that estimates a property's value from sales and public-record data without anyone inspecting the property. Lenders use it for quick screening; it is not an appraisal.
The housing payment plus all other monthly debt payments, divided by gross monthly income.
An offer accepted subject to an existing contract failing; it moves into first position only if the earlier deal falls through.
The buyer's debits minus credits: the cash the buyer must bring to closing.
The seller's credits minus debits: the cash the seller receives at closing.
A large lump sum due at the end of a partially amortized or interest-only loan.
A deed that implies the grantor holds title but gives no express warranties against encumbrances.
A main east–west line in the rectangular survey system that crosses a principal meridian; township tiers are numbered north and south of it.
A property owner's starting tax investment, usually the purchase price plus certain acquisition costs.

Business email compromise. A scam in which criminals hack or impersonate a legitimate email account, often a broker's or title company's, to send fake wiring instructions. Brokers should warn clients to confirm wire instructions by phone using a known number.
The person who receives the benefit of property held in a trust.
A contract in which each party exchanges a promise and both are obligated.
A written document that transfers ownership of personal property, such as a business's equipment and inventory.
One loan secured by several parcels, usually with a release clause so individual parcels can be released as they are paid down or sold.
Inducing owners to sell by suggesting that members of a protected class are moving into the area.
A local board, also called a zoning board of appeals, that hears variance requests and appeals of zoning decisions.
In an oil and gas lease, the one-time payment made to the mineral owner when the lease is signed.
Cash, debt relief or other non-like-kind property received in an exchange; gain is taxable up to the amount of boot.
Broker price opinion. A broker's estimate of a property's value, often ordered by a lender or asset manager. It is not an appraisal and can't be presented as one.
Failure to perform a contract promise without legal excuse.
The gross sales level above which percentage rent is owed; the natural breakpoint equals annual base rent divided by the percentage rate.
A short-term loan that lets a buyer use equity in a current home to buy a new one before the first sells.

The only kind of real estate license Colorado issues; anyone who performs real estate brokerage activities for others for compensation must hold one. Colorado has no salesperson license: brokers differ only by level (associate, independent, or employing broker).
A broker's estimate of value, often ordered by a lender or asset manager; it is not an appraisal.

The written statement of the broker's relationship with a party, required before confidential information is discussed. It is made in a signed engagement contract or on a Commission brokerage disclosure form (to buyer, tenant, seller or landlord).
The Commission's Brokerage Duties Addendum to Property Management Agreement. It attaches to an attorney-drafted management agreement and sets out the brokerage relationship and duties.
aliases: Brokerage Duties Addendum to Property Management Agreement

glossary.definition: The commission or fee paid to a brokerage for its services, as set by the listing or buyer agreement and the contract. On a closing statement it is a debit to the party paying it.
A strip of land, such as a park or a light-use district, that separates incompatible uses like homes and heavy industry.
Local standards for construction, plumbing, electrical, and fire safety, enforced through permits and inspections.
Permission from the local building department to construct or alter a building, which lets the department enforce building codes through inspections.
A transfer of a major part of a business's inventory or equipment outside the ordinary course of business, which in some states triggers notice requirements.
The set of legal rights that come with owning real property: possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, and disposition.
A scam in which criminals hack or imitate a legitimate email account to trick recipients into sending money or information.
Insurance that replaces lost rent or income while damage to the property is being repaired.
The sale or lease of an operating business, including its assets, inventory and goodwill.
An upfront payment to the lender, often by a seller or builder, that lowers the borrower's interest rate, usually for the first years of the loan.
A relationship in which the broker represents the buyer as a client.
A single agent who represents only the buyer. In leasing, the tenant's agent plays the same role.
The association's rules for running itself: board, elections, officers and meetings.
Colorado Revised Statutes. The codified laws of Colorado, cited by title, article and section (for example, C.R.S. 38-35-109). The real estate license law is in Title 12, Article 10.
A 365-day year using the actual number of days in each month for prorations; daily rate = annual amount ÷ 365.

Common area maintenance. The costs of running and maintaining shared areas of a multi-tenant commercial property, such as parking lots and lobbies. Leases usually pass them through to tenants by their pro rata share of the space.

Controlling the Assault of Non-Solicited Pornography And Marketing Act. The 2003 federal law governing commercial email. Marketing emails must have accurate headers and subject lines, identify themselves as ads, include a valid postal address and offer a working opt-out that is honored promptly.
Federal law governing commercial email, requiring accurate headers, a postal address and a working opt-out.
The legal ability to enter a contract: being of legal age and mentally competent.
A budget that plans for large replacements and improvements, such as a new roof, HVAC system or parking lot.
Profit from selling a capital asset; long-term if held more than one year, short-term if held one year or less.
Additions or upgrades that add value, prolong useful life or adapt property to new uses; they increase basis, unlike ordinary repairs.
The rate used to convert net operating income into value: value = NOI ÷ cap rate.

An alarm Colorado requires in a home that has a fuel-fired heater or appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage, plus a bedroom: an operational alarm within 15 feet of each bedroom entrance (or where the building code requires).
"Let the buyer beware" — the old rule that buyers must discover defects themselves.

Colorado Bureau of Investigation. Colorado's state investigative agency, which processes the fingerprint background checks required of broker license applicants. Fingerprints must be submitted before applying for a license.

Comp Better, Subtract. A memory aid for sales comparison adjustments: when a comparable property is better than the subject, subtract the value of the difference from the comp's price. You always adjust the comp, never the subject.

Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Residential). The Colorado Commission-approved purchase contract for single-family homes, condos and townhomes. It is the form the exam's Colorado contract questions are built around.

Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Income-Residential). The Colorado Commission-approved purchase contract for income-producing residential property such as rentals. It adds provisions for leases, rent rolls, tenant estoppel statements and security deposits.

Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Commercial). The Colorado Commission-approved purchase contract for office, retail, industrial and mixed-use property. It adds commercial due-diligence items such as environmental assessments, ADA review and estoppels.
Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Land). The Colorado Commission-approved purchase contract for vacant or rural land. It addresses items such as growing crops, water rights and mineral rights.

Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Residential) (Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act). The Colorado Commission-approved contract for buying an owner-occupied home in foreclosure when the buyer won't live there. It includes the terms the Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act requires to protect the homeowner from equity stripping.

Covenants, conditions and restrictions. The private restrictions recorded for a subdivision, condominium or other planned community that bind every owner, covering things like architecture, fences, pets and rentals. An HOA usually enforces them, and where they are stricter than zoning, the stricter rule controls.

Colorado Common Interest Ownership Act. The Colorado statute (C.R.S. 38-33.3) governing common interest communities such as condos, townhomes and HOA subdivisions and their associations. It sets rules on governing documents, assessments, records and owner rights, with only some sections applying to communities created before July 1, 1992.

Code of Colorado Regulations. The official compilation of Colorado agency rules. The Real Estate Commission's rules for brokers appear at 4 CCR 725-1 and have the force of law, so violating one is grounds for discipline.

Colorado Civil Rights Division. The Colorado agency, within the Department of Regulatory Agencies, that investigates discrimination complaints, including housing discrimination under Colorado's fair housing law. Cases may go on to the Colorado Civil Rights Commission.

Closing Disclosure. The TRID form showing a borrower's final loan terms and closing costs, which the borrower must receive at least three business days before closing. Only an APR that becomes inaccurate, a change in loan product or an added prepayment penalty restarts that waiting period.

Continuing education. The coursework a licensed broker must complete during each license cycle to renew. In Colorado it includes the Annual Commission Update course plus Commission-approved electives.
A formal public reprimand imposed as discipline.

Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act. The federal Superfund law for cleaning up hazardous-waste sites. Liability is strict, joint and several, and retroactive, so current and past owners can be liable even if they didn't cause the contamination, which is why buyers order Phase I environmental assessments.
aliases: Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act

glossary.definition: A document the building department issues after a building passes final inspection, allowing people to legally occupy it.
Document given to the winning bidder at a public trustee sale, later exchanged for a confirmation deed.

A certificate from the county treasurer showing any unpaid property taxes, special assessments and tax liens on a property. The title company usually orders one for closing, and the contract says who pays for it.
The state-issued title document for a manufactured home that hasn't been converted to real property. It transfers ownership instead of a deed.
Highest appraiser credential, allowed to appraise all types of real property, including commercial and income property.
Appraiser credential for 1–4 unit residential properties regardless of value or complexity.

Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act. The Colorado law (C.R.S. 6-1-1101 et seq.) protecting homeowners in foreclosure from foreclosure consultants and equity purchasers who might strip their equity. Brokers dealing with distressed sellers must know when it applies and use the matching Commission contract.

Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. The federal agency that writes and enforces consumer-finance rules, including TILA/Regulation Z, RESPA and the TRID disclosures. It also administers the Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act.
Code of Federal Regulations. The official compilation of federal agency rules, cited by title and section. For example, HUD's fair housing advertising rule appears in Title 24 of the CFR.
The recorded history of conveyances from the original source of title to the current owner.

The Colorado Division of Water Resources form that records a new owner of a well. On a residential sale with an exempt household well, the buyer completes it and the closing company files it within 60 days after closing.
Commission-approved disclosure given when a broker moves from single agent for one party to transaction-broker for both, no later than when the consumer signs the contract.

Comp Inferior, Add. A memory aid for sales comparison adjustments: when a comparable property is worse than the subject, add the value of the difference to the comp's price. It pairs with CBS (Comp Better, Subtract).

Common interest community. Real estate where owning a unit or lot obligates the owner to pay for common elements or other units' expenses, such as condominiums, townhome communities and HOA subdivisions. In Colorado, CCIOA governs them.
Federal law prohibiting all racial discrimination in property transactions, with no exemptions.
A category of criminal offense under Colorado law. Acting as a real estate broker without a license, or while a license is suspended or revoked, is a class 2 misdemeanor.
A higher standard of proof than "more likely than not," requiring evidence that makes a claim highly probable. Colorado adverse possession claimants must meet it.
Common term for a party who has engaged the broker as a single agent or transaction-broker.
The event at which the buyer pays, the seller delivers the deed, liens are paid off, the new loan is funded, and documents are recorded. Also called settlement.
The title company or other settlement provider that prepares closing figures, collects and disburses funds, and records documents.
Federal TRID form giving a borrower final loan terms and closing costs, for most consumer mortgage loans.
The charge the closing company (usually a title company) makes for conducting the closing. Under the Colorado contract the parties choose whether the buyer, the seller or both split it.
The Commission form signed by buyer, seller and closing company that engages the closing company to prepare documents, close and disburse funds.
An itemized accounting of each party's debits and credits at closing; Colorado requires brokers to ensure parties receive an accurate one signed by the broker.
A claim or document that casts doubt on title, such as an unreleased lien or a possible heir's claim.

Comparative market analysis. A broker's estimate of a property's likely selling price based on recent sales, active listings and expired listings of similar properties. It helps set a list price or an offer but is not an appraisal.
Cooperation between two brokerages on one transaction, with the commission split set by agreement.
Two brokers sharing a listing. Partnering or co-listing with a qualified broker is one acceptable way to handle a task you lack the competency to do alone.
A written amendment to a will.
An insurance provision requiring the owner to insure for at least a stated percentage of the property's value to collect full payment on a loss.
Property pledged to secure a loan. In a mortgage loan it is the real estate, and its value is supported by the appraisal.
State agency that investigates discrimination complaints, including housing.

C.R.S. 38-33.3, the statute governing Colorado common interest communities and their associations. It applies to communities created on or after July 1, 1992, and only listed sections apply to older ones.
Colorado's intermediate appellate court. A final Commission order in a disciplinary case or license denial is reviewed there, not in a district court.
Colorado's housing discrimination law (C.R.S. 24-34-501 et seq.), covering more protected classes than federal law.
Law (C.R.S. 6-1-1101 et seq.) protecting homeowners in foreclosure from foreclosure consultants and equity purchasers.

Colorado's rule that when a nonresident seller sells Colorado real estate for more than $100,000, the closing company withholds the lesser of 2% of the price or the seller's net proceeds and sends it to the Department of Revenue. It is a prepayment of the seller's Colorado income tax, with exceptions such as a former principal residence.
The five-member, governor-appointed board that makes rules for Colorado brokers, approves standard forms, and decides disciplinary cases.
Mixing a broker's or firm's own money with money belonging to others. Prohibited.
A compensation model in which the firm keeps an agreed share of each commission and pays the rest to the broker.
A standard contract or form promulgated by the Commission; brokers must use it when one exists and fits the transaction.
Costs of operating and maintaining shared areas of a multi-tenant property, passed through to tenants by their pro rata shares.
Real estate where owning a unit or lot obligates the owner to pay for common elements or other units' expenses. Examples are condos, townhome communities and HOA subdivisions.

The bold-type statement C.R.S. 38-35.7-102 requires in contracts for residential property in a CIC. It covers membership, assessments, liens, architectural approval and the buyer's need to investigate.
A system in some states under which property acquired during marriage is owned equally by both spouses. Colorado is not a community property state.
A firm's own list of people who've asked not to be called; requests must be honored within a reasonable time and kept for five years.
Recently sold properties similar to the subject, used in the sales comparison approach and adjusted toward the subject.
A broker's estimate of a property's likely price based on recent sales, listings and expired listings of similar properties.
Money a court awards to cover the actual loss caused by a breach of contract.
Having the experience, training and knowledge needed for a particular brokerage task, and keeping up with the laws that apply to it.
An allegation filed with the Division that a licensee violated the license law or Commission rules. The licensee must respond in writing by the deadline, and complaint files are closed to the public.
A local government's long-range plan for growth and land use, carried out through zoning and other regulations. Also called a master plan.
Hiding or staying silent about a material fact when there's a duty to disclose it; it can count as misrepresentation.
A deed restriction that, if broken, may let the grantor reclaim title. Courts prefer to treat restrictions as covenants to avoid this forfeiture.
A contingency that makes the purchase depend on the buyer selling another property named in the contract. The buyer must terminate by the Conditional Sale Deadline or lose that right.
Permission for a use the zoning ordinance allows only under specified conditions, such as a church in a residential zone.
Ownership of an individual unit in fee simple plus an undivided interest in common elements shared with other owners.
The fiduciary duty to keep the client's private information, such as motivation or bottom-line price, secret, even after the agency ends.
The deed the public trustee issues to the holder of the certificate of purchase after all redemption periods end without redemption. It transfers title to the foreclosed property.
A real or apparent personal or professional interest that could affect a broker's duties to a client; must be disclosed in writing.
A conventional loan that meets Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac guidelines, including the loan-size limit, so it can be sold to them.
Appraisal principle: value is maximized when a property is reasonably similar in style, size and quality to the others around it.
A recorded, usually permanent restriction on development that the owner grants to a land trust or government agency while keeping ownership.
A fiduciary deed from a court-appointed conservator conveying a protected person's property, usually with limited warranties.
Something of legal value — money, property, or a promise — exchanged by each party to a contract.
A legal claim against a builder or developer over defects in the design or construction of the property. Notices of such actions from the past six months are part of the association documents.
A short-term interim loan that funds building improvements, paid out in draws as work is completed.
A single loan, usually with one closing, that funds construction and then converts to a permanent mortgage.
A landlord's act or neglect that makes premises unusable, allowing the tenant to leave and end the lease.
Notice the law presumes everyone has, from public records or from inspecting the property.
A loan to an individual mainly for personal, family or household purposes. Federal and state lending laws can apply, so the Commission forms tell the parties to consult legal counsel.
A condition that must be met before a party is obligated to perform under a contract.

glossary.term: Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Commercial)
glossary.definition: The Commission's sales contract (CBS3) for office, retail, industrial and mixed-use property. It adds commercial due diligence such as environmental (Phase I/II) review and an ADA evaluation.

glossary.term: Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Income-Residential)
glossary.definition: The Commission's sales contract (CBS2) for residential property bought for income, from 1–4 units up to apartment buildings. It adds tenant items such as leases, the rent roll, tenant estoppel statements and security deposits.

glossary.term: Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Land)
glossary.definition: The Commission's sales contract (CBS4) for vacant, rural or agricultural land. It focuses on water rights, mineral rights and growing crops. Not to be confused with a "land contract" (contract for deed).

glossary.term: Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Residential)
glossary.definition: The Commission's standard residential sales contract (CBS1), used for single-family homes, condos and townhomes. It holds the Dates and Deadlines table and the rules for title, inspections, financing, closing and default.
Principle that a component's value equals what it adds to the whole property, not its cost.
A life estate created on purpose by a deed or will, usually lasting for the life tenant's own lifetime.
A mortgage loan that is not insured or guaranteed by a government agency.
Using money belonging to others for the broker's own purposes or for a different beneficiary.
The 1957 Colorado Supreme Court case allowing brokers to fill in standard forms in their own transactions without charging beyond their commission.
aliases: Conway-Bogue Realty v. Denver Bar Association

glossary.definition: Ownership in which a corporation holds title to a building and residents own shares plus a proprietary lease for their units.
A legal entity separate from its shareholders that can hold title in severalty. Shareholders have limited liability, but a C corporation's income is taxed twice.
An east–west line (standard parallel) drawn every 24 miles north and south of a base line to adjust the survey grid for the curvature of the earth.
Repairs to something that has already broken.
What it took, or would take, to build an improvement (land plus construction). Cost can differ from both value and price.

Tax depreciation: the annual deduction that recovers the cost of buildings used in business or held for investment (27.5 years residential rental, 39 years nonresidential, straight-line); land isn't depreciable. Unlike appraisal depreciation, it isn't an actual loss in value.
A response that changes an offer's terms; it rejects the original offer and becomes a new offer.
Separate copies of the same contract, each signed by one or more parties, that together form one agreement.
The Commission form used to respond to an offer with changed terms. It supersedes earlier counterproposals and expires without timely notice of acceptance.
The county official who sets the actual value of each property for property tax purposes. A Colorado owner who disagrees with a valuation protests to the assessor first.
The county body (usually the county commissioners) that hears a property owner's appeal after the assessor denies a valuation protest.

The county official who records deeds, deeds of trust and other documents in the public records. In Colorado the clerk and recorder also collects the documentary fee and passes the transfer declaration to the assessor.
A promise in a deed or recorded declaration about how property will or won't be used. A breach is usually remedied by an injunction or damages.
The deed covenant that the property has no encumbrances except those listed in the deed.

Commission Position. The label for the Colorado Real Estate Commission's position statements (CP-1, CP-2 and so on) in the Colorado Real Estate Manual. They explain how the Commission views common practice issues; they guide conduct but aren't rules themselves.

Certified public accountant. A state-licensed accountant. Brokers should refer clients with tax questions, such as 1031 exchanges or capital gains, to a CPA or tax attorney rather than give tax advice.
Consumer Price Index. A government measure of changes in consumer prices over time. Index leases often tie rent increases to the CPI.

Colorado Real Estate Commission. The governor-appointed board that makes rules for Colorado brokers, approves the standard forms, and decides disciplinary cases. The Division of Real Estate does its day-to-day staff work.
An amount in a party's favor on a closing statement — something they receive or have already paid.
Zoning that allows "higher" uses, such as homes, in a zone set aside for "lower" uses, such as commercial.
Paying past-due amounts and costs before the sale to stop a foreclosure and reinstate the loan.
What the seller actually knows at the time of the disclosure. The Seller's Property Disclosure is completed on this basis and is not a warranty of the property's condition.
A party to a transaction who has not engaged the broker, so the broker has no brokerage relationship with that party.
The table near the front of a Colorado contract that lists every deadline (title, inspection, loan, appraisal, closing, possession) as a date or a number of days after MEC.
A reference point or surface, such as mean sea level or a local benchmark, from which surveyors measure elevations and heights.
A charge to a party on a closing statement — something they owe.
The recorded document that creates a common interest community. It defines units and common elements, allocates assessments and sets restrictions.
A written instrument that conveys title to real property from a grantor to a grantee.
A borrower's voluntary conveyance of the property to the lender to avoid foreclosure.
The security instrument used in Colorado. The borrower conveys title to the county Public Trustee as security for the lender's note.
A private limit on property use written into a deed or recorded declaration.
Provision requiring the lender to release the lien once the debt is fully paid.
A personal judgment against a borrower for the amount still owed when a foreclosure sale brings less than the debt, where state law allows it.
A specific end date that every Colorado listing or other brokerage agreement must have. Open-ended terms such as "until sold" are not allowed.

Commission-approved form defining seller's agent, buyer's agent, transaction-broker and customer. Required when a party asks about a relationship the firm doesn't offer. Its definitions alone are not the brokerage disclosure, and it is not a contract.
A payment that keeps an oil and gas lease in force during the primary term when drilling has not started.
The final steps that make a deed transfer title: the grantor delivers it and the grantee accepts it during the grantor's lifetime.
Written notice a landlord must give before filing eviction, usually 10 days for residential tenants in Colorado.

The signed agreement between the firm and the bank that opens an account. For a Colorado trust account it must identify the account as a fiduciary account using the word "trust" or "escrow," and the firm keeps a copy for Commission inspection.
In appraisal, any loss in value from any cause: physical deterioration, functional obsolescence or external obsolescence.
Taxing, at sale, the part of a gain that came from depreciation deductions taken during ownership.
The passing of a deceased person's property to heirs under state law when there is no valid will.
An arrangement in which the employing broker assigns different licensees in the same firm to represent the buyer and the seller.
A broker the employing broker designates in writing to work with a particular party. The relationship does not extend to the employing broker, other brokers or the firm.
A fixed fee a broker pays the firm (monthly or per transaction) in exchange for keeping most or all of each commission.
A gift of real property by will.
The person who receives real property by will.

For fair housing, a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, a record of such an impairment, or being regarded as having one. The statute uses the word "handicap."
The ending of a contract, whether by performance, agreement, impossibility, operation of law, or breach.
The fiduciary duty to tell the client every material fact the agent knows or should know that affects the client's interests.
Prepaid interest paid to lower a loan's rate; one point equals 1% of the loan amount.
An ad or statement that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on a protected class; prohibited even for sellers who are otherwise exempt.
A complaint outcome where there's no jurisdiction or no violation is found, so no discipline is imposed.
The state agency within the Department of Regulatory Agencies that staffs the Commission, investigates complaints, audits brokers, and enforces the license law.
Do Not Call. Refers to the national Do-Not-Call Registry and to a company's own do-not-call list. Brokers who cold-call must check the registry regularly and honor anyone's request not to be called.
The national list of phone numbers that telemarketers may not call without an exception; checked at least every 31 days.
Colorado state fee of one cent per $100 of consideration, collected by the county clerk and recorder when a deed is recorded.
An exempt Colorado well permit, usually on 35 acres or more, that can serve up to three homes, water up to one acre of lawn and garden, and water livestock.
A closing item that passes between buyer and seller, debited to one and credited to the other in the same amount.
Rezoning land to a less intense use, such as from commercial to residential.
Staged disbursements of a construction loan, released after the lender verifies completed work.

Division of Real Estate. The Colorado agency within the Department of Regulatory Agencies that staffs the Real Estate Commission, licenses brokers, investigates complaints, audits brokerages and enforces the license law.
One broker acting as agent for both sides of a transaction. Prohibited in Colorado by statute.
Documents the seller delivers under the contract, such as leases, leased-item and encumbered-inclusion documents and a septic permit if required, each with its own delivery and objection deadlines.
A Commission deed of trust version under which the lender may call the loan due on a transfer only if the person receiving the property isn't creditworthy.
A Commission deed of trust version under which the lender may call the whole loan due if the property is transferred.
A copy of a document, including a photocopy, fax or electronic copy with electronic signatures.
A power of attorney written to stay in effect if the principal becomes incapacitated; like any power of attorney, it ends at the principal's death.
Forcing a person to agree through threats or force; makes a contract voidable.
Demand, Utility, Scarcity, Transferability. A memory aid for the four elements a property needs to have value. On the exam, demand means effective demand: desire backed by the ability to pay.

Errors and omissions. Professional liability insurance covering a broker's negligent mistakes. Colorado requires every active broker to carry it, and it serves in place of a recovery fund for protecting consumers.

Electronic Signatures in Global and National Commerce Act. The 2000 federal law giving electronic signatures and records the same legal effect as paper ones in interstate commerce. It works alongside UETA, which states adopt.
Federal law (2000) giving electronic signatures and records the same legal effect as paper ones.
aliases: Electronic Signatures in Global and National Commerce Act

glossary.definition: A buyer's good-faith deposit under a purchase contract, held in trust for both parties.
The party named in the contract to hold the earnest money, usually the listing brokerage or a title company.
The Commission form, signed by buyer and seller, that directs how earnest money is paid out and mutually releases the parties.
A non-possessory right to use another person's land for a specific purpose.
An easement that benefits a neighboring (dominant) parcel and burdens the servient parcel. It runs with the land.
An easement implied from the circumstances and prior use of the land when a parcel is divided.
An easement created by law when a parcel is sold without access to a road and the parcels were once under common ownership. It ends when the need ends.
An easement that benefits a person or company rather than a neighboring parcel, such as a utility line easement.

Established business relationship. An exception to Do-Not-Call rules that lets a business call someone on the registry for a limited time after that person's last transaction with it or after their inquiry or application.

Equal Credit Opportunity Act. The federal law, implemented by Regulation B, that bars lenders from discriminating against credit applicants based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, receipt of public assistance, or good-faith exercise of consumer-credit rights.
Effective gross income. Potential gross income minus vacancy and collection losses (plus any other income). In the income approach, subtract operating expenses from EGI to get net operating income.
Delivering documents under the contract by email, by a link or website, or by fax.
Giving a contract notice electronically, such as by email or fax, through the methods the parties list in the contract. Like any notice, it is effective when received.
An electronic mark or process adopted to sign a record. Under Colorado's UETA it satisfies a legal signature requirement.
Annual crops produced by labor. They're treated as personal property, and a tenant farmer may harvest them after the tenancy ends if the tenant didn't cause it to end.

Earnest money deposit. A buyer's good-faith deposit under a purchase contract, held in trust for both parties until closing or termination. In Colorado it must be handled under the trust-account rules and the contract's earnest money provisions.
Government's power to take private property for public use with just compensation, through condemnation.
The broker who runs a brokerage firm, employs or engages other brokers, and is responsible for supervising them and the firm's trust accounts.
A state law that gives local governments the authority to enact zoning and other land use regulations.
Sealing or covering a hazardous material, such as asbestos, so it can't release fibers, instead of removing it.
An improvement that extends onto a neighbor's property or into a setback or easement.
An included item that has a lien or other debt against it. The buyer chooses whether to assume the obligation, and the lienholder's written approval is needed before closing.
Any claim or right held by someone other than the owner that limits the property's use or lowers its value, such as a lien, easement, or restriction.

Environmental Protection Agency. The federal agency that enforces environmental laws such as CERCLA (Superfund) and, together with HUD, the lead-based paint disclosure rule for housing built before 1978.

Federal law barring credit discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, receipt of public-assistance income, or good-faith exercise of consumer credit rights.
The HUD fair housing poster brokerage offices must display; failing to display it can be treated as evidence of discrimination.
A buyer's interest in property under a signed purchase contract before legal title passes at closing.
The owner's interest in a property: market value minus all loan balances.
A borrower's right to stop a foreclosure by paying off the debt before the sale.

Under the Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act, a buyer of a residence in foreclosure who won't occupy it as a principal residence. These sales carry special contract protections and cancellation rights.
A predatory practice of lending based on a homeowner's equity without regard to the borrower's ability to repay, setting up foreclosure.
The gradual wearing away of land by water, wind, or other natural forces, which reduces the owner's land.
Professional liability insurance required of every Active Colorado broker; minimum $100,000 per claim and $300,000 aggregate.

Exclusive Right-to-Sell Listing Contract. The Colorado Commission-approved listing form under which the seller owes the brokerage a commission no matter who finds the buyer during the listing period. It is the most common type of residential listing.
Transfer of property to the state when an owner dies without a will and without heirs.
A Do-Not-Call exception allowing calls to a registered number within 18 months of the person's last transaction with you or 3 months after their inquiry or application.
The degree, quantity, and duration of a person's interest in real property. Estates are either freehold (ownership) or leasehold (tenancy).
A leasehold with a definite start and end date that ends automatically without notice.
A federal tax on the right to transfer property at death, based on the fair market value of the estate; most estates fall below the filing threshold.
Electric vehicle. Used in the course in the context of Colorado HOA law, which limits an association's ability to prohibit owners from installing EV charging stations.

A Commission addendum that lets either party structure the sale as a Section 1031 exchange. The other party cooperates at no added cost, and the contract binds both parties even if the exchange fails.
In a 1031 exchange, the 180 days (or the tax return due date, if earlier) after transferring the old property within which the replacement must be acquired.
Items the contract lists as staying with the seller, even if they are attached to the property (for example, a chandelier the seller wants to keep).
A listing with one broker in which the owner keeps the right to sell the property alone without owing a commission.

A listing that gives one brokerage firm exclusive rights to market a property for a set term, such as an exclusive right-to-sell or exclusive agency listing. Another broker may not negotiate a listing directly with an owner who has an unexpired exclusive listing with a different firm.
A listing in which the broker earns a commission no matter who sells the property during the term, including the owner.
The Commission's landlord-side listing contract. It hires a brokerage to market a property for lease and find a tenant.
aliases: Exclusive Right to Lease Listing Contract

glossary.definition: A listing in which the brokerage earns its fee if the property sells during the listing period, no matter who finds the buyer.
The Commission's tenant-side listing contract, under which a broker finds a rental for the tenant and negotiates the lease for the tenant.
Zoning that allows only the use listed for the zone.
A contract that all parties have fully performed.
A contract with obligations still to be performed.
A small household or domestic well permitted by the State Engineer outside the priority system, with limited uses.
Agency created by words, oral or written, such as a signed listing agreement.
A contract whose terms are stated in words, oral or written.
An easement created on purpose in writing, either granted to someone in a deed or agreement or reserved by a seller when conveying land.
Title insurance that removes some or all standard exceptions, such as survey matters and parties in possession, usually after a survey and inspection.
Coverage, often called tail coverage, that lets claims be reported after an E&O policy ends; Colorado requires a 365-day option.
A Commission form, new for 2026, where one party proposes extending deadlines in Part I. If Part I isn't signed by both and accepted in time, Part II works as that party's notice to terminate.
Loss in value from conditions outside the property, such as noise or a declining local economy; always incurable.
Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, as amended, which prohibits housing discrimination based on seven protected classes.
The amendment to the federal Fair Housing Act that added disability (handicap) and familial status as protected classes and strengthened enforcement.
Having one or more children under 18 living with a parent, custodian or designee; includes pregnancy and someone securing custody.
Federal Bureau of Investigation. The federal law-enforcement agency that runs the Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), where victims of wire fraud should report quickly.

Federal Communications Commission. The federal agency that regulates telecommunications and enforces the TCPA's rules on autodialed and prerecorded calls and texts, alongside the FTC's Do-Not-Call rules.

Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. The federal agency that insures deposits in banks and savings institutions. Colorado requires brokerage trust accounts to be held in a recognized institution with federally insured deposits, such as an FDIC- or NCUA-insured one.

Forcible entry and detainer. Colorado's name for the court eviction process. A landlord must go through an FED action to remove a tenant and may not use self-help such as changing the locks or cutting off utilities.
A general lien the IRS holds on all of a taxpayer's property after an assessed tax goes unpaid; a public notice is filed to establish priority against most creditors.
The most complete form of ownership, unlimited in duration and freely transferable or inheritable.
A fee estate that can end if a stated condition occurs or stops, such as a fee simple determinable or a fee simple subject to a condition subsequent.

glossary.term: Fee simple subject to a condition subsequent
glossary.definition: Fee ownership that the grantor can end if a stated condition is broken, using words like "on condition that." The grantor must take action (right of reentry) to get the property back.

Federal Emergency Management Agency. The federal agency that maps flood zones and runs the National Flood Insurance Program. Property in a FEMA special flood hazard area financed with a federally backed or regulated loan must carry flood insurance.

Federal Housing Administration. The agency within HUD that insures loans made by approved lenders, allowing low down payments in exchange for mortgage insurance premiums. FHA insures loans; it doesn't lend money.
A loan insured by the Federal Housing Administration and made by an approved lender, known for low down payments.
Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation. Freddie Mac, a government-sponsored enterprise that buys conventional mortgages from lenders in the secondary market, giving lenders more money to lend.
A person in a position of trust who must act in the best interests of the client.

Foreign Investment in Real Property Tax Act. The federal law requiring a buyer to withhold a portion of the amount realized when buying U.S. real estate from a foreign seller, with some exceptions. The withholding is usually handled at closing.
aliases: Foreign Investment in Real Property Tax Act

glossary.definition: Financial Institutions Reform, Recovery, and Enforcement Act. The 1989 law passed after the savings and loan crisis. Its Title XI created the modern system of appraiser regulation: USPAP standards, minimum qualifications and state licensing or certification of appraisers for federally related transactions.
Formerly personal property that has been attached to real estate so that it becomes part of the real property.
Federal National Mortgage Association. Fannie Mae, a government-sponsored enterprise that buys mortgages from lenders in the secondary market and packages them into securities.

Colorado's rule (HB24-1098) that a landlord generally needs a legal cause, such as nonpayment or serious lease violations, to evict a covered residential tenant or refuse to renew the lease after the tenant has lived there 12 months.
The legal process by which a lender forces the sale of property to satisfy a defaulted loan.
Person who, for pay, offers to stop or delay a foreclosure or arrange relief for a homeowner; regulated by the CFPA.

For FIRPTA, a nonresident alien individual or a foreign corporation, partnership, trust or estate. When the seller is a foreign person, the buyer generally must withhold part of the amount realized for the IRS.

The four things a lender weighs in underwriting: capacity (ability to afford the payment), credit (history of paying debts), capital (cash for down payment, costs and reserves) and collateral (the property).
The four requirements traditionally needed to create a joint tenancy: possession, interest, time, and title. Tenancy in common requires only unity of possession.
Intentional misstatement or concealment of a material fact to induce someone to act, causing them harm.
An ownership interest of indefinite duration, such as a fee simple or life estate.
The housing payment (PITI plus items like HOA dues) divided by gross monthly income.
Trees, perennial shrubs, grass, and other plants that grow without being planted each year. They're treated as part of the real property.

For sale by owner. A property the owner is selling without a listing broker. A FSBO isn't exempt from Do-Not-Call rules just because it's publicly advertised, and Colorado has a brokerage disclosure form for working with one.
Federal Trade Commission. The federal consumer-protection agency that runs the national Do-Not-Call Registry and enforces CAN-SPAM and data-security rules for businesses, including brokerages.
Completion of all contract terms by both parties; the normal way a contract is discharged and becomes executed.
Loss in value from poor design or outdated features within the property; may be curable or incurable.
The deed covenant that the grantor will sign any additional documents needed to perfect the grantee's title.
A missing link in the chain of title, where the records don't show how title passed from one owner to the next.
An agent authorized to handle a range of matters in a particular business, such as a property manager.
A lien that attaches to all of the debtor's property, real and personal, such as a federal tax lien or a judgment lien.
A business in which all partners share management and have unlimited personal liability for the partnership's debts.
A power of attorney giving the attorney-in-fact broad authority to act for the principal in many matters, creating a universal agency.
A deed in which the grantor warrants title against all defects, including those arising before the grantor owned the property.
Gross income multiplier. Sales price divided by annual gross income, used to estimate the value of larger or commercial income properties. Compare GRM, which uses monthly rent.

Government National Mortgage Association. Ginnie Mae, a government-owned corporation within HUD that guarantees securities backed by government-insured or guaranteed loans such as FHA and VA loans. It doesn't buy loans itself.
Funds received and available for immediate withdrawal, such as wires or cashier's checks, required before a Colorado closing provider disburses.
The intangible value of a business's reputation, name and customer relationships.
An irregular parcel in the rectangular survey system that can't be a full quarter-quarter section, usually because it lies along a body of water or at the edge of a township.
A lease with rent that increases in scheduled steps.
The person who receives title by deed.
The part of a deed with words of conveyance, such as "grants" or "conveys," showing the grantor's intent to transfer title.
The person who conveys title by deed.
Gross rent multiplier. Sales price divided by monthly gross rent, used to estimate the value of one- to four-unit rental homes. Compare GIM, which uses annual income.
Sales price divided by annual gross income; used for larger or commercial income property.
A lease where the tenant pays fixed rent and the landlord pays property expenses.
Sales price divided by monthly gross rent; used to estimate value of 1–4 unit rentals.
A long-term lease of land only, on which the tenant usually builds.
Competitors agreeing not to do business with a particular person or firm.

The errors and omissions insurance policy the Division arranges with an insurer through competitive bid, open to every Colorado licensee. The insurer can drop a licensee only for limited reasons such as nonpayment or the license going inactive.
A fiduciary deed from a court-appointed guardian conveying a ward's property, usually with limited warranties.
The "to have and to hold" clause of a deed, which defines the estate being granted.
The implied warranty in most states that residential rental premises are fit to live in.

House Bill. Prefix for bills introduced in the Colorado House of Representatives; the two digits after it are the session year and the last digits are the bill number (HB24-1098 is House Bill 1098 from 2024). Colorado landlord-tenant law has changed through several recent bills, so check current law.
Held by production. Describes an oil and gas lease that continues past its primary term because the well keeps producing in paying quantities.
Highest and best use. The use that is legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible and produces the highest value. It is a basic principle of appraisal.

Home Equity Conversion Mortgage. The FHA-insured reverse mortgage for older homeowners. The lender pays the owner, the balance grows, and the loan is repaid when the owner sells, permanently moves out or dies.
Describes an oil and gas lease that continues past its primary term because production in paying quantities continues.
Home equity line of credit. A revolving credit line secured by the borrower's home, usually in a junior lien position. The borrower can draw on it, repay and draw again up to the limit.
The closer supervision an employing broker must give new brokers: training, contract help, transaction monitoring, and closing review.
The legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible use that produces the highest value.

Home Mortgage Disclosure Act. The federal law requiring many lenders to report data on mortgage applications and loans by location and borrower characteristics. The data help regulators spot redlining and other lending discrimination.

Homeowners' association. The organization of owners in a planned community or condominium that enforces the CC&Rs, maintains common areas and collects assessments. In Colorado, CCIOA governs most HOAs and limits some restrictions they can impose.
The Division of Real Estate office that registers HOAs, educates owners and logs complaints. It is not a regulator and has no enforcement power.
A listing provision that protects the commission for a period after expiration, limited to buyers whose names were given to the seller in writing during the term.
A period after a listing or buyer agreement ends during which the broker can still earn compensation from prospects named in writing during the term.
A professional examination of a home's condition and systems that a buyer orders before closing. Brokers should recommend one on virtually every purchase.
Federal law (Regulation C) requiring many lenders to report data about mortgage applications and loans so regulators can spot discriminatory lending patterns such as redlining.
Federal rule (Section 121) letting a seller exclude up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 married filing jointly) on a main home owned and used at least 2 of the last 5 years.

A Commission-approved notice attached to the Foreclosure Protection Act contract warning the homeowner that the sale has serious legal consequences, including a right to cancel, and urging them to consult an attorney or housing counselor. It must be translated into the seller's main language if needed, but not by the broker.
An organization of owners in a planned community or condominium that enforces CC&Rs, maintains common areas, and collects assessments.
A state-law protection that shields part of the value of a family's home from certain creditors.
An exempt Colorado well permit that allows water for ordinary household uses inside a home only, with no lawn or garden watering or livestock. It is common on smaller parcels.
Senior housing (all occupants 62+, or at least 80% of occupied units with one resident 55+ plus required policies) that is exempt from the familial status rules only.
U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. The federal department that enforces the Fair Housing Act and oversees FHA and Ginnie Mae. Fair housing complaints can be filed with HUD.

Heating, ventilation and air conditioning. A building's heating and cooling systems. HVAC replacement is a typical big-ticket item in a property manager's capital budget and a common inspection issue.
Internet Crime Complaint Center. The FBI's center for reporting internet crimes such as wire fraud. Victims should report immediately, because funds can sometimes be frozen if the report is fast.
In a 1031 exchange, the 45 days after transferring the old property within which the investor must identify replacement property in writing.
Internet Data Exchange. The MLS feature that lets participating brokers show other participants' listings on their own websites, subject to MLS display rules.

Improvement Location Certificate. A Colorado surveyor's drawing showing where improvements sit relative to the property lines. It is cheaper and less precise than a full survey and can't be relied on to set boundary lines; the purchase contract states who orders and pays for an ILC or survey.
A charge on developers to help pay for public facilities, such as schools, parks, and roads, that new development requires.
Agency created by the conduct of the parties rather than by an express agreement.
A contract created by the parties' conduct rather than stated words.
Discharge of a contract because performance can't legally be done, for example because the property was destroyed or a party to a personal services contract died.

An account the lender sets up to collect a share of property taxes and insurance with each monthly payment and pay those bills when due. Also called an escrow account; RESPA limits how much cushion the lender can hold.
A drawing by a surveyor showing where improvements sit relative to the boundaries. It is less precise than a full survey.
Knowledge legally treated as known by someone else. In Colorado, a designated single agent's knowledge is not imputed to non-designated brokers in the firm.
A license that remains renewed but can't be used for brokerage activity; no E&O required while inactive.

Items that convey with the property under the sales contract: attached items unless excluded, plus listed items such as window coverings, storm windows, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors and all keys.
A broker who runs their own one-person brokerage and doesn't employ or supervise other brokers; requires two years of Active licensure.
A worker who controls how the work is done and pays their own self-employment taxes, as opposed to an employee.
An errors and omissions insurance policy bought on the open market instead of through the Division's group plan. It must meet the Commission's minimum terms and be certified.
The published market rate an adjustable-rate loan is tied to; it changes over time.
A lease whose rent adjusts with an economic index, such as the Consumer Price Index.
Permission given after the person understands what will be disclosed or done and its consequences.
A court order requiring a person to do or stop doing something, such as removing an encroachment or obeying a deed restriction.
The contract deadline by which the buyer delivers an Inspection Objection Notice listing unsatisfactory items and the corrections requested.
The buyer's written notice listing unsatisfactory conditions and the corrections requested, delivered by the Inspection Objection Deadline.
The Commission form, signed by buyer and seller, in which the seller agrees to specific corrections. It amends the contract.

The contract deadline for a signed written agreement (usually the Inspection Resolution form) on the buyer's inspection objection. If there's none, the contract terminates unless the buyer withdraws the objection in writing first.
The contract deadline by which the buyer may simply terminate over any unsatisfactory condition, as long as the buyer hasn't already delivered an Inspection Objection.
A sale in which the seller receives at least one payment after the tax year of the sale, usually reporting gain as payments are received.
A loan whose payments cover only interest for a period, so the principal is not reduced during that time.
A court action in which a holder of disputed money deposits it with the court and asks the court to decide who gets it.

glossary.term: Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act
glossary.definition: A federal law requiring developers who sell or lease certain unimproved lots through interstate commerce to register and give buyers a property report. Subdivisions under 25 lots are exempt.
Dying without a valid will. Property then passes to heirs under state succession laws.
A lawsuit by an owner seeking compensation when government action has effectively taken or damaged the property without formal condemnation.
Transfer of title without the owner's consent, such as by foreclosure, eminent domain, escheat, or adverse possession.
Internal Revenue Service. The federal tax agency. It matters to brokers for 1031 exchanges, FIRPTA withholding, closing-agent reporting of sales and federal tax liens.
Income = Rate × Value. A memory aid for capitalization math: net operating income equals cap rate times value. Rearranged, value = NOI ÷ cap rate and cap rate = NOI ÷ value.
Specific deductible expenses, such as mortgage interest and property taxes, that a taxpayer lists in place of taking the standard deduction.
Liability under which any one responsible party can be made to pay the entire amount, such as a whole CERCLA cleanup.
Co-ownership with equal shares and the right of survivorship, traditionally requiring the four unities of possession, interest, time, and title.
Two or more parties joining together for a single project or investment. It isn't a separate legal form and is often organized as a partnership or LLC.

glossary.term: Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co.
glossary.definition: The 1968 U.S. Supreme Court case holding that the Civil Rights Act of 1866 bars all racial discrimination, private or public, in the sale or rental of property.
A trust account's chronological record of every receipt and disbursement, with a running balance.

Joint tenants with right of survivorship. Wording that creates a joint tenancy, in which a deceased owner's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenants rather than through the estate.
A general, involuntary lien created when a court judgment against a person is recorded. It attaches to that person's real property in the county.
Foreclosure in which the lender sues and a court orders the property sold, often by a sheriff.
A conventional loan that exceeds the conforming loan limit set for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.
A lienholder whose lien is lower in priority than the one being foreclosed, such as a second mortgage lender. In Colorado, eligible junior lienors may redeem after a public trustee sale.
Under prior appropriation, a water right with a later appropriation date. When there isn't enough water, junior users must stop diverting so senior rights can be filled.
The payment the government must make when it takes property by eminent domain, usually the property's fair market value.
A doctrine that lets a court refuse to enforce a right when the person waited unreasonably long to assert it.
The earth's surface, everything below it to the center of the earth, and the airspace above it, including natural things attached to it such as trees and minerals in place.
A sale in which the seller keeps legal title until the buyer pays in full; the buyer has possession and equitable title.
A hidden defect not discoverable by ordinary inspection.

Loan Estimate. The TRID form a lender must deliver or mail within three business days after receiving a loan application, showing estimated loan terms and closing costs so borrowers can compare offers.
The federally required disclosure for housing built before 1978, including known hazards, the EPA pamphlet and the buyer's inspection opportunity.
A lease that gives the tenant the right, but not the obligation, to buy the property.
An arrangement in which a tenant agrees to buy the property, often with part of the rent credited to the price; unlike a lease option, both sides are obligated to complete the sale.
Included items the seller leases rather than owns, such as leased solar panels. The buyer chooses whether to assume the lease, and the lessor's written approval is needed before closing.
A tenant's right to possess property for a period under a lease. It's treated as personal property.
A trust account record kept separately for each beneficiary, showing that person's receipts, disbursements and balance.
A description of land precise enough to identify exactly one parcel, written using metes and bounds, lot and block, or the rectangular survey system.
A life estate created by state law rather than by a deed or will, such as historical dower and curtesy rights of a surviving spouse.
The essential element requiring that a contract's object be lawful; a contract to do something illegal is void.
The tenant who receives possession of property under a lease and holds a leasehold estate.
The owner or landlord who grants possession of property under a lease.
An informal reprimand sent by certified mail for minor misconduct; the licensee can reject it by requesting formal proceedings within 20 days.
A preliminary document summarizing proposed deal terms, usually non-binding on the main transaction.
Insurance covering the owner's legal responsibility for injuries to others on the property.
Personal, revocable permission to enter another's land for a specific purpose. It isn't an interest in land.
Appraiser credential for simpler 1–4 unit residential properties, up to set value and complexity limits.
A Commission addendum for a purchase contract in which a licensee buys the seller's property. The seller may terminate at any time and reimburses the licensee's expenses up to a stated cap.
A creditor's claim against property as security for a debt, which can be enforced by forcing a sale.
The order in which liens are paid. The basic rule is first in time, first in right by recording date, except that property tax and special assessment liens generally come first.
The view, followed in most states, that a mortgage creates only a lien and the borrower keeps title; contrasts with title theory.
A signed statement from a contractor or supplier giving up mechanic's lien rights for work or materials that have been paid for. Construction lenders often require them before releasing a draw.
An estate that lasts for the lifetime of a named person, after which the property passes to a remainderman or reverts to the grantor.
A life estate measured by the life of someone other than the life tenant, such as "to Ann for the life of Bob."
A Section 1031 trade of real property held for investment or business use for other such property, deferring tax on the gain.
Colorado's term for a single agent whose duties are only those set by statute plus any additional duties agreed in writing.
Common elements of a condominium reserved for the use of one or a few units, such as an assigned parking space or a balcony.
A business entity whose members have limited liability and flexible pass-through tax treatment. It's commonly used to hold investment property.
A partnership with at least one general partner who manages and has unlimited liability, plus limited partners who are passive investors liable only up to their investment.
A power of attorney that authorizes only a defined act or set of acts, such as signing closing documents for one sale.
An amount agreed in advance as the remedy for breach. In the Colorado contract, it is the earnest money kept by the seller as the seller's only remedy unless specific performance is selected.
The time a listing contract runs: from its start date to the earlier of a completed sale or the end date, plus any written extensions.
The rights of owners whose land borders a lake, sea, or ocean to use and enjoy the water and the shoreline.

Limited liability company. A business entity whose members have limited personal liability and flexible, usually pass-through, tax treatment. Many Colorado brokerages are organized as LLCs, but team names may not use terms like LLC that suggest a separate entity.

Limited liability partnership. A partnership in which partners generally aren't personally liable for other partners' misconduct. Like LLC, it's a term Colorado bans from team names because it implies a separate entity.
A buyer taking over the seller's existing loan; the balance is debited to the seller and credited to the buyer.
TRID form the lender must deliver or mail within three business days after receiving a loan application.
A predatory practice of repeatedly refinancing a borrower's loan to generate fees, with little or no benefit to the borrower.
The loan amount divided by the lesser of the sales price or appraised value.
Letter of intent. A preliminary document, common in commercial leasing and sales, that summarizes proposed key terms such as rent, term and allowances. It is usually non-binding as to the main deal.
A legal description that identifies a parcel by lot and block number on a recorded subdivision plat.
A rental agreement for the space a manufactured home sits on, usually in a park. A buyer of the home must be approved by the lot owner and take over the lease or sign a new one.
The fiduciary duty to put the client's interests first, ahead of the agent's own and any other party's, with no self-dealing.

Limited partnership. A partnership with at least one general partner who manages the business and is personally liable, plus limited partners whose liability is limited to their investment. It's often used for real estate syndications.

Loan-to-value ratio. The loan amount divided by the lower of the sales price or appraised value. A higher LTV means more risk to the lender, so conventional loans above 80% LTV usually need private mortgage insurance.
The written contract between an owner and a property manager that creates the agency and sets duties and compensation.

A Commission addendum attached to the Land or Commercial contract when the property sold includes a manufactured home. It adds the home's serial number and VIN, the certificate-of-title steps and a UCC lien search.

glossary.term: Manufactured Home Contract to Buy and Sell (Lot Lease Only)
glossary.definition: The Commission contract (MHC1) for a manufactured home on a rented space, such as in a park. No land changes hands: title passes by the home's certificate of title, and the deal depends on the park owner approving the buyer and assigning or issuing a lot lease.
The fixed percentage a lender adds to the index to set an ARM's rate.

Method of attachment, Adaptability, Relationship of the parties, Intention, Agreement. A memory aid for the tests courts use to decide whether an item is a fixture that stays with the property. A written agreement between the parties overrides the other tests, and otherwise intention is treated as the most important.
Competitors dividing markets by territory, customers or property type.
Studying comparable properties, vacancy rates, location, condition and amenities to set rent or estimate value.
The price actually paid for a property in a specific sale; it may differ from market value.
The most probable price a property should bring in a competitive, open market with typically motivated, informed parties and reasonable exposure time.
Title free enough from reasonable doubt that a prudent buyer would accept it.
A fact that would affect a reasonable person's decision to buy or the price they'd pay.
Mutual execution of contract. The date both parties have signed the Colorado purchase contract. Deadlines stated as a number of days are counted from MEC.
A specific, involuntary lien for unpaid contractors, subcontractors, or suppliers who improved the property.
A nonbinding process in which a neutral third party helps the parties settle. Colorado contracts require it before arbitration or litigation.

Laws requiring sex offenders to register and making registry information available to the public. In Colorado, a buyer who cares about nearby registered offenders gets that information from local law enforcement.
The ending of a lesser interest when it and a greater interest come under the same owner, such as an easement ending when one person owns both the dominant and servient parcels.
A legal description that traces a parcel's boundaries using distances, directions, and monuments from a point of beginning back to that point.
The seller's required disclosure of known methamphetamine manufacture, use or storage on the property, unless the property was remediated to state standards.
The fixture test that asks how an item is attached to the property (bolted, nailed, plumbed, or wired in) and whether removing it would cause damage.

Manufactured Home Contract to Buy and Sell (Lot Lease Only). The Colorado Commission-approved contract for buying a manufactured home on a leased lot, such as in a park. Title passes by certificate of title rather than a deed.

Mortgage insurance. Insurance that protects the lender if the borrower defaults. Examples are private mortgage insurance on conventional loans and mortgage insurance premiums on FHA loans; VA loans have no monthly MI.
Property tax rate expressed in mills (thousandths of a dollar) per dollar of assessed value.
Ownership of minerals beneath the surface, which can be severed from surface ownership.
The Commission's position that every broker must perform all statutory duties of a single agent or transaction-broker; those duties can't be waived.
Routine help a broker may give a customer, such as showing property, filling in forms, or conveying offers, without creating a brokerage relationship.
A person under the legal age of majority. A contract with a minor is generally voidable by the minor, not by the adult.
A false statement of material fact that the other party relies on; it may be innocent, negligent or intentional.
An error about a fact or term of a contract. Depending on whether it is mutual or one-sided, it may or may not let a party avoid the contract.

Mortgage loan originator. A separately licensed person who takes residential loan applications or negotiates residential loan terms. A Colorado broker without an MLO license shouldn't negotiate loan terms, though the law has limited exemptions such as a broker representing a seller who carries financing.
Multiple listing service. A private, cooperative database through which member brokers share listings and cooperate in finding buyers. Its rules are set by the MLS, not by state or federal law.
Funds a broker holds that are not the broker's own, such as earnest money, rents, security deposits and advance payments.

A fixed natural or artificial object, such as an iron pin, tree, or road, used to mark a boundary in a metes and bounds description. When a monument and a measured distance conflict, the monument generally controls.
A two-party security instrument in which the borrower (mortgagor) pledges property to the lender (mortgagee) as collateral.
A federal income tax deduction for interest on a loan secured by a main or second home, available only if the taxpayer itemizes and subject to loan-amount limits.
A separately licensed person who takes residential loan applications or negotiates residential loan terms; brokers without this license shouldn't negotiate seller-financing loan terms.
Fair Housing Act exemption for renting rooms or units in an owner-occupied building of up to four units where families live independently.
Mountain Time. The time zone used for Colorado contract deadlines; under the Commission forms, a day ends at 11:59 p.m. MT unless an earlier time of day is set.
A package insurance policy combining several coverages, such as property and liability, in one policy.
A private organization through which member brokers share listing information to cooperate in finding buyers.

A company formed by water users to own and run a ditch or canal, with each shareholder entitled to a share of the water. In Colorado its shares are personal property and transfer by stock assignment, not by deed.
A mistake shared by both parties about a material fact; it can make a contract void or voidable.
Discharge of a contract by both parties agreeing to cancel it and release each other.

National Association of REALTORS. The national trade association whose members may use the REALTOR trademark and must follow its Code of Ethics. After its 2024 settlement, NAR-affiliated MLS participants must have a written buyer agreement before touring a home with a buyer.

National Credit Union Administration. The federal agency that insures deposits in credit unions. Like FDIC insurance, NCUA insurance qualifies an institution to hold a Colorado brokerage's trust account.
Notice of election and demand. The document the public trustee records to start a Colorado non-judicial foreclosure. Its recording starts the foreclosure timeline.
An increase in loan balance when payments are too small to cover the interest due.
A false statement of material fact the licensee didn't know was false but should have known, such as repeating an unchecked claim as fact.
A lease where the tenant pays rent plus some or all of the property's expenses.
A listing in which the seller names a net price and the broker keeps anything above it; not expressly prohibited in Colorado but discouraged, with no Commission-approved form.
Effective gross income minus operating expenses; excludes debt service and income tax depreciation.
The contract deadline by which the buyer must have applied for the new loan.
The deadline by which the buyer may terminate if the lender's underwriting is unsatisfactory. Missing it can make the earnest money nonrefundable.
The contract deadline by which the buyer may terminate if the new loan's terms are unsatisfactory, in the buyer's sole discretion.

National Flood Insurance Program. The federal program, run by FEMA, that provides flood insurance. Standard homeowners policies don't cover flood, so buyers in flood zones get coverage through the NFIP or private insurers.
Double net. A lease in which the tenant pays rent plus property taxes and insurance (the exact split depends on the lease). It falls between a single net and a triple net lease.

Triple net. A lease in which the tenant pays rent plus property taxes, insurance and maintenance or repairs. It is common for single-tenant retail and gives the landlord the most predictable net income.
