A non-renewal or eviction allowed under Colorado's for-cause law even though the tenant did nothing wrong, such as for demolition, substantial renovation, the owner or a family member moving in, or a sale. It generally requires longer written notice.
Net operating income. Effective gross income minus operating expenses. It excludes debt service and income-tax depreciation, and dividing it by a cap rate gives value in the income approach.

A well that needs more water or broader uses than an exempt permit allows, such as irrigation or a multi-home system. In Colorado it usually needs a water court-approved augmentation plan so it doesn't injure senior water rights.
A conventional loan that does not meet Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac guidelines, for example because it exceeds the loan limit (a jumbo loan).
A use that was lawful before a zoning change but doesn't meet the current ordinance. It may continue, usually with limits.
Foreclosure without a lawsuit, under a power of sale in the deed of trust. Colorado uses a public trustee for most of these.

A Commission-approved form attached to the Foreclosure Protection Act contract that tells the homeowner they may cancel without penalty and how to do it. Its deadline must match the contract's cancellation date.
Document recorded by the public trustee that starts a Colorado foreclosure.
A written notice a Colorado owner (or other eligible party) files with the public trustee at least 15 calendar days before a foreclosure sale to preserve the right to cure the default.
A recording statute under which a later buyer without notice of an earlier unrecorded deed wins.
The written notice a party delivers to end the contract under a specific provision. It is effective when the other party receives it by the deadline.
Replacing a contract or party with a new one by agreement, releasing the original party.
The fiduciary duty to follow the client's lawful instructions; an agent must refuse illegal or unethical instructions.

Open, Continuous, Exclusive, Adverse, Notorious. A memory aid for the elements of adverse possession; the same letters are sometimes arranged as ONCEA. The possession must be open and notorious, continuous for the statutory period, exclusive and adverse (without the owner's permission).

Owner's extended coverage. Optional title insurance coverage that removes the standard exceptions for unrecorded matters such as parties in possession, survey issues and unrecorded mechanics' liens. The Colorado purchase contract lets the parties choose whether to buy it and who pays.
Matters affecting title that don't appear in the public records, such as unrecorded easements, boundary disputes or parties in possession.
The contract deadline by which the seller delivers existing surveys and discloses known off-record matters, such as unrecorded easements, boundary disputes and parties in possession.
The contract deadline by which the buyer may object to off-record title matters, including what the buyer finds by inspecting the property.
A proposal showing willingness to be bound on definite terms, which becomes a contract when accepted.
The essential element of mutual assent: one party makes a definite offer and the other accepts those exact terms without conditions, creating a meeting of the minds.
The written policies every employing broker must adopt and have each associate receive and sign, including brokerage relationships and confidentiality.
A lease in which a mineral owner (lessor) grants an oil company (lessee) the right to explore for and produce oil and gas in exchange for a bonus, rentals and royalties.

Obedience, Loyalty, Disclosure, Confidentiality, Accounting, Reasonable care. A memory aid for the six fiduciary duties an agent owes a client under common-law agency. Colorado's statute spells out its own duties for single agents and transaction-brokers, so know both.

A manager who works at an apartment building or condominium and is paid a salary or other non-commission pay rather than commissions. Doing customary duties such as showing units and collecting rents, they don't need a license, but they can't negotiate material lease terms.
A nonexclusive listing given to one or more brokers; only the broker who is the procuring cause earns a fee.
A loan that lets the borrower borrow more later under the same security instrument.
A projection of a property's income and expenses for a year.
Discharge of a contract by a legal rule rather than the parties' actions, such as bankruptcy, the statute of limitations, or alteration of the contract without consent.
A contract giving the optionee the right, but not the obligation, to buy property at a set price within a set time, for consideration.
Optional title coverage that removes the standard exceptions for unrecorded matters such as parties in possession, survey issues and unrecorded mechanics' liens.
Title policy protecting the buyer's ownership; under the Colorado contract default, the seller pays for it.
For the home-sale exclusion, the seller must have owned the home for at least two years during the five years before the sale.
Principal and interest. The part of a mortgage payment that repays the loan balance and pays interest. Add taxes and insurance to get PITI.
A loan that covers real property plus personal property, such as furniture or appliances.
A predatory practice of adding unnecessary products, such as credit insurance, to a loan.
Paid after the period it covers; Colorado property taxes are paid the year after they're levied.
A court action that divides co-owned property among the owners or, if it can't be divided fairly, orders it sold and divides the proceeds.
A wall shared by two adjoining properties along the property line, with each owner holding an easement in the other's half.
A defect visible on reasonable inspection, such as a broken window or stained ceiling. Buyers are expected to notice obvious problems.
The amount needed to pay a loan in full at closing, including accrued interest; a seller debit when the seller's loan is retired.
A lease with base rent plus a percentage of the tenant's gross sales, common in retail.
A leasehold that renews automatically for successive periods, such as month to month, until notice is given.
Movable property that isn't real property, such as furniture or vehicles. It transfers by bill of sale.
A fiduciary deed used by the court-appointed representative of a deceased person's estate to convey estate property.
A contract that depends on a particular person's skill or judgment, such as a listing agreement. It generally can't be assigned without consent and may end if that person dies.
Police power, Eminent domain, Taxation, Escheat. A memory aid for the four powers government holds over private property. Only eminent domain requires just compensation to the owner.
Potential gross income. The total income a property would produce if fully rented with all rent collected. Subtract vacancy and collection losses to get effective gross income.
A study of a property's history and records to identify possible contamination, used to support CERCLA defenses.
Loss in value from wear and tear, such as a worn roof or peeling paint. It can be curable or incurable.
Principal, interest, taxes and insurance. The components of a typical full monthly mortgage payment when taxes and insurance are paid through an escrow account. Lenders use PITI in qualifying ratios.
Possession, Interest, Time, Title. A memory aid for the four unities traditionally required to create a joint tenancy. A tenancy in common needs only unity of possession.
A map of a subdivision, prepared by a surveyor and recorded with the county, that shows each lot and block along with streets and easements.

Public Land Survey System. The rectangular (government) survey system of principal meridians, base lines, townships and sections used in most western and midwestern states, including Colorado. A township is 36 sections, and a section is one square mile (640 acres).

Private mortgage insurance. Insurance protecting the lender on a conventional loan when the borrower's down payment is small. It is usually required above 80% loan-to-value and can be cancelled once enough equity builds.
Point of beginning. The fixed starting point of a metes and bounds legal description. The description must return to the POB to close the boundary.
The fixed starting point of a metes and bounds description, where the description must also end.
Government's authority to regulate property use to protect public health, safety, and welfare. It's the basis of zoning and building codes.
Commission guidance (CP-1, CP-2, etc.) explaining how it views practice issues; best practices, not binding law.

Physical occupancy and control of the property. Under the contract the seller delivers it on the Possession Date and Time, and a seller who holds over owes the per-day amount set in the contract plus actual damages.
The future interest a grantor keeps in a fee simple determinable. If the stated condition is broken, title returns to the grantor automatically.
A Commission optional form for a seller rent-back: the seller stays in the home after closing for a short term of no more than 60 days.
A written document authorizing one person (the attorney-in-fact) to act for another.
A clause in a deed of trust or mortgage that allows the property to be sold without a court action if the borrower defaults.
A buyer moving into the property before closing. There is no Commission form for it, and because the buyer has possession but no title, the agreement should be drafted by an attorney.
Abusive lending practices that strip borrowers' equity or load them with unfair costs, such as loan flipping, equity stripping and packing.
An expense the seller paid in advance for a period that extends past closing. At closing the seller is credited, and the buyer debited, for the unused portion.
A loan clause that charges the borrower a fee for paying the loan off early. Without one, the borrower can generally prepay without a fee.
An easement acquired by open, continuous, hostile use of another's land for the period set by state law.
Scheduled upkeep designed to prevent problems and preserve value.
Competitors agreeing on prices or commission rates.
Where loans are made directly to borrowers by banks, credit unions and mortgage companies.
The initial period of an oil and gas lease during which the lessee must begin drilling or production.
A party to a transaction acting for themselves, such as a broker buying or selling their own property.

A main north–south line in the rectangular survey system from which ranges are numbered east and west. Colorado uses the Sixth Principal Meridian, the New Mexico Principal Meridian, and the Ute Meridian.

A party a transaction is actually for, such as the buyer, seller, landlord or tenant, as opposed to the brokers working on it. A principal party may ask a broker to produce the transaction's required records.
The home a person actually lives in as their main home. The term matters for Colorado nonresident withholding exemptions, the Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act and the federal home-sale exclusion.
Appraisal principle that nothing stays the same: neighborhoods move through stages of growth, stability, decline and renewal, so values change over time.
Colorado's water doctrine: the first person to put water to beneficial use has the senior right.
aliases: first in time, first in right

glossary.definition: Fair Housing Act exemption letting a private club limit non-commercial lodging it provides to its members.
A fair housing suit filed directly in federal or state court, due within two years of the discriminatory act.
Insurance protecting a conventional lender against borrower default, typically required with a small down payment.
A legal relationship between parties, such as a seller and buyer, that lets one succeed to the other's rights.
A tenant's proportional share of building expenses: its square footage divided by the building's total leasable square footage.
The court-supervised process of proving a will, paying the deceased person's debts, and distributing the property.
A disciplinary order letting a licensee keep practicing subject to conditions set by the Commission.
The broker whose efforts started an unbroken chain of events that resulted in the sale; usually the one entitled to the commission when more than one broker claims it.
The borrower's written promise to repay a debt on stated terms. In seller financing, it is secured by a deed of trust.
Insurance covering a building and its contents against fire and other hazards.
A licensee or firm hired as a general agent to operate income property for an owner.
The disclosure document a developer must give lot buyers under the Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act before they sign. Buyers can generally revoke within 7 days.

An annual ad valorem tax that local governments levy on real property based on its value; Colorado calculates it as actual value × assessment rate × mill levy. Colorado property taxes are paid in arrears, the year after they accrue.
A specific, involuntary lien created by law for unpaid property taxes. It generally takes priority over all other liens.
The lease a cooperative corporation gives a shareholder, granting the right to occupy a particular unit.
Dividing an expense or income between buyer and seller according to the time each owned the property.
A group protected from discrimination by law; federally: race, color, religion, national origin, sex, disability and familial status.
Property associated with facts like a homicide, other felony or suicide, or an occupant's disease highly unlikely to spread by occupancy. Not material facts under C.R.S. 38-35.5-101.
Under the ADA, a privately operated business or facility open to the public, such as a store, office or a brokerage or leasing office.
The county official who serves as trustee under Colorado deeds of trust and conducts foreclosures and releases.
A use that benefits the public, such as a road or school. Eminent domain can be used only for a public use.
Planned unit development. A zoning and development type that allows flexible lot sizes and mixed uses in exchange for planned common areas, usually governed by an HOA.
Exaggerated opinion or sales talk that a reasonable person would not rely on as fact.
A mortgage given to finance the purchase of the property itself; often refers to the seller taking back a note and mortgage as lender.

Qualified intermediary. An independent party who holds the sale proceeds during a 1031 exchange so the investor never controls the cash. The investor's own agent, attorney or accountant generally can't serve as QI.
In the rectangular survey system, a square about 24 miles on a side containing 16 townships, bounded by guide meridians and correction lines.
An independent party who holds sale proceeds during a 1031 exchange so the investor never has control of the cash.

A mortgage that meets stricter federal standards (for example, no negative amortization or interest-only payments, a term of 30 years or less, and limited points and fees), giving the lender legal protection under the ability-to-repay rule.
Federal tax category for a licensed agent paid on output under a written non-employee contract; not treated as an employee for federal employment taxes.
A tenant's or owner's right to possess and use property without interference from the landlord or someone with superior title.
A lawsuit to establish ownership and remove clouds on title.
A deed that conveys whatever interest the grantor has, if any, with no warranties.
A recording statute under which the first buyer to record wins, regardless of notice.
Recording system where a later buyer without notice of an earlier unrecorded interest wins by recording first; Colorado's system.
A naturally occurring, odorless radioactive gas from uranium decay in soil; EPA action level is 4 pCi/L.
A north–south line in the rectangular survey system drawn every 6 miles east and west of a principal meridian. The columns between them are called ranges.
A limit on how much an adjustable-rate mortgage's interest rate can change, at the first adjustment, at each later adjustment, or over the life of the loan.
Annual profit or income divided by the amount invested, expressed as a percentage.
A principal's approval, after the fact, of an act an agent performed without authority, creating agency for that act.
Land plus everything people have permanently attached to it, such as buildings, fences, and paving.
The Commission's term for a broker's licensed or unlicensed assistant; unlicensed REAPs may do clerical work but not negotiate or advise.

A company that pools investors' money to own or finance real estate and avoids corporate income tax on income it distributes if it meets federal requirements, such as paying out at least 90% of taxable income.
A state fund some states keep to pay consumers who can't collect judgments against licensees. Colorado repealed its fund in 2005 and has none today.
Land, everything permanently attached to it, and the legal rights of ownership.
Form TD-1000 filed with a deed to report the sale price to the county assessor; confidential.

Real Estate Administrative Professional. The Colorado Real Estate Commission's term for a broker's assistant. An unlicensed REAP may do clerical and administrative work but may not negotiate, advise or perform other licensed activities.
A change in rules, policies, practices or services that gives a person with a disability equal opportunity to use housing.
The fiduciary duty to act with the skill and competence expected of a licensee and to refer the client to other experts when needed.
A physical change to the premises that a person with a disability needs; generally at the tenant's expense in private housing.
Returning part of the firm's earned commission to its own client; allowed in Colorado with proper written and lender disclosure.
A bank, savings and loan or credit union insured by the FDIC or NCUA. For Colorado trust accounts it must be in Colorado.

The trust account's bank statement balance adjusted for items the bank hasn't processed yet, such as deposits in transit and outstanding checks. In a three-way reconciliation it must equal the journal balance and the total of all ledger balances.
The appraiser's final step of weighing the value indications from the different approaches into one opinion of value, giving most weight to the approach best suited to the property.
Title as shown in the public records and the title commitment, including recorded liens, easements and covenants.
The contract deadline by which the seller delivers the title commitment and copies of the recorded exception documents.
The contract deadline by which the buyer may object to record title problems. A buyer who doesn't object accepts title as shown.
Filing a document affecting real property in the county public records, which gives constructive notice.
A grid-based legal description system using principal meridians, base lines, townships, and sections. It's used in most western and midwestern states.
Buying back property after a foreclosure sale; in Colorado available to junior lienors, not the owner.
Illegally refusing to lend, or lending on worse terms, in an area because of its racial or ethnic makeup.
Compensation for referring a client; allowed between licensees with reasonable cause and if RESPA permits, but never to unlicensed persons.
Principle that a superior property loses value when surrounded by lesser properties; its opposite is progression.
The routine monthly or quarterly HOA dues that fund the association's budget, including reserves.

Real estate investment trust. A company that pools investors' money to own or finance income-producing real estate. If it pays out most of its taxable income as dividends, it generally avoids corporate income tax.
The offeree's refusal of an offer. A rejection ends the offer, and it can't later be accepted unless it is renewed.
A written document in which the holder of a right, such as an easement or lien, gives it up.
Provision in a blanket loan that frees individual parcels from the lien as they are paid down.
Fair Housing Act exemption letting a religious organization limit non-commercial housing it owns to members of its religion, unless membership is restricted by race, color or national origin.
The future interest held by a remainderman, who takes the property when a life estate ends.
The third party named to receive the property when a life estate ends.
Real estate owned. Property a lender owns after it failed to sell at a foreclosure sale. Lenders selling REO often convey with a special warranty deed rather than a general warranty deed.
The cost to build a building with the same usefulness (utility) as the existing one, using modern materials and methods. Used more often than reproduction cost.
The cost to build an exact replica of the existing building, using the same materials and design.
Canceling a contract and returning the parties to their original positions.
Money set aside for future capital replacements and emergencies.
A study of an association's major common components (roofs, paving, and the like) that estimates their remaining life and replacement cost, used to plan how much to set aside in reserves.
Under the CFPA, an owner's principal residence with a home loan at least 30 days delinquent or in default.
A Commission addendum attached to the Commercial or Land contract when the property includes dwellings. It brings in residential disclosures such as lead-based paint and carbon monoxide alarms.

A written contract that makes a residential seller, buyer, landlord or tenant a broker's client. Under C.R.S. 12-10-403.5 it may not run with the land or bind future owners, may not be assigned without the owner's notice and agreement, and may not create a lien or other recordable interest in the property.

Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act. The federal law covering most residential mortgage closings. It requires settlement-cost disclosures, limits escrow accounts and bans kickbacks and unearned fees for referrals of settlement services.
Liability that applies to conduct or conditions that existed before the law was passed; CERCLA liability reaches contamination that predates the law.
A loan for older homeowners in which the lender pays the owner and the balance grows, repaid when the owner sells, moves or dies.
The future interest a grantor keeps when the property returns to the grantor or the grantor's heirs after a life estate ends.
The most severe license discipline: the Commission cancels the license outright. After a revocation, the Commission won't consider a new license application from that person for one year.
Changing the zoning of an area through the legislative process. Also called a zoning amendment.
The right to match a third-party offer before the owner sells to that third party.
The future interest a grantor keeps in a fee simple subject to a condition subsequent. If the condition is broken, the grantor must act to reclaim the property. Also called a power of termination.
Under TILA, a borrower's right to cancel certain refinances and home-equity loans on a principal residence within three business days. It does not apply to a loan used to buy the home.
The feature of joint tenancy under which a deceased owner's interest passes automatically to the surviving co-owners.
Rights of owners of land along a river or stream to make reasonable use of the water.
Managing risk by removing the activity that creates it, such as closing a swimming pool.
Managing risk by reducing the chance or size of a loss, such as with better lighting, sprinklers or handrails.
Managing exposure to loss by avoiding, controlling, transferring or retaining risk.
Managing risk by accepting it yourself, such as carrying a large deductible or self-insuring small losses.
Managing risk by shifting it to someone else, such as buying insurance or requiring tenant liability insurance.
Right of first refusal. The right to match a third party's offer before the owner can sell to that third party. Unlike an option, it doesn't let the holder force a sale.
Day-to-day custodial upkeep of a property, such as cleaning common areas and landscaping.
The mineral owner's fractional share of oil or gas production, paid free of production costs.

A limited Colorado court proceeding in a public trustee foreclosure that authorizes the sale. It mainly checks whether a default has probably occurred and whether the borrower is protected as a servicemember.
Day-to-day rules adopted by an association's board, such as parking, pets and amenities. They must be consistent with the declaration.
Describes a right or restriction that stays attached to the property and binds or benefits later owners when the property is sold.
Senate Bill. Prefix for bills introduced in the Colorado Senate; the two digits after it are the session year and the last digits are the bill number (SB26-054 is Senate Bill 54 from 2026).
The market where existing loans are bought, sold and securitized by entities such as Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and Ginnie Mae.
In the rectangular survey system, a 1-mile-square area containing 640 acres. There are 36 in a township.
A tax-deferred like-kind exchange of investment or business real estate under Internal Revenue Code Section 1031.
An investment in which the buyer expects a profit from others' management efforts, such as a condo unit that must go into a rental pool. Selling one requires a securities license and registration.
Money a tenant pays to secure performance of a lease; in Colorado capped at two months' rent and returned within 30 days (up to 60 days by lease).
The document that pledges real property as collateral for a loan, such as a mortgage or a deed of trust. The promissory note is the debt; the security instrument secures it.
The deed covenant that the grantor owns the property and has the right to convey it.
A brokerage relationship in which the listing broker acts as the seller's agent, owing the seller the duties of a single agent (including loyalty) rather than acting as a neutral transaction-broker.
Seller financing in which the seller accepts the buyer's note for part of the price; debited to the seller and credited to the buyer.
A credit from the seller to the buyer at closing, typically toward closing costs or other costs the buyer's lender allows.

A Commission-approved form attached to the Foreclosure Protection Act contract that warns the seller the buyer is not assuming the seller's loans or liens, so the seller remains liable for them and any deficiency. The seller reads and signs it.
A single agent who represents only the seller (listing agent). In leasing, the landlord's agent plays the same role.
The Commission form a seller completes from current actual knowledge about the property's condition. It is not a warranty.
Under prior appropriation, a water right with an earlier appropriation date. Senior rights are filled first in a shortage, and juniors must stop diverting to satisfy them.
In community property states, property a spouse owned before marriage or received by gift or inheritance, which belongs to that spouse alone.
The minimum distance a building must be from a lot line, street, or other boundary under zoning rules.
A working spreadsheet used to compute closing figures, with debit and credit columns for the seller, the buyer and the broker's cash; Colorado courses teach a six-column version.
Ownership by a single person or legal entity.
Compensation for the loss in value of the remaining land when only part of a property is taken by eminent domain.

Special flood hazard area. Land on FEMA flood maps with a 1% annual chance of flooding (the 100-year floodplain), labeled Zones A and V. Flood insurance is required when such property is financed with a federally backed or regulated loan.
A deed given to the buyer at a court-ordered sale, such as a judicial foreclosure. It carries no warranties.
Sale where the lender agrees to accept less than the loan balance and release its lien.
The Short Sale Addendum deadline for written acceptance of the short sale by the seller's lienholders. If acceptance doesn't arrive by then, the contract terminates.

The Commission-approved addendum to the Contract to Buy and Sell used when the seller's lender must approve a sale for less than the payoff. Using it helps keep a short sale outside the CFPA's equity-purchaser rules.
Negotiating a listing directly with an owner who has an unexpired exclusive listing with another firm; prohibited.
A broker engaged by and representing only one party in a transaction: a seller's, buyer's, landlord's or tenant's agent.
A closing item between one party and an outside payee or source, entered in that party's column and the cash column.
Fair Housing Act exemption for a private owner of no more than three single-family homes who sells or rents without a broker and without discriminatory advertising; lost once a broker is used.
Colorado protected class covering lawful, verifiable income, including rental assistance and vouchers.
The Commission addendum in which the seller identifies the property's water source: a well (with permit number), a water provider, or another source.

Information on where the property's water comes from (a well, a water provider or another source). In the contract, the buyer acknowledges receiving it, plus well permit information if there's a well.

Seller's Property Disclosure. The Colorado Commission-approved form a seller completes from current actual knowledge about the property's condition. It isn't a warranty or a substitute for an inspection, and the broker shouldn't fill it out for the seller.
An agent authorized for one specific act or transaction, such as a listing broker.
A one-time association charge for a specific expense, such as a major repair, on top of regular dues.
FEMA-mapped area with a 1% annual chance of flooding (Zones A and V); flood insurance required with federally backed or federally regulated loans.
Local government unit, such as a metropolitan district, that can issue debt and levy property taxes for services or infrastructure.
A deed in which the grantor warrants title only against defects arising during the grantor's ownership.
A lien that attaches only to one particular property, such as a mortgage, mechanic's lien, or property tax lien.
A court order requiring a party to carry out the contract, for example to convey the property.
Rezoning a single parcel to benefit one owner in a way that conflicts with the comprehensive plan. It's often struck down as illegal.
The Commission form, completed by the listing licensee, stating how square footage was measured or sourced. It is for marketing only.
Social Security number. One of the six pieces of information that make up a loan application under TRID, which triggers the Loan Estimate deadline. It is also sensitive data brokers must protect.
A budget that averages expenses over several years to smooth out year-to-year spikes.
Title insurance that covers defects in the public records plus certain hidden risks like forgery, but excludes matters only a survey or inspection would reveal.
A statement from the owners' association showing the owner's account status and fees, requested by the seller before closing.
Law requiring certain contracts, including contracts to sell real estate, to be in writing and signed to be enforceable.
The deadline set by state law for filing a lawsuit; after it passes, the claim can't be enforced.
IRS status for a licensed real estate agent who is paid on results rather than hours and has a written agreement saying they won't be treated as an employee for tax purposes.
A right some states give to buy back the property after a foreclosure sale within a set period.
A 360-day year (twelve 30-day months) used for some prorations; daily rate = annual amount ÷ 360.
Directing buyers or renters toward or away from areas based on a protected class.
Property that buyers may avoid for psychological reasons, such as a death or crime there, rather than physical defects.
A negotiated settlement of a disciplinary case between the licensee and the Commission; it becomes a public record.

Short-term rental. A rental for a short stay, such as a vacation rental. In Colorado, deposits a broker collects from STR guests, even for the broker's own property, must go into a trust or escrow account.
A term loan with interest-only payments and the entire principal due at maturity.
Depreciation spread evenly over the asset's life: the same amount each year (cost of the improvement ÷ its life). Applies to buildings, never land.
Liability that applies without any showing of fault or negligence; CERCLA cleanup liability is strict.
A broker engaged to act for another broker on a principal's behalf. Colorado single agents and transaction-brokers may not create subagents.
Buying "subject to" an existing loan: the buyer takes title and makes the payments but is not personally liable for the debt; the seller stays liable.
A tenant's transfer of part of its leasehold interest; the original tenant remains liable and acts as the subtenant's landlord.
Under the listing contract, a person the broker negotiated with whose name was given to the seller in writing during the listing period.
An agreement by which a lien holder accepts a lower priority than another lien.
Completion of most of a contract's terms; the other party may still owe payment, minus damages for minor shortfalls.
Principle that a buyer won't pay more for a property than the cost of an equally desirable alternative.
Colorado's limited priority for an HOA's assessment lien over a first deed of trust, for up to six months of regular common-expense assessments.
A broker, such as a managing broker or team lead, to whom the employing broker has delegated supervisory duties in writing.
Appraisal principle: more supply relative to demand pushes prices down; less supply relative to demand pushes them up.
Ownership of the land's surface, which can be held and sold separately from the mineral rights below it.
A professional measurement of a property's boundaries and improvements, used to find encroachments and confirm boundaries, fences, and easements.
A group of investors pooling money for a real estate investment, usually organized as a partnership or LLC rather than a separate legal form.
Adding together the periods of possession of successive adverse possessors who are in privity to reach the required statutory time.
The permanent, long-term loan that pays off the construction lender when the project is finished.

Transaction-broker. A broker who helps one or more parties through a transaction without being an agent or advocate for any of them. In Colorado it is the presumed relationship unless there is a written agency agreement.

Telephone Consumer Protection Act. The federal law restricting autodialed, prerecorded and artificial-voice calls and texts. Robocalls and automated texts to cell phones generally need the recipient's prior express consent.
Real Property Transfer Declaration. The Colorado form filed with a deed so the county assessor learns the sale price and terms. It is confidential and isn't recorded with the deed.
Two or more brokers in the same brokerage firm who regularly work together; team names can't suggest a separate company.

A short-term license the Division director can issue so a brokerage firm can keep operating after its employing broker leaves. It lasts up to 90 days, with one extension of up to 90 days for good cause, while the firm finds a new employing broker.
Occupancy by a tenant who stays after the lease ends without the landlord's consent.
A leasehold of no fixed term that lasts as long as both parties wish.
A form of co-ownership for married couples, recognized in some states, with survivorship and protection from one spouse acting alone. Colorado does not recognize it.
Co-ownership with undivided interests that may be unequal, transferable without consent, and inheritable, with no right of survivorship.
Alterations made to leased space to suit a tenant's use, often funded partly by a landlord allowance.
Evaluating rental applicants (credit, income, rental history) using the same written criteria for everyone to avoid discrimination.
A person who makes a will.
A private nonprofit authorized by Congress under FIRREA that houses the boards setting appraisal standards (USPAP) and appraiser qualifications; it does not license appraisers.
Money or tangible non-monetary assets exchanged in a transaction; must be itemized in contracts and can't be paid as illegal referral kickbacks.
Compensation paid to the broker by someone other than the broker's client. Under the listing contract, the broker may not accept it without the seller's written consent.
A monthly check that the journal balance, the total of all ledgers, and the reconciled bank balance agree on the same date.
Tenant improvements. Changes made to leased commercial space to fit a tenant's use, such as walls, finishes and wiring. The landlord often pays part of the cost through a TI allowance.

Tenancy in common. Co-ownership with undivided interests that may be unequal, can be transferred without the other owners' consent and pass to heirs, with no right of survivorship. In Colorado, co-owners are presumed to be tenants in common unless the deed says otherwise.
Conditioning the sale of one product or service on the purchase of another.

Truth in Lending Act. The federal law, implemented by Regulation Z, requiring disclosure of credit costs, including the APR. It also regulates credit advertising: certain trigger terms in an ad require full disclosures.
A contract clause making deadlines strict. A late performance or notice is a breach or is ineffective.

An optional time in the Dates and Deadlines table that sets the cutoff for objection, resolution, examination and termination deadlines. If blank or N/A, those deadlines end at 11:59 p.m. Mountain Time.
Ownership or use of property divided by recurring time periods, either as a fee interest (timeshare estate) or a contractual right to use.
A timeshare that conveys a fee ownership interest in a property for a recurring period, such as the same week every year.
A timeshare that gives a contractual or lease-type right to use a property for a period, without real property ownership.
Ownership of real property, and the evidence of that ownership.
A title insurer's promise, issued before closing, to issue a policy once listed requirements are met, showing the exceptions the policy won't cover.
The part of the Americans with Disabilities Act covering public accommodations and commercial facilities, which must remove barriers where readily achievable.
A policy that protects an owner or lender against covered losses from title defects. It's paid for with a one-time premium.
The contract deadline for resolving a title objection in writing. If it isn't resolved by then, the contract terminates unless the buyer withdraws the objection in writing before the deadline.

glossary.term: Title, Survey and Due Diligence-Related Objection Notice
glossary.definition: The new name, in the Commission forms mandatory January 1, 2027, for the title objection notice. The buyer uses it to object in writing to title, survey and related due-diligence matters by the contract deadlines.
In the rectangular survey system, a square 6 miles on a side (36 square miles) divided into 36 sections.
An east–west line in the rectangular survey system drawn every 6 miles north and south of a base line. The rows between them are called township tiers.
Equipment a tenant installs for business use. It remains the tenant's personal property and must be removed by the end of the lease.
A business name other than the firm's legal name, filed with the Commission; a firm may use only one.
A licensee who assists one or both parties in a transaction without acting as an advocate for either; duties are set by state law.
The documents a broker must keep for each transaction, per the Commission's checklist, for four years.

A Colorado Real Estate Commission checklist of the documents that must be kept in sales and property management transaction files, such as contracts, listing agreements, brokerage disclosures, amendments, notices and closing statements. A firm may require more.
A broker who helps one or more parties through a transaction without being an agent or advocate for any of them. Colorado's presumed relationship absent a written agency agreement.

TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure. The CFPB rule, branded "Know Before You Owe," that combined the older federal mortgage disclosures into the Loan Estimate and the Closing Disclosure, with set delivery deadlines.
Specific credit terms in an advertisement (down payment, number of payments, payment amount, finance charge) that require full TILA disclosures.
A net lease where the tenant pays rent plus property taxes, insurance and maintenance.
An arrangement in which a trustor conveys property to a trustee, who holds legal title and manages it for a beneficiary.
A separate fiduciary account at a recognized depository that holds money belonging to others. Colorado rules call it a trust or escrow account.
The person or institution that holds legal title to property in a trust and manages it for the beneficiary.
A deed from a trustee conveying property held in a trust or sold at a deed-of-trust foreclosure. It generally carries only limited warranties.
The person who creates a trust by conveying property to a trustee. Also called the settlor or grantor.
Federal law, implemented by Regulation Z, requiring disclosure of credit costs including the APR.
A monthly check that the journal balance matches the reconciled bank balance; used for a broker's own non-brokerage trust account.
Head of the U.S. Department of Justice, who can sue under the Fair Housing Act when there's a pattern or practice of discrimination.

Uniform Commercial Code. A model set of state laws on commercial transactions such as sales of goods and security interests in personal property. A UCC search shows liens on personal property, such as a manufactured home or business equipment.

Uniform Electronic Transactions Act. A uniform state law, adopted by nearly every state including Colorado, that gives electronic records and signatures the same legal effect as paper ones when the parties agree to do business electronically.
Urea-formaldehyde foam insulation. An insulation used mainly in the 1970s that can release formaldehyde gas. Known UFFI is a material fact a broker should disclose.
Giving legal advice or drafting legal documents without a law license, such as advising on title exceptions or writing custom contract clauses.
A buried tank holding fuel or chemicals that can leak and contaminate soil and groundwater.
The lender's process of evaluating a borrower's capacity, credit, capital and collateral to decide whether to make a loan.
Representing both parties in a transaction without their knowledge and consent; illegal everywhere and grounds for license discipline and loss of the commission.
A co-owner's share in a whole property, with the right to use all of it, rather than ownership of any particular physical part.
Using a position of trust or control to obtain someone's agreement unfairly; makes a contract voidable.
A contract that seems valid but that a court will not enforce, such as an oral contract to sell real estate or a claim filed after the statute of limitations has run.
A contract in which one party promises something in exchange for an act; only that party is bound.
A mistake by only one party; it usually doesn't undo the contract unless the other party knew of it and took advantage.
An agent with broad authority to do anything the principal could legally delegate.

Unauthorized practice of law. Giving legal advice or drafting legal documents without a law license. Colorado brokers may fill in Commission-approved forms but may not draft custom legal language or advise on legal matters.
Insulation used in the 1970s that can release formaldehyde gas.
United States Department of Agriculture. The federal department whose Rural Development program guarantees and makes home loans in eligible rural areas, often with no down payment.
A loan backed by the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Rural Development program for eligible borrowers in eligible rural areas, often with no down payment.
For the home-sale exclusion, the seller must have lived in the home as a main home for at least two years during the five years before the sale.

Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice. The ethical and performance standards appraisers follow, written by The Appraisal Foundation's Appraisal Standards Board. Federally related transactions require appraisals that comply with USPAP.
aliases: Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice

glossary.definition: Underground storage tank. A buried tank holding fuel oil, gasoline or chemicals that can leak and contaminate soil and groundwater. A known or suspected UST is a material environmental issue for buyers and lenders.

U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. The federal department that guarantees part of home loans made to eligible veterans and service members. VA loans can allow no down payment and have no monthly mortgage insurance, but usually charge a funding fee.
A loan to an eligible veteran or service member that is partly guaranteed by the Department of Veterans Affairs.
A contract that has all the required elements and can be enforced by either party.
A general term for a lease whose rent can change over its term; graduated and index leases are examples.
Permission to depart from the strict requirements of a zoning ordinance because they would cause an unusual hardship.
Legal responsibility for someone else's acts. Colorado clients are not vicariously liable for broker acts they did not approve, direct or ratify.
Vehicle identification number. An identifying number that, with the serial number, describes a manufactured home on the contract's addendum and on its certificate of title.
An agreement with no legal effect, such as one for an illegal purpose.
A contract that is valid until the protected party chooses to cancel it, such as one signed by a minor.
The deed covenant that the grantor will defend the title against all lawful claims.
Implied promise in every Colorado residential lease that the unit is fit for human habitation; cannot be waived.
Damage, neglect, or misuse of property by a life tenant or tenant that lowers its value for the future owner.
A special district court that decides water-right matters in each of Colorado's seven water divisions, including approving new water rights, changes of water rights and augmentation plans.
A property right to divert and use a certain amount of water, which in Colorado can be conveyed separately from land.
Land saturated with water much of the time, protected under the Clean Water Act.
A written document directing how a person's property passes at death.
In real estate, the theft of closing funds by tricking a party into wiring money to a criminal's account, usually with fake wiring instructions.
Insurance covering on-the-job injuries to employees of the owner or manager.
A new loan that includes an existing loan, with the wrap lender continuing to pay the underlying loan.
Local laws dividing land into districts and regulating the uses, density, and building dimensions allowed in each.

references.title: The exam at a glance
references.body:
The Colorado broker exam is given by PSI in two portions. Each is scored separately, and you must pass both. Source: PSI's Colorado Real Estate Broker candidate information bulletin (updated 10/1/2023); check the current bulletin before you schedule.

| | National portion | State portion |
|---|---|---|
| Scored questions | 80 | 74 |
| Time | 120 minutes | 110 minutes |
| To pass | 60 correct (75%) | 53 correct (about 72%) |

- PSI may add 5 to 10 unscored "experimental" questions. They don't count toward your score but do use up exam time, and you can't tell which ones they are, so answer everything.
- You can pass the portions on different days and retake only the portion you failed. A passing score on either portion is accepted for no more than one year, and you must apply for your license within one year of passing the whole exam or retake both portions.
- No reference materials are allowed in the room, and personal calculators are on PSI's prohibited list. You get scratch paper.

## National portion: where the points are

| Area | Weight | About this many questions |
|---|---|---|
| Contracts | 19% | 15 |
| Agency | 13% | 10 |
| Practice of real estate (fair housing, antitrust, advertising, supervision) | 12% | 10 |
| Property ownership | 10% | 8 |
| Financing | 9% | 7 |
| Valuation | 8% | 6 |
| Property disclosures | 7% | 6 |
| Transfer of title | 6% | 5 |
| Real estate calculations | 6% | 5 |
| Land use controls | 5% | 4 |
| Property management | 5% | 4 |

## State portion: where the points are

| Area | Questions (of 74) |
|---|---|
| Colorado forms and contracts | 23 |
| Activities of licensees | 11 |
| Brokerage relationships | 11 |
| Closing and settlement | 10 |
| Additional topics: property management and landlord-tenant, water rights and wells, Colorado taxes, Colorado Fair Housing Act, foreclosure | 7 |
| Licensing requirements | 5 |
| Record keeping and trust accounts | 5 |
| Commission duties and powers | 2 |

> **Strategy:** Contracts are the largest area on both portions. Colorado forms alone are almost a third of the state exam, so know the residential Contract to Buy and Sell well: who does what, by which deadline, and what happens if they don't.

## How this course's practice exams work

Each timed practice exam draws 80 national and 74 state questions at random from the question bank and scores each portion against its own pass mark, like the real thing. Each portion has its own timer: 120 minutes national, 110 minutes state.

references.title: Math formulas
references.body:
## Core formulas

| To find | Formula |
|---|---|
| Commission | Sale price × commission rate |
| Seller's net | Sale price − commission − loan payoff − seller's other costs |
| Price needed to net a target | (Desired net + seller's costs) ÷ (1 − commission rate) |
| Loan amount | Price (or appraised value, if lower) × LTV |
| LTV | Loan ÷ value |
| Points | Loan amount × number of points × 1% |
| Annual interest (simple) | Principal × annual rate |
| Monthly interest | Principal × annual rate ÷ 12 |
| Equity | Market value − debts against the property |
| NOI | Gross potential income − vacancy and collection loss − operating expenses (not debt service) |
| Cap rate | NOI ÷ value |
| Value by income approach | NOI ÷ cap rate |
| Gross rent multiplier value | Monthly gross rent × GRM |
| Percent profit | (Sale price − cost) ÷ cost |
| Property tax | Assessed value × mill levy ÷ 1,000 |

## The "IRV" triangle

Income = Rate × Value. Cover the one you want: Value = Income ÷ Rate, Rate = Income ÷ Value. The same pattern works for commission (Commission = Rate × Price) and interest (Interest = Rate × Principal).

## Land

- 1 acre = 43,560 square feet
- 1 section = 1 square mile = 640 acres
- 1 township = 36 sections = 6 miles × 6 miles
- Rectangular survey shortcut: multiply 640 by each fraction in the description. For example, the NE ¼ of the SW ¼ is 640 × ¼ × ¼ = 40 acres.
- 1 mile = 5,280 feet; 1 square yard = 9 square feet

## Prorations

1. Find the amount per day (or per month).
2. Count the days the party is responsible for.
3. Multiply. Decide who gets the credit.

| Item | Typical direction |
|---|---|
| Colorado property taxes (paid in arrears) | The seller hasn't paid this year's taxes yet: **debit seller, credit buyer** for the seller's days |
| Rent the seller already collected for the month | **Debit seller, credit buyer** for the buyer's days |
| HOA dues the seller prepaid | **Credit seller, debit buyer** for the buyer's days |
| Security deposits held by the seller | **Debit seller, credit buyer** (the buyer takes over the obligation) |

- The Colorado residential contract prorates to the closing date. Unless the parties choose otherwise, taxes are based on the calendar year before closing, using the most recent mill levy and valuation.
- The exam question will tell you the day count convention (365-day year or 30-day "banker's" months) and who owns the closing day. Read for it.

## Colorado-specific numbers

- **Documentary fee:** one cent per $100 of consideration, with a major fraction counted as $100. No fee if the consideration is $500 or less. A $485,000 sale: 4,850 × $0.01 = $48.50.
- **Nonresident withholding:** the closing company withholds the lesser of 2% of the sale price or the net proceeds when a nonresident sells. Nothing is withheld if the price is $100,000 or less, and there are exemptions by affirmation.

references.title: Colorado numbers and deadlines
references.body:
Numbers and deadlines from Colorado statutes (C.R.S.) and Real Estate Commission rules. Forms and rules change; when in doubt, check the current Colorado Real Estate Manual.

## Licensing

| Item | Rule |
|---|---|
| Minimum age | 18 |
| Pre-license education | 168 hours: Law and Practice 48, Colorado Real Estate Contracts 48, Trust Accounts and Record-Keeping 8, Current Legal Issues 8, Closings 24, Practical Applications 32 |
| Background check | Fingerprints submitted to the CBI before applying |
| Exam score | Good for 1 year |
| First license expires | December 31 of the year it's issued; then 3-year calendar-year cycles |
| Continuing education | 24 hours per 3-year cycle, including a different 4-hour Annual Commission Update course each year (12 hours). No CE in the first partial period. |
| Missed Annual Commission Update | Can't be made up; you need one of the alternatives (such as the 24-hour Broker Reactivation course) |
| Late renewal (reinstatement) | Within 31 days: renewal fee. 31 days to 1 year: plus half the fee. 1 to 3 years: plus the full fee. Over 3 years: apply as a new licensee. |
| Independent broker | 2 years active as an associate broker first |
| Employing broker | 2 years active in the last 5, 50 experience points, plus 24-hour Brokerage Administration |
| Change of employer or business address | Notify the Division immediately; failure inactivates the license |
| Conviction, plea or discipline elsewhere | Written notice to the Commission within 30 calendar days |

## Errors and omissions insurance

| Item | Rule |
|---|---|
| Who needs it | Every active broker. Inactive brokers (and attorneys with malpractice coverage) are exempt. |
| Individual policy minimums | $100,000 per claim, $300,000 aggregate, deductible no more than $1,000 |
| If it lapses | License goes inactive immediately |

## The Commission

- 5 members appointed by the governor: 3 brokers with at least 5 years' Colorado experience (one with substantial property management experience) and 2 members of the public; 3-year terms.
- Fines up to $2,500 per separate offense; also censure, probation, suspension and revocation. A licensee who gets a letter of admonition has 20 days to request formal disciplinary proceedings, which vacates the letter.
- After revocation, no new application is considered for 1 year.
- Unlicensed brokerage activity is a class 2 misdemeanor.
- Colorado's real estate recovery fund was repealed in 2005.

## Money and records

| Item | Rule |
|---|---|
| Earnest money and other funds | Deposit within 3 business days after receipt or mutual execution, whichever is later |
| Property management funds | Deposit within 5 business days after receipt or mutual execution of the lease, whichever is later |
| Trust account | Insured depository in Colorado, labeled "trust" or "escrow" |
| Property management accounts | Rents and security deposits in separate accounts |
| Records | Keep 4 years from closing, or from listing expiration if it never closed |

## Landlord-tenant

| Item | Rule |
|---|---|
| Security deposit cap | Two months' rent |
| Deposit return | Within 30 days after the lease ends or the tenant surrenders, whichever is later; the lease can extend this to 60 days at most (rule in effect since Jan 1, 2026). Deductions need a written itemized statement. Wrongful retention can cost treble damages. |
| Habitability | Landlord responds within 24 hours of notice; remedial action within 24 hours for conditions that materially interfere with life, health or safety, 96 hours for other conditions |
| Demand for rent or compliance | 10 days' written notice for most residential tenancies; 5 days under an "exempt residential agreement" (landlord owns 5 or fewer single-family rentals and the lease says so); 3 days for nonresidential or employer-provided housing |

## Foreclosure and the Foreclosure Protection Act

| Item | Rule |
|---|---|
| Public trustee sale | 110–125 days after the notice of election and demand is recorded (215–230 for agricultural property) |
| Owner's cure | File intent to cure at least 15 calendar days before the sale; pay by noon the day before |
| Redemption after sale | Junior lienors only; the owner has no post-sale redemption right |
| Equity purchase cancellation | Until midnight of the third business day after signing, or noon the day before the sale, whichever is earlier |
| Foreclosure consultant | No fees until every promised service is fully performed |

## Other

| Item | Rule |
|---|---|
| Adverse possession | 18 years |
| Documentary fee | $0.01 per $100; none at $500 or less |
| Well change of ownership | Closing company files with the Division of Water Resources within 60 days after closing |
| Fair housing complaint (Colorado Civil Rights Division) | Within 1 year; private lawsuit within 2 years |
| Federal fair housing complaint (HUD) | Within 1 year; lawsuit within 2 years |

references.title: Brokerage relationships
references.body:
## Colorado's brokerage relationships

| Relationship | Represents | Created by |
|---|---|---|
| Seller's (landlord's) agent | The seller only, as an advocate | Written agreement |
| Buyer's (tenant's) agent | The buyer only, as an advocate | Written agreement |
| Transaction-broker | Nobody; assists one or both parties | **Presumed** unless there's a written single-agency agreement |
| Customer | Not a relationship: a party who hasn't engaged the broker | |
| Dual agent | **Not allowed in Colorado**, even with consent | |

## Disclosure timing

- A written disclosure of the relationship is required **before the broker elicits or discusses confidential information**. Small talk about price range, area and style of home isn't confidential.
- Single agency needs a written agreement **before** the broker acts as that agent.
- The Commission's Definitions of Working Relationships form is a separate rule: it's required when a party asks about a relationship the firm doesn't offer.
- **Change of status** (for example, a buyer's agent who will now work with their own seller-client on the same deal): written disclosure no later than when the party signs the contract.

## Designated brokerage

The employing broker can designate, in writing, specific brokers to work with a party. The relationship is with those brokers only, not the whole firm, so two designated brokers in one firm can represent opposite sides without either being a dual agent.

## Duties side by side

| Duty | Single agent | Transaction-broker |
|---|---|---|
| Reasonable skill and care | Yes | Yes |
| Present offers and counteroffers in a timely way | Yes | Yes |
| Account for money and property | Yes | Yes |
| Counsel the party on material benefits and risks of the transaction | Yes | No |
| Keep the parties fully informed about the transaction | Not a separately listed duty | Yes |
| Disclose adverse material facts actually known | Yes | Yes |
| Advocate for the party, promote their interests | **Yes** | No |
| Negotiate for the best terms for one side | **Yes** | No |
| Keep confidential a party's motivation and willingness to take less or pay more | Yes, unless the client gives informed consent | Yes, unless **all** parties give informed consent |
| Independently inspect or verify | Not required | Not required |
| Duties that survive after the relationship ends | Accounting for money and property, and confidentiality | Accounting for money and property only |

> **Exam tip:** A seller's agent need not disclose to a buyer that the property was the site of a homicide, felony or suicide, or that an occupant had HIV/AIDS. Colorado law says these aren't material facts (C.R.S. 38-35.5-101).

## Compensation

- Commissions aren't set by law and are fully negotiable.
- Payment alone doesn't create an agency relationship. Compensation can come from either party, a third party, or be split.
- Parties must be told about compensation arrangements before signing the brokerage agreement or the contract.
- A buyer's agent needs the buyer's written approval before asking to be paid from the seller's side.

references.title: Colorado forms map
references.body:
## Which form?

Brokers must use the Commission-approved form whenever one exists for the situation. They may fill in blanks and add simple factual provisions, but may not draft legal language. A brokerage may use an attorney-drafted form only when no appropriate Commission form exists; it must name the attorney and the firm and say it isn't Commission-approved. A party's own attorney may also draft documents for that party.

| Situation | Form |
|---|---|
| Residential property | Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Residential) |
| Residential income property | Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Income-Residential) |
| Commercial | Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Commercial) |
| Vacant land | Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Land) |
| Manufactured home on a leased lot | Manufactured Home (Lot Lease Only) contract |
| Residence in foreclosure (Foreclosure Protection Act) | The CFPA version of the residential contract. If there's a leaseback, repurchase option or loan assumption, an attorney must draft the contract. |
| Responding to an offer with changes | Counterproposal |
| Changing deadlines or terms after acceptance | Agreement to Amend/Extend Contract |
| Releasing earnest money | Earnest Money Release |
| Reviving a contract that terminated | Agreement to Revive Contract |
| Extending or ending a pending contract | Extension or Termination of Contract |
| Listing a property | Exclusive Right-to-Sell Listing Contract |
| Representing a buyer | Exclusive Right to Buy Listing Contract |
| Selling a short sale | Short Sale Addendum (one version for the listing contract, one for the purchase contract) |

## Disclosures that travel with the contract

- Seller's Property Disclosure (the seller's duty to disclose continues if new adverse facts come up)
- Lead-Based Paint Disclosure for housing built before 1978
- Square Footage Disclosure
- Source of Water Addendum
- Brokerage relationship disclosures

## How the residential contract works

- **Dates and deadlines** sit in one table at the front. Most contingencies are tied to a named deadline.
- **Time is of the essence.** Missing a deadline usually means losing the right tied to it.
- **Inspection:** the buyer either terminates by the Inspection Termination Deadline or sends an Inspection Objection by the Inspection Objection Deadline. Sending an objection gives up the right to terminate under the termination deadline; if the objection isn't resolved by the Inspection Resolution Deadline, the contract terminates unless the buyer withdraws the objection. If the buyer does nothing in time, they've accepted the condition.
- **Earnest money release:** when one party is entitled to the earnest money, the other party has 3 days after receiving the Earnest Money Release to sign it.
- **Notices** to a party's broker count as notice to the party, with exceptions; electronic delivery is allowed.
- **Default (buyer):** liquidated damages apply by default: the seller cancels and keeps the earnest money as the sole remedy. If the specific-performance box is checked instead, the seller may sue for specific performance, or cancel, keep the earnest money and also recover damages.
- **Disputes:** mediation is required before arbitration or a lawsuit, with exceptions in the contract.

> **Current forms:** The Commission revises its forms periodically. A set of revised forms becomes mandatory January 1, 2027. Always use the current version.

references.title: Federal laws and fair housing
references.body:
## Fair housing

| | Federal (Fair Housing Act) | Colorado adds |
|---|---|---|
| Protected classes | Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability | Creed, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, marital status, ancestry, veteran or military status, source of income |
| File a complaint | HUD, within 1 year | Colorado Civil Rights Division, within 1 year |
| Lawsuit | Within 2 years | Within 2 years |

- **Federal exemptions:** a single-family home sold or rented by an owner without a broker or discriminatory ads; owner-occupied buildings with up to 4 units; religious organizations and private clubs (limited); qualifying housing for older persons (55+ or 62+). Hiring a broker ends the single-family exemption.
- The Civil Rights Act of 1866 bans all racial discrimination in property, with **no exemptions**.
- **Prohibited:** steering, blockbusting, redlining, discriminatory advertising, refusing reasonable accommodations (rules) or modifications (physical changes, usually at the tenant's cost).

## Lending laws

| Law | What to know |
|---|---|
| RESPA | No kickbacks or referral fees for settlement services. Commission splits between brokers are allowed. Affiliated business arrangements need disclosure. |
| TILA / Regulation Z | Trigger terms in ads (down payment amount, number of payments, payment amount, finance charge) require full disclosure: down payment, terms of repayment, and APR. |
| TRID | Loan Estimate by the 3rd business day after application. Closing Disclosure received at least 3 business days before closing. A new 3-day wait if the APR becomes inaccurate, the loan product changes, or a prepayment penalty is added. |
| ECOA | No credit discrimination by race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, receipt of public assistance, or exercising consumer credit rights |

## Disclosures and environment

| Item | Rule |
|---|---|
| Lead-based paint | Housing built before 1978. Give the EPA pamphlet and known information, allow a 10-day inspection opportunity (can be changed or waived in writing), keep records 3 years. |
| Radon | EPA action level is 4 pCi/L |
| Flood | Special flood hazard areas (A and V zones) have a 1% annual chance of flooding; flood insurance is required with federally backed loans in those zones |

## Marketing and business practice

| Rule | What to know |
|---|---|
| Do-Not-Call | Check the registry every 31 days; call only 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. (called party's local time); established business relationship lasts 18 months after a transaction or 3 months after an inquiry; honor a person's do-not-call request within 10 business days, for 5 years |
| CAN-SPAM | Identify the email as an ad; honor opt-outs within 10 business days (opt-out must work for 30 days after sending); include a valid physical postal address |
| Antitrust | Never agree on (or even discuss) commission rates with competing firms (price fixing); no group boycotts, market allocation or tie-ins. Each firm sets its own rates, negotiated with each client |

references.title: Ownership, estates and deeds
references.body:
## Forms of co-ownership

| | Tenancy in common | Joint tenancy |
|---|---|---|
| Shares | Can be unequal | Equal |
| On death | Share passes by will or inheritance | Passes to surviving joint tenants (right of survivorship) |
| Unities required | Possession only | Possession, interest, time, title |
| In Colorado | **Presumed** when a deed to two or more natural persons says nothing | Must be expressly stated (for example, "as joint tenants" or "JTWROS"); only natural persons can be joint tenants, except co-fiduciaries such as co-trustees, who are presumed joint tenants |

- Colorado doesn't recognize tenancy by the entirety. A deed that attempts one creates a joint tenancy instead.
- Colorado isn't a community property state.

## Estates

| Estate | Key point |
|---|---|
| Fee simple absolute | The most complete ownership |
| Fee simple defeasible | Can be lost if a condition is broken |
| Life estate | Lasts for a life; then goes to the remainderman or reverts |
| Estate for years | Lease with a definite end date |
| Periodic tenancy | Renews automatically (month to month) |
| Tenancy at will | No fixed term; ends by notice |
| Tenancy at sufferance | Tenant stays without permission after the lease ends |

## Deeds (most to least protection for the buyer)

| Deed | Warranties |
|---|---|
| General warranty | Covers title against defects from any time |
| Special warranty | Covers only defects arising while the grantor owned it |
| Bargain and sale | Implies the grantor has title, with no warranties against defects |
| Quitclaim | No warranties; conveys whatever interest the grantor has, if any |

## Recording

Colorado's recording statute is a **race-notice** statute: a later buyer who records first and didn't know about the earlier unrecorded deed wins.

## Land use

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Police power | Government's power to regulate for health, safety and welfare (zoning, codes) |
| Eminent domain | Taking private property for public use, with just compensation |
| Escheat | Property passes to the state when there's no will and no heirs |
| Variance | Permission to deviate from zoning |
| Nonconforming use | A use allowed to continue after zoning changes |

drills.title: Total commission
drills.prompt: A home sells for {price:money0}. The listing contract sets a total commission of {rate}% of the sale price. What is the total commission?
drills.solution: Commission = price × rate = {price:money0} × {rate}% = **{comm:money}**.

drills.title: Commission split to the broker
drills.prompt: A home sells for {price:money0} with a {rate}% total commission. The listing firm keeps {listShare}% of the commission and pays the rest to the buyer's firm. The listing broker's agreement with her employing broker gives her {brokerShare}% of what her firm receives. How much does the listing broker earn?
drills.solution:
1. Total commission: {price:money0} × {rate}% = {total:money}.
2. Listing firm's share: {total:money} × {listShare}% = {firm:money}.
3. Broker's share: {firm:money} × {brokerShare}% = **{mine:money}**.

drills.title: Seller's net proceeds
drills.prompt: A seller accepts {price:money0}. She owes {payoff:money0} on her loan, will pay a {rate}% commission, and has {costs:money0} in other closing costs. What are her net proceeds?
drills.solution:
Commission: {price:money0} × {rate}% = {comm:money}.
Net = {price:money0} − {comm:money} − {payoff:money0} − {costs:money0} = **{net:money}**.

drills.title: Price needed to net a target
drills.prompt: A seller wants to walk away with {target:money0} after paying {costs:money0} in closing costs and a {rate}% commission on the sale price. What's the lowest sale price that does it? Round to the nearest dollar.
drills.solution:
The commission comes out of the sale price, so the seller keeps {keep}% of it.
Price = (net + costs) ÷ (1 − commission rate) = {sum:money0} ÷ {keep}% = **{price:money0}**.

A common mistake is adding {rate}% to the net, which comes up short.

drills.title: Loan amount from LTV
drills.prompt: A buyer contracts to pay {price:money0}. The home appraises at {appraised:money0}. The lender will lend {ltv}% of the price or the appraised value, whichever is lower. What is the maximum loan?
drills.solution:
Lenders use the lower of price and appraised value: {basis:money0}.
Loan = {basis:money0} × {ltv}% = **{loan:money}**.

drills.title: Discount points
drills.prompt: A buyer pays {price:money0} with {down}% down and pays {points} discount points on the loan. How much do the points cost?
drills.solution:
Points are charged on the **loan**, not the price.
Loan = {price:money0} × (100% − {down}%) = {loan:money}.
Points = {loan:money} × {points}% = **{cost:money}**.

drills.title: First month's interest
drills.prompt: A {loan:money0} loan carries {rate}% annual interest. How much interest is due for the first month?
drills.solution: Annual interest = {loan:money0} × {rate}%. Divide by 12 for one month: **{interest:money}**.

drills.title: Principal paid in the first payment
drills.prompt: A borrower's monthly principal and interest payment on a 30-year {loan:money0} loan at {rate}% is {pmt:money}. How much of the first payment goes to principal?
drills.solution:
First month's interest = {loan:money0} × {rate}% ÷ 12 = {interest:money}.
Principal = payment − interest = {pmt:money} − {interest:money} = **{principal:money}**.

drills.title: Square feet to acres
drills.prompt: A rectangular parcel measures {w} feet by {d} feet. How many acres is it? Round to two decimal places.
drills.solution:
Area = {w} × {d} = {sqft:int} sq ft.
Acres = {sqft:int} ÷ 43,560 = **{acres:num2}** acres.

drills.title: Rectangular survey acreage
drills.prompt: How many acres are in the {a} of the {b} of the {c} of Section {sec}?
drills.solution:
A section is 640 acres. Divide by each fraction's denominator: 640 ÷ {dc:int} ÷ {db:int} ÷ {da:int} = **{acres:num2} acres**.
The order doesn't matter for the math; only the denominators do.

drills.title: Value by cap rate
drills.prompt: A {units}-unit building rents each unit for {rent:money0} a month. Expect {vac}% vacancy and collection loss and {opex:money0} a year in operating expenses. Comparable sales indicate a {cap}% cap rate. What is the indicated value? Round to the nearest dollar.
drills.solution:
1. Potential gross income: {units} × {rent:money0} × 12 = {pgi:money0}.
2. Effective gross income: {pgi:money0} × (100% − {vac}%) = {egi:money0}.
3. NOI: {egi:money0} − {opex:money0} = {noi:money0}. (Mortgage payments are not operating expenses.)
4. Value = NOI ÷ cap rate = {noi:money0} ÷ {cap}% = **{value:money0}**.

drills.title: Find the cap rate
drills.prompt: An investor pays {price:money0} for a property with net operating income of {noi:money0}. What is the cap rate? Answer as a percentage rounded to two decimal places.
drills.solution: Cap rate = NOI ÷ price = {noi:money0} ÷ {price:money0} = **{cap}%**.

drills.title: Gross rent multiplier
drills.prompt: Similar rental homes in the neighborhood sell for about {grm} times their monthly rent. What is the indicated value of a home renting for {rent:money0} a month?
drills.solution: Value = monthly rent × GRM = {rent:money0} × {grm} = **{value:money0}**.

drills.title: Property tax from a mill levy
drills.prompt: A home's assessed value is {assessed:money0} and the total mill levy is {mills} mills. What is the annual property tax?
drills.solution:
One mill = $1 per $1,000 of assessed value (0.001).
Tax = {assessed:money0} × {mills} ÷ 1,000 = **{tax:money}**.

drills.title: Colorado documentary fee
drills.prompt: What is the Colorado documentary fee on a {price:money0} sale?
drills.solution:
The fee is one cent per $100 of consideration (C.R.S. 39-13-102).
{price:money0} ÷ $100 = {units:int} units × $0.01 = **{fee:money}**. Shortcut: move the decimal point four places left.

drills.title: Colorado tax proration at closing
drills.prompt: A Colorado sale closes on {m:month} {d} (not a leap year). Last year's taxes were {tax:money0}, and the contract prorates on that basis using a 365-day year. The buyer owns the day of closing. Colorado taxes are paid in arrears, so the seller hasn't paid any of this year's taxes. How much will the seller be debited (and the buyer credited)?
drills.solution:
The seller owns January 1 through the day before closing: {days} days.
Daily tax = {tax:money0} ÷ 365 = {daily:num4}.
Seller's share = {tax:money0} × {days} ÷ 365 = **{share:money}**, debited to the seller and credited to the buyer, who will pay the whole year's bill next year.

drills.title: Rent proration at closing
drills.prompt: A seller collected {rent:money0} rent for the month in which the sale of a rental home closes, on day {d}. Use a 30-day month; the buyer owns the day of closing. What credit does the buyer receive for rent?
drills.solution:
The buyer owns days {d} through 30: {buyerDays} days.
Daily rent = {rent:money0} ÷ 30.
Buyer's credit = {rent:money0} ÷ 30 × {buyerDays} = **{credit:money}** (debit seller, credit buyer). Security deposits transfer separately, also as a debit to the seller and credit to the buyer.

drills.title: Colorado nonresident withholding
drills.prompt: A nonresident seller with no exemption sells Colorado property for {price:money0}. Net proceeds to the seller will be {net:money0}. How much must the closing company withhold for Colorado?
drills.solution:
Colorado withholding is the **lesser** of 2% of the sale price or the net proceeds (C.R.S. 39-22-604.5).
2% of {price:money0} = {twoPct:money}; net = {net:money0}. The lesser is **{withheld:money}**.

drills.title: Percent profit on a sale
drills.prompt: An investor bought a property for {cost:money0} and sold it for {sale:money0}. What percent profit did she make on her purchase price?
drills.solution: Profit = {sale:money0} − {cost:money0}. Divide by what she **paid**, not the sale price: ({sale:money0} − {cost:money0}) ÷ {cost:money0} = **{pct}%**.

drills.title: Owner's equity
drills.prompt: A home's market value is {value:money0}. The owner owes {first:money0} on the first mortgage and {heloc:money0} on a home equity line. What is the owner's equity?
drills.solution: Equity = market value − all debts secured by the property = {value:money0} − {first:money0} − {heloc:money0} = **{equity:money0}**.

drills.title: Maximum Colorado security deposit
drills.prompt: A Colorado residential lease sets rent at {rent:money0} a month. What is the largest security deposit the landlord may charge?
drills.solution: Colorado caps residential security deposits at two months' rent (C.R.S. 38-12-102.5): {rent:money0} × 2 = **{max:money0}**.

drills.title: Property management fee
drills.prompt: A property manager earns {fee}% of rents actually collected. The building has {units} units renting at {rent:money0}, and {occ}% of the rent was collected this month. What is the manager's fee for the month?
drills.solution:
Collected = {units} × {rent:money0} × {occ}% = {collected:money}.
Fee = {collected:money} × {fee}% = **{pay:money}**.

drills.title: Buyer's cash to close with a new loan
drills.prompt: A Colorado buyer pays {price:money0} with {down}% down and a new loan for the rest. The buyer has deposited {em:money0} earnest money, will pay {costs:money0} in loan and closing costs, and, as agreed in the contract, pays the state documentary fee. The buyer is credited {taxcr:money0} for the seller's share of unpaid current-year taxes. How much cash must the buyer bring to closing?
drills.solution:
Loan = {price:money0} × {pct}% = {loan:money}.
Documentary fee = {price:money0} ÷ 100 × $0.01 = {doc:money}.
Buyer debits: price + costs + doc fee = {debits:money}.
Buyer credits: earnest money + loan + tax credit = {credits:money}.
Cash due from buyer = {debits:money} − {credits:money} = **{cash:money}**.

drills.title: Seller's net with payoff, fee and tax proration
drills.prompt: A Colorado sale for {price:money0} closes on {m:month} {d} (not a leap year). The seller owes {payoff:money0} on her loan, pays a {rate}% brokerage fee and the {title:money0} owner's title premium, and is charged her share of this year's unpaid taxes, prorated on last year's {tax:money0} bill with a 365-day year. The buyer owns the day of closing. What is the balance due to the seller?
drills.solution:
Brokerage fee = {price:money0} × {rate}% = {comm:money}.
Taxes: the seller owns January 1 through the day before closing = {days} days. {tax:money0} ÷ 365 = {daily:money} a day × {days} = {share:money} (debit seller; Colorado taxes are paid in arrears).
Seller debits = {payoff:money0} + {comm:money} + {title:money0} + {share:money} = {debits:money}.
Balance due to seller = {price:money0} − {debits:money} = **{net:money}**.

drills.title: Buyer's cash with a loan assumption
drills.prompt: A buyer pays {price:money0} by assuming the seller's loan, which has a {bal:money0} balance at {rate}% interest paid in arrears; the seller made the payment due on the 1st. Closing is on day {d} of the month (use a 30-day month; the buyer owns the closing day). The buyer deposited {em:money0} earnest money, reimburses the seller for the {resv:money0} lender escrow reserve, and pays a {fee:money0} assumption fee. Ignoring taxes and other costs, how much cash must the buyer bring?
drills.solution:
Interest: {bal:money0} × {rate}% ÷ 12 = {monthly:money} a month. The seller owns days 1–{days}, so accrued interest = {monthly:money} ÷ 30 × {days} = {interest:money} (debit seller, credit buyer — the buyer's next payment covers it).
Buyer debits: price + reserve + fee = {debits:money}.
Buyer credits: earnest money + assumed balance + interest = {credits:money}.
Cash due = **{cash:money}**.
